userFlow.persona: Renée Okafor — Senior NOC Engineer on-call during a tentpole live streaming event
userFlow.goal: Detect, diagnose, and resolve a streaming latency spike before it becomes viewer-facing, and capture the incident record automatically
userFlow.entryPoint: Renée is watching the Data Mesh unified topology view on the NOC video wall as concurrency ramps into the millions.
userFlow.exitPoint: The fault is resolved before rebuffering spreads, blast radius is confirmed contained, and a complete incident timeline is saved to the review workspace — all from one surface.

steps.label: Data Mesh flags a latency anomaly on one streaming path
steps.description: The topology view highlights a single packaging→CDN edge where segment latency is drifting above its learned baseline, before error rates or rebuffering have climbed.
steps.systemState: One high-signal anomaly card appears at the top of the incident feed with the affected topology node lit; no alert storm.

branches.condition: If the drift stays within baseline variance
branches.outcome: The card auto-resolves and is logged quietly without paging anyone

branches.condition: If drift crosses the impact threshold
branches.outcome: Data Mesh escalates and pre-fills an incident with the affected node and blast radius

steps.friction: Engineer may hesitate to trust a pre-emptive flag before symptoms are visible
steps.errorPath: If baseline data is thin for this path, the card is labeled low-confidence rather than suppressed or over-escalated

steps.label: Renée opens the anomaly and reads the correlated context
steps.description: She clicks the anomaly; Data Mesh shows the upstream transcode profile, the packager, and the CDN edge as one traced path, with latency, throughput, and error trends aligned on a single clock.
steps.systemState: Incident workspace opens with correlated metrics, the topology trace highlighted, and a probable root-cause candidate suggested.

branches.outcome: Root-cause candidate is shown with confidence and the upstream stage highlighted
Data Mesh ranks candidates and lets her pivot the trace stage by stage

steps.friction: Too much detail at once could slow triage in a high-pressure moment
steps.errorPath: If a stage lacks telemetry, the trace marks the gap explicitly instead of implying the fault is elsewhere

steps.label: Decide: fix upstream now, or watch for confirmation?
steps.description: Renée weighs the confidence of the root-cause candidate and the impact severity against acting before the fault is fully viewer-facing.
steps.systemState: Data Mesh displays impact-ranked severity — affected channels, regions, and projected viewers — next to the candidate.

branches.condition: If severity is high and confidence is high
branches.outcome: She moves immediately to coordinate the upstream fix
She pins the anomaly to watch a 60-second confirmation window while prepping the fix

steps.friction: Acting too early risks a needless change; acting too late risks viewers seeing it
steps.errorPath: If severity data is incomplete, Data Mesh defaults to the more cautious high-impact assumption and says so

steps.label: Coordinate the fix and confirm blast radius contained
steps.description: From the incident, she pages the packaging team with the pre-filled context and watches the traced path recover as the bad transcode profile is rolled back.
steps.systemState: Latency and error trends fall back toward baseline; the topology node returns to green; blast radius shows contained to two regions.

branches.outcome: Data Mesh marks the incident resolved and freezes the timeline
Severity auto-escalates and adjacent affected nodes are added to the same incident

steps.friction: Hand-off context must be complete enough that the packaging team acts without re-investigating
steps.errorPath: If recovery stalls, Data Mesh keeps the incident open and prompts an escalation path rather than closing prematurely

steps.label: Data Mesh saves the authoritative incident timeline
steps.description: As the incident closes, the platform has already assembled a clock-aligned record — detection time, correlated trace, actions taken, blast radius, and recovery — ready for the morning review.
steps.systemState: Incident record is stored with MTTD/MTTR computed automatically and exportable to the review workspace.

branches.condition: If review flags a recurring pattern
branches.outcome: The pattern is added to baselines to sharpen future detection
It is tagged for a follow-up runbook so the next occurrence is caught faster

steps.friction: Auto-generated records must be trusted as authoritative, not second-guessed against old screenshots
steps.errorPath: If a data source was briefly unavailable during the incident, the timeline marks the gap rather than silently omitting it

experienceMap.overview: End-to-end operational experience of a NOC engineer (Renée) and the ops manager she reports to (Daniel), from the fragmented status quo through onboarding Data Mesh to detecting, resolving, and learning from a live-event incident. Every phase turns on the same shift: from stitching a dozen tools by hand to reading one supply-chain-aware nervous system.

phases.name: Status Quo — The Wall of Tabs
phases.channel: NOC video wall · vendor dashboards · Grafana · Slack/PagerDuty
phases.experience: Engineers monitor linear, cable, and streaming through a dozen disconnected tools, holding "normal" in their heads. Detection depends on human attention split across screens; managers get status by asking.
phases.emotion: Stretched and reactive (engineer) / anxious about blind spots (manager)
insights: The signal is almost always present in hindsight — the gap is unified, in-time visibility, not data

phases.name: Onboarding — One Path, Read-Only
phases.channel: Data Mesh web app · existing telemetry feeds
phases.experience: A single distribution path is piped into Data Mesh read-only and run beside the old tools. Renée sees latency, throughput, and errors for that path in one place with a learned baseline, and starts glancing at it first.
insights: Read-only side-by-side is the trust on-ramp: adoption is earned by catching one real thing earlier

phases.name: Detection — The Anomaly Before the Storm
phases.experience: During a live event, Data Mesh flags a latency drift on one edge before rebuffering spreads. Instead of an alert storm, Renée sees one high-signal card pointing at the topology node that matters.
insights: Detecting the cause before the symptoms is the entire value — minutes here are viewer-facing minutes saved

phases.name: Diagnosis & Resolution — Trace, Rank, Fix
phases.experience: She opens the incident, follows the traced path upstream to a bad transcode profile, sees blast radius and impact severity, and coordinates the fix from one surface as metrics recover.
insights: Correlation plus impact severity turns a chaotic war-room into a ranked, guided response

phases.name: Learning — The Review That Writes Itself
phases.experience: The next morning the incident record already exists — clock-aligned, with detection and resolution times computed. Daniel reviews it in minutes; the pattern feeds back into detection so it is caught faster next time.
phases.emotion: Relieved and in control (engineer) / confident and informed (manager)
insights: When the record writes itself, the org actually learns — each incident sharpens the next detection

storyboard.scenario: It is the fourth quarter of a marquee Sunday Night Football stream with millions of concurrent viewers. A bad transcode profile is about to ripple downstream into rebuffering — the kind of failure that trends on social media within minutes. Renée is on-call in the NOC, and this is the first tentpole event where Data Mesh is her primary detection surface.
storyboard.persona: Renée Okafor (Senior NOC Engineer) & Daniel Cho (NOC Operations Manager)

frames.description: The NOC video wall glows with the Data Mesh unified topology — linear, cable, and streaming as one connected graph, all green, as concurrency climbs into the millions during the live game.
frames.dialogue: 'Everything's green — but this is exactly when it bites you.'

frames.description: One node on the streaming path pulses amber. A single anomaly card rises to the top of the incident feed: segment latency drifting above baseline on a packaging→CDN edge — before any rebuffering appears.
frames.dialogue: 'Latency's drifting on one edge. No errors yet. Data Mesh caught it early.'

frames.description: Renée opens the incident. The workspace traces the path upstream — transcode profile to packager to CDN — with latency, throughput, and errors aligned on one clock and a probable root-cause candidate flagged.
frames.dialogue: 'It's pointing straight at the new transcode profile. Two regions in the blast radius.'

frames.description: Daniel leans over her shoulder as the severity panel ranks the incident by projected viewers affected. In the old world this would already be a war-room; now it is one screen and one clear next action.
frames.dialogue: 'High impact, high confidence. Page packaging — roll it back now.'

frames.description: The bad profile is rolled back. On the wall the amber node fades back to green; latency and error trends fall to baseline. Viewers never saw a spinner. The game plays on uninterrupted.
frames.dialogue: 'Recovered. Blast radius held to two regions. Nobody at home noticed a thing.'

frames.description: The next morning, Daniel opens the incident review. The timeline already exists — detection time, trace, actions, recovery, MTTD and MTTR computed — no screenshots, no reconciling clocks.
frames.dialogue: 'Detected before symptoms, resolved in four minutes, and the review wrote itself. This is the difference.'

projects.name: Abode — Transparency-First Real Estate Platform

hypothesis.problem: A brokerage's online presence today is a patchwork nobody built for real estate: a generic IDX website template, a separate CRM, spreadsheets for inventory, a bolt-on 3D-tour vendor, and disconnected lead forms — none of which talk to each other. Standing it up takes weeks of vendor wrangling and a monthly stack that runs $800–$2,500 with no single source of truth. On the other side of the same transaction, the homebuyer is making the largest purchase of their life on remarkably thin information: staged photos that hide the real space, vague listing copy, no honest sense of dimensions or flaws, buried disclosures, and an agent whose incentives they quietly distrust. The result is expensive, low-converting tooling for the agency and buyer's remorse for the consumer. No platform lets an agency launch a real-estate-native, transparency-first storefront in an afternoon while giving buyers 3D walkthroughs, an AI agent that answers honestly, and full visibility into every data point on a listing.

segments.name: Independent & boutique brokerages (5–50 agents)
segments.description: Owner-operators of independent and boutique brokerages, roughly 5–50 agents, competing against national franchises and the portals without their budgets, engineering teams, or in-house tooling.
segments.painPoint: Their online presence is a patchwork nobody built for real estate — a generic IDX template, a separate CRM, inventory spreadsheets, a bolt-on 3D vendor, and disconnected lead forms — that takes weeks to stand up, runs $800–$2,500 a month with no single source of truth, and still loses their own buyers back to Zillow.
segments.resolution: A same-afternoon, MLS-connected transparency storefront with inventory ops, per-listing buyer-intent analytics, an AI lead-qualification agent, and a lightweight CRM in one system — replacing the entire stack at lower cost and handing the brokerage back ownership of its own audience.

segments.name: Top-producing individual agents
segments.description: High-performing individual agents who live by conversion and referrals, investing in a personal brand independent of their brokerage while juggling inbound leads, follow-ups, and showings.
segments.painPoint: Leads arrive across disconnected forms and portals with no behavioral context, so agents burn hours chasing cold contacts while warm buyers slip away; staged listings pull low-intent inquiries, and they have no branded, transparent presence to stand out from every other agent on Zillow.
segments.resolution: A personal, transparency-first storefront plus per-listing intent analytics (who viewed, how long, which rooms, where they dropped off) and an AI agent that qualifies inbound leads and surfaces exactly who is ready to transact — so agents spend time on buyers about to move and earn the referral by volunteering the truth.

segments.name: New-development sales teams (pre-construction / off-plan)
segments.description: In-house and outsourced sales teams marketing pre-construction and off-plan developments — selling units that buyers often cannot walk because they have not been built yet.
segments.painPoint: Selling the unbuilt means leaning on renderings and sales-center visits: buyers can not gauge true space, sightlines, or finishes; disclosures and pricing across a release are hard to present transparently; and demand across dozens of units is invisible until someone calls.
segments.resolution: Photorealistic 3D walkthroughs of model units and floor-plan types, transparent release-wide pricing and disclosure panels, and per-unit buyer-intent analytics that show which layouts and price points are pulling demand — so teams market off-plan inventory with in-person-grade confidence and prioritize the hottest units.

segments.name: Remote & relocating homebuyers
segments.description: Job movers, military families, and international and out-of-state buyers who must evaluate — and often commit to — homes they cannot physically visit.
segments.painPoint: They can not walk the house or gauge true space and condition from staged photos, so they are forced to trust a remote agent’s word or fly in repeatedly — making the highest-stakes purchase of their life essentially blind, with the most to lose from buyer’s remorse.
segments.resolution: Photorealistic in-browser 3D walkthroughs paired with natural-language search and an honest AI buyer’s agent that answers every question from disclosed data — letting them tour, vet, and shortlist properties remotely with the same confidence as an in-person visit.

hypothesis.solution: 1. Abode is Shopify for real estate agencies. A brokerage signs up, picks a theme, connects its MLS/IDX feed, and has a listing-first storefront live the same afternoon — no developer required. The B2B layer runs the business inventory management, per-listing buyer-intent analytics (who viewed, how long, which rooms, drop-off points), an AI lead-generation and qualification agent, and a lightweight CRM. The B2C layer wins the buyer: photorealistic 3D models, in-browser interior walkthroughs, and an AI buyer's agent that finds homes by natural-language criteria and answers questions honestly from every disclosed data point. The same agent infrastructure is harnessed on both sides — qualifying leads for the broker and guiding buyers for the consumer. The organizing principle across all of it is radical transparency: surface days-on-market, full price history, disclosures, true dimensions, and neighborhood data by default so buyers choose with zero remorse.
hypothesis.hook: Launch a transparency-first listing storefront in an afternoon — and let buyers walk the house before they ever book a showing.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Large national franchise brokerages with custom-built portals and in-house engineering; pure iBuyers and flippers optimizing for spread, not relationships; and any operator whose model depends on obscuring listing information rather than exposing it — Abode makes them look worse, not better.

advantage.capability: Abode is the only platform that is simultaneously the brokerage's storefront builder, its operations backend, and the buyer's discovery experience — with one AI agent layer serving both sides of the transaction. Website builders (Luxury Presence, AgentFire, Placester) give an agency a pretty IDX site but no inventory ops, no honest buyer agent, and no native 3D. CRM/lead platforms (kvCORE, BoomTown) run the back office but bolt onto a separate website and treat the buyer as a lead to be captured, not a person to be informed. Portals (Zillow, Realtor.com) own the buyer but rent the agency its own leads back. 3D vendors (Matterport) sell tours as a disconnected media file. Abode collapses all four into one system where a single listing object flows from MLS ingest → 3D capture → transparent public page → buyer-intent analytics → qualified lead → CRM — and the AI agent reads that entire object to answer buyers truthfully and to tell the broker exactly which lead is ready to transact.
advantage.motivation: Every brokerage owner already pays for four disconnected tools and still loses buyers to Zillow. Abode replaces the stack and hands the agency back its own audience — the buyer relationship, the intent data, and the lead — at lower total cost. The pull is that transparency is now a growth lever, not a risk: the agent who shows price history and flaws closes faster and earns the referral. Abode lets a boutique brokerage present like a national franchise and out-inform the portals, which is the one thing money can't buy them off the shelf today.
advantage.insight: The transparency homebuyers crave is exactly the transparency that closes deals faster. For decades agents treated information asymmetry as leverage — hold back the days-on-market, stage over the flaws, control the flow. The market has inverted: buyers now trust the agent who volunteers the price history and points out the foundation crack. Zero buyer's remorse isn't a consumer nicety bolted onto a brokerage tool — it is the brokerage's fastest path to a closed sale and a referral. Whoever makes total transparency the default wins both sides at once.

principles: Transparency by default — every listing surfaces price history, days-on-market, disclosures, true dimensions, and neighborhood data unless legally prohibited; hiding information is a deliberate, logged choice, never the default state

One listing object, everywhere — MLS data, 3D capture, public page, analytics, and CRM all read and write the same canonical listing; the agency never re-enters a fact twice and the buyer never sees a stale one
The AI agent is honest before it is helpful — the buyer-facing agent answers from disclosed data and says "the seller has not disclosed that" rather than guessing or spinning; trust is the product
Live in an afternoon — a non-technical broker must go from signup to a public, MLS-connected storefront in a single sitting; every feature is measured against that activation moment
The agency owns its audience — buyer intent, contact, and behavioral data belong to the brokerage, never resold or rented back to them the way portals do

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Brokerages will replace their existing IDX website + CRM + 3D-vendor stack with a single platform — AND believe that radical transparency wins them more listings and clients rather than commoditizing the very information advantage that justifies their commission. The whole model fails if brokers conclude that showing buyers everything makes the agent less necessary, or if they treat Abode as 'just another website builder' and keep their back-office tools separate.
clickTest.testMethod: Concierge MVP with 3 boutique brokerages (8–20 agents each). For 8 weeks, manually stand up an Abode-style transparency storefront for each: ingest their active listings, hand-produce 3D walkthroughs for 5 flagship properties, publish full price-history + disclosure panels, and run a scripted 'AI buyer agent' as a human-in-the-loop chat for inbound buyers. Instrument every buyer session. In week 8, interview each broker owner: 'Would you pay to run your whole business on this? What would you cancel to afford it? Did transparency win or cost you a listing?' Separately survey the buyers who used the transparent listings vs. the brokerage's normal site on confidence and remorse.
clickTest.successMetric: At least 2 of 3 broker owners commit to a paid pilot and name specific tools they would cancel (website + one of CRM/3D). AND transparent listings show a measurably higher showing-request rate and buyers self-report ≥30% higher purchase confidence than on the brokerage's standard listings — with zero brokers reporting that transparency cost them a deal they would otherwise have won.

milestones: M1 — Concierge pilot: Manually operate the transparency storefront + human-in-the-loop buyer agent for 3 brokerages for 8 weeks. Validate that brokers will pay and that transparency lifts buyer confidence and showing requests (2 weeks to set up, 8 weeks to run)

M2 — Storefront + MLS/IDX ingest: Self-serve theme picker and MLS/IDX/RETS connector that produces a live listing-first storefront in under an afternoon. Canonical listing object with price history, disclosures, and true dimensions rendered by default (5 weeks)
M3 — B2B ops layer: Inventory management, per-listing buyer-intent analytics (dwell time, room-level engagement, drop-off), and lightweight CRM writing to the same listing object (5 weeks)

M4 — AI agent layer (both sides): One agent infrastructure — buyer-facing honest discovery/Q&A grounded in disclosed data, and broker-facing lead qualification + intent summaries. Guardrailed to never fabricate undisclosed facts (6 weeks)

M5 — 3D & interior walkthrough: Capture pipeline (Matterport/LiDAR ingest + photogrammetry fallback) rendering photorealistic models and in-browser walkthroughs embedded in the transparent listing page (7 weeks)
M6 — Billing, roles & launch: Multi-agent brokerage accounts, role-based permissions, transparency audit log, subscription billing, and public launch to the boutique-brokerage segment (4 weeks)
blockers: MLS/IDX data-access rules vary by regional MLS and often restrict how listing data may be displayed and syndicated — legal/display compliance is a per-market gate
3D capture still requires someone physically in the home; the walkthrough experience is only as good as capture coverage and adds field-ops cost
Fair-housing and disclosure liability: an AI agent answering buyer questions must be provably guardrailed against steering, redlining language, and asserting undisclosed facts
Two-sided cold start — the storefront is worthless to buyers without listings and worthless to brokers without buyers; must seed via existing brokerage audiences, not open marketplace
blueprint.timelineNotes: Sequence deliberately front-loads the concierge pilot to de-risk the transparency-vs-commoditization assumption before any 3D or AI engineering spend. 3D (M5) is intentionally last among build items because it is the highest-cost, most operationally heavy feature and is not required to validate the core wedge. Target: paid pilots by end of M1, self-serve beta by end of M4 (~5 months of build after the pilot).

sources.title: Abode founder brief
sources.content: Web-based application: essentially Shopify for real estate agencies. Brokers and agencies can create a site for their business — not ecommerce, primarily a site for listings. Two layers. B2B layer: analytics on the site's performance to potential buyers, inventory management, lead-generation tool, and other solutions to streamline the brokerage's work. B2C layer: 3D models of houses, interior walkthroughs via the site, and a chatbot/AI agent to find homes with more accuracy. The AI agents should be harnessed for both B2B and B2C use cases. Goal: provide as much transparency to homebuyers as possible so they make choices with zero buyer's remorse.

journey.persona: Marcus Delgado — Owner/Broker of a 14-agent boutique brokerage
journey.goal: Replace a fragmented, expensive tool stack with one platform that wins listings, informs buyers, and gives him back ownership of his audience — without needing to hire an engineer

stages.name: The Stack Tax — Paying Four Vendors to Still Lose Buyers to Zillow
steps: Marcus pays monthly for an IDX website template, a CRM, a 3D-tour vendor, and lead forms — none of which share data
His agents re-enter listing details across three systems; something is always stale or wrong on the public site

steps.label: Describe the home in natural language to the AI buyer agent
steps.description: Priya types "3-bed under $650k, quiet street, good light, home office, within 20 min of downtown, no major foundation issues." The agent parses intent rather than making her fill out filter dropdowns.
steps.systemState: AI agent returns a ranked short-list of matching listings with a one-line honest rationale each, drawn from disclosed data.

branches.condition: If no listings match all criteria

Agent asks one clarifying question to rank, e.g. light vs. commute priority

steps.friction: Buyer may distrust an AI agent that sounds like a salesperson

steps.label: Open a transparent listing page

branches.condition: If the seller withheld a disclosure

Price-history panel highlights the reduction and days-on-market context

steps.friction: Information density could overwhelm; must be progressively disclosed
steps.errorPath: Missing MLS fields render as explicit unknowns, never as fabricated values

steps.label: Walk the interior in-browser

branches.outcome: Page falls back to a photogrammetry preview and clearly labels it as partial capture

branches.condition: If she lingers in a room

steps.friction: Walkthrough performance on lower-end devices

steps.label: Ask the agent hard questions and get honest answers

branches.condition: If the buyer asks something requiring an agent

projects.name: Behavioral Analytics

hypothesis.problem: Traditional web analytics tools (Google Analytics, Mixpanel) tell teams WHAT users do — page views, clicks, funnels — but not WHY they do it. Teams are left guessing at root causes, running expensive user interviews, and shipping fixes that miss the mark. The user's mental model is a blur to these product teams and they rely on assumptions to make product changes.
hypothesis.solution: A behavioral analytics platform that automatically synthesizes website traffic data into qualitative artifacts — AI-generated User Personas, Journey Maps, and User Flows — so teams can understand the human intent and emotion behind every metric, without manual research.
hypothesis.hook: Stop guessing why users leave. Get research-grade UX insights from your existing traffic data — automatically.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Early-stage startups with <1,000 monthly visitors (insufficient data), and enterprise companies with dedicated in-house research teams and existing qualitative tooling.

segments.name:
1. Product managers
2. UX researchers
3. Growth Teams at Saa
segments.description:
1. Product managers
2. UX researchers
3. Growth Teams at SaaS companies (50–500 employees)

The common theme across all these customer segments is that they rely on quantitative data that cannot explain the reasoning behind recurring user behaviors like churn, drop-offs, low engagement time, minimal scroll depth, and lack of any kind of interaction.
segments.painPoint: Traditional web analytics tools (Google Analytics, Mixpanel) tell teams WHAT users do — page views, clicks, funnels — but not WHY they do it. Teams are left guessing at root causes, running expensive user interviews, and shipping fixes that miss the mark. The user's mental model is a blur to these product teams and they rely on assumptions to make product changes.
segments.resolution: A behavioral analytics platform that automatically synthesizes website traffic data into qualitative artifacts — AI-generated User Personas, Journey Maps, and User Flows — so teams can understand the human intent and emotion behind every metric, without manual research.

advantage.capability: We can bridge quantitative event data with LLM-based synthesis to generate living, continuously-updated UX artifacts at a fraction of the cost of manual research. Since the data is consistently incoming, we do not have to hunt down users to conduct research.
advantage.motivation: We believe most product teams are flying blind because the gap between analytics and research is too wide and too expensive to close manually. Product teams are at the mercy of standard analytic tools that do not tell a story about their user traffic that will help them understand how their products are perceived.
advantage.insight: Teams do not lack data — they lack interpretation. The same behavioral signals that analytics tools discard (scroll depth, rage clicks, hesitation patterns, exit timing) contain the WHY that researchers spend weeks uncovering.

principles: WHY > WHAT — always surface intent, not just events
Boring > Exciting — accurate, reliable artifacts beat flashy dashboards
Living artifacts — everything updates as traffic changes, never goes stale
Research-grade without research budgets

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Product teams will trust AI-generated artifacts and interpretations enough to act on them without manual validation.
clickTest.testMethod: Sales deck pitched to 8 growth/PM teams at mid-size SaaS companies, offering a free pilot connecting their analytics to our artifact generator.
clickTest.successMetric: 3 teams complete the pilot and at least 1 uses an AI-generated artifact to inform a shipped product decision.

milestones: Week 1–2: Integrate with GA4 / Segment event stream
Week 3–4: Build behavioral clustering engine (segment users by pattern)
Week 5–6: LLM synthesis layer — generate Personas, Journey Maps, User Flows from cluster data
Week 7–8: Dashboard UI + artifact export (PDF, Figma)
blockers: Data privacy / GDPR compliance for processing behavioral data
Minimum traffic threshold needed for statistically valid persona generation
Model accuracy — artifacts must feel authentic, not generic

Clicks 'Generate Journey Map' — sees a loading state with session count
Waits while AI clusters sessions, detects patterns, and synthesizes narrative
Views the completed 5-stage Journey Map with WHY Score and persona context
Reads stage-by-stage behavioral annotations for the first time
painPoints: Currently spends 2 full days per sprint watching Hotjar session recordings to find the same patterns
Manual journey mapping in Figma or Miro takes a UX researcher 2–3 weeks
AI tools like ChatGPT give generic journeys with no grounding in actual traffic data
No existing tool produces a WHY-focused narrative — only WHAT-focused funnels
opportunities: Show a sample insight preview while real data processes to eliminate the dead-wait anxiety
Display 'Analyzing X sessions across Y pages' as a progress message — make the work visible
Deliver the first Journey Map in under 5 minutes from connection to output
WHY Score badge (e.g. '87% confidence') immediately signals how much to trust the output

stages.name: Review & Validate Insights
steps: Reads each journey stage — name, steps, emotion, pain points, and opportunities
Checks the WHY Score confidence rating and the session count cited per stage
Compares AI-flagged friction points against their own intuition from past recordings
Clicks into a friction annotation to see the behavioral evidence behind it
Decides whether the output is ready to share or needs refinement via Ask WHY
painPoints: Qualitative insights from manual research are always subjective and hard to defend to stakeholders
No existing tool cites its behavioral evidence — insights feel like guesses
Stakeholders routinely push back on journey maps with 'how do you know this?'
Validating a manually built journey map requires a separate round of user interviews
opportunities: Every friction annotation links to the behavioral evidence (session count, event patterns) behind it
WHY Score gives stakeholders a data-backed confidence signal — removes the 'how do you know?' objection
Allow users to accept, reject, or annotate each AI-generated insight inline
Surface a 'compared to last 30 days' delta on key stage metrics to show trend direction

stages.name: Ask WHY for Deeper Context
steps: Navigates to Ask WHY from the AI Tools section in the sidebar
Types a plain-English behavioral question (e.g. 'Why do users drop off at checkout?')
Reads the AI response — structured analysis with behavioral evidence and cited session volumes
Uses suggested follow-up chips to drill deeper into a specific segment or time period
Copies a key finding to share directly in Slack
painPoints: Every behavioral question currently requires a data analyst and a 2–3 day turnaround
Natural language queries don't exist in Mixpanel or GA4 — you need SQL or custom reports
Answers from manual data pulls lack narrative context — they're numbers without a story
Can't ask a follow-up question without starting the whole analysis request over
opportunities: Plain-English query with a response in under 10 seconds — replaces the analyst request entirely
Structure the AI response as a brief, a root cause, and a recommendation — not just data
Suggested follow-up chips reduce the cognitive load of knowing what to ask next
Allow users to save frequently asked questions as pinned queries for reuse

stages.name: Export & Share with Team
steps: Clicks 'Export' on the Journey Map view
Selects PDF format or copies a shareable link with configurable access
Drops the PDF or link into the #product Slack channel with a short summary
Presents the Journey Map in a stakeholder sync — VP of Product responds positively
Team agrees on a next action based on the behavioral findings
painPoints: Currently formats journey maps in Figma or Google Slides — takes hours per deck
Manually built artifacts can't be shared as a live URL — they go stale immediately
Stakeholders can't interact with or comment on shared insights without a Figma or Miro license
No audit trail for who viewed or acted on a shared insight
opportunities: One-click PDF export that generates a stakeholder-ready, branded artifact in under 5 seconds
Shareable link with expiry control and view-only access — no tool license required for recipients
Slack integration to post artifact previews directly into a channel without leaving the app
Track who has viewed a shared artifact — give the PM visibility into stakeholder engagement

stages.name: Monitor & Return Weekly
steps: Receives the weekly behavioral digest email every Monday morning
Opens the email, sees a summary of what changed in user behavior that week
Clicks a deep-link into the specific insight or updated artifact that changed
Checks the WHY Score trend — up means growing confidence, down means a behavioral shift
Uses Ask WHY to investigate any anomalies flagged in the digest
painPoints: There is no proactive alert for behavioral changes — problems are only discovered reactively after conversion drops
Analytics dashboards require the PM to visit and know what to look for — no push intelligence
Weekly insights require manual re-running of the same reports every sprint
No way to compare behavioral patterns week-over-week without building a custom Mixpanel report
opportunities: Weekly digest email surfaces the 3 most significant behavioral changes automatically — no dashboard visit required
WHY Score trend indicator (↑ or ↓) at the top of the digest gives an at-a-glance behavioral health signal
Deep-link every digest item back to the live artifact in the app — one click from email to insight
Behavioral anomaly alerts fire in real time when session patterns deviate significantly from the 30-day baseline

experienceMap.overview: Tracks the emotional and cognitive arc of a PM from manual research frustration through discovering, adopting, and advocating for Behavioral Analytics — spanning roughly 8 weeks from pre-awareness to post-activation.

phases.name: Pre-Awareness
phases.experience: The PM is stuck in a manual research loop. After each sprint, 2 full days go toward watching session recordings and building spreadsheet narratives — with no clear 'why' at the end.
phases.insights: Target 'why are users dropping off' search queries with case studies showing time saved — not just feature lists

phases.name: Discovery
phases.experience: Encounters Behavioral Analytics via a G2 comparison article or LinkedIn ad. The WHAT vs WHY framing immediately resonates — it names the exact frustration they've been living with.
phases.insights: Lead with 'stop guessing why users leave' in all acquisition — the framing problem is the headline, not the feature

phases.name: Evaluation
phases.experience: Spends 3 days comparing pricing and features. Returns to the pricing page 3 times over 3 days. Key anxiety: 'Is this actually different from Amplitude, or just better marketing?'
phases.insights: Add a side-by-side 'WHAT you get elsewhere vs WHY you get here' comparison directly on the pricing page

phases.name: Onboarding
phases.experience: Signs up and connects GA4. Excited at first, then impatient — Step 3 of the wizard has no progress feedback and the first insight takes over 4 minutes. Nearly bounces.
phases.insights: Show a sample insight preview while real data processes — the dead-wait state is the highest churn risk in onboarding

phases.name: Value Realization
phases.experience: Generates and shares the first Journey Map. VP of Product responds positively within minutes. This is the 'aha' moment — the tool just saved 2 days of manual research.
phases.insights: Trigger a 'you saved X hours this week' milestone message after the first artifact export — make the ROI explicit

phases.name: Habit Formation
phases.experience: Returns weekly via the digest email. Uses Ask WHY 3–4× per week. The tool has replaced the manual research sprint entirely.
phases.insights: Deep-link every digest highlight back to the live insight in the app — remove the friction between notification and action

phases.name: Advocacy
phases.experience: Recommends the tool to two other PMs at a networking event. Shares a Journey Map screenshot on LinkedIn with a caption about cutting research time.
phases.insights: Trigger a referral prompt after 3 successful artifact exports — that's when advocacy intent peaks

serviceBlueprint.overview: End-to-end service delivery for generating and delivering a behavioral AI insight — from user trigger through data pipeline, AI synthesis, and artifact delivery to the customer's stakeholders.

storyboard.scenario: A PM discovers a checkout abandonment spike on Monday morning and uses Behavioral Analytics to go from raw drop-off data to a stakeholder-ready explanation — in under 15 minutes, without watching a single session recording.
storyboard.persona: Marcus Chen — Senior PM at a 120-person B2B SaaS company

frames.description: Marcus opens his laptop Monday morning. His Mixpanel dashboard shows checkout conversion dropped 12% over the weekend. The funnel stops at the checkout step — but gives no explanation.
frames.dialogue: Something broke on Saturday. But what?

frames.description: He opens Hotjar to start reviewing session recordings. The queue shows 200 new sessions from the weekend. His shoulders drop — last time this took two full days.
frames.dialogue: 200 recordings. I don't have time for this.

frames.description: He opens Behavioral Analytics instead. The WHY Score on the dashboard has dropped from 81 to 61 — a visual alert he's learned to recognize as a behavioral shift in progress.
frames.dialogue: WHY Score is down. Something changed in how users behave.

frames.description: He types 'Why did checkout abandonment spike on Saturday?' into Ask WHY. The AI responds in 8 seconds with a structured analysis citing 47,000 sessions.
frames.dialogue: 67% of drop-offs happened after users viewed the Seat Limits row.

frames.description: He opens Journey Maps. Stage 2 (Consideration) already has a new friction annotation added by the AI: 'Pricing ambiguity detected — seat limit language unclear to 67% of exiting users.'
frames.dialogue: It already updated the Journey Map. Exactly where I would have flagged it.

frames.description: Marcus exports the Journey Map as a PDF and drops it in the #product Slack channel with a two-line summary. His VP responds within three minutes. Total time elapsed: 11 minutes.
frames.dialogue: This is exactly what we needed. Let's fix the pricing copy today.

projects.name: VelocityHealth Dashboard

hypothesis.problem: UI infrastructure debt compounds invisibly. Component libraries drift from their intended patterns. New engineers bypass governed components because discoverability is poor. Reuse rates fall quarter over quarter. Duplicate implementations proliferate. None of this registers in the dashboards an engineering leader watches today — sprint velocity, DORA metrics, deployment frequency look fine right up until a $300K remediation sprint appears on the roadmap. There is no 'infrastructure P&L' for the UI layer: no single report that shows what the component library is worth, whether its value is growing or eroding, where the debt is accumulating fastest, and what it will cost if left unaddressed. CTOs can't justify platform team investment without data, and they can't get data without a tool that understands UI infrastructure health as a concept — which no existing tool does.
hypothesis.solution: VelocityHealth — an executive-level UI infrastructure health dashboard that ingests data from the codebase, CI/CD pipeline, and onboarding tooling to surface KPIs that make UI infrastructure health visible at the leadership level. Tracks five core metrics: Component Reuse Rate (% of UI built from governed components), Drift Frequency (rate at which components deviate from canonical patterns per week), Time-to-First-Feature for new hires (onboarding velocity), Technical Debt Surface Area (count of deprecated components with active usage in production files), and Coverage Score (% of UI surface area with governed component coverage). Delivers a weekly 'Infrastructure Health Report' — a single score with trend, top 3 risks, and a business cost estimate — formatted for a Monday morning executive briefing, not a terminal window.
hypothesis.hook: Your architecture is accumulating debt at a rate your sprint metrics can't see. VelocityHealth makes it visible before it's catastrophic.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Engineering teams without a component library or design system — there's no infrastructure to measure. Companies with fewer than 20 engineers where infrastructure health is still manageable by intuition and direct communication. CTOs who are still writing code and can observe the library's health firsthand. Teams whose primary technical debt is in backend systems or data infrastructure rather than the UI layer.

advantage.capability: VelocityHealth uniquely sits at the intersection of static code analysis and engineering leadership reporting — a gap no existing tool occupies. Linters track violations but don't aggregate to trend metrics. DORA tools measure deployment velocity but have no concept of component library health. Storybook tracks component coverage but doesn't connect it to engineering velocity or business cost. DataDog tracks production system health, not code architecture health. VelocityHealth ingests from all of these data sources (GitHub for component usage patterns, CI/CD for PR rejection rates, onboarding tooling for time-to-first-feature) and translates them into a single Infrastructure Health Score with business cost attribution. The report format — a Monday morning digest built for an inbox, not a dashboard — removes the activation energy that kills most developer analytics tools. Leaders don't need to log in to get value; the value comes to them.
advantage.motivation: The ROI of UI infrastructure investment has always been hard to quantify — which is precisely why platform team budget requests get cut when DORA metrics look healthy. VelocityHealth is the first tool that makes this quantification tractable and defensible. Every CTO who installs it gets, within 30 days, a number they can put in a board deck: 'Our component reuse rate is 64%, down from 71% last quarter. At current drift trajectory, remediation will cost an estimated 3.2 engineer-months by Q4.' That number transforms the budget conversation from 'trust me, the architecture is degrading' to 'here is the evidence and the cost of inaction.' The tool creates the business case for the investment it measures.
advantage.insight: The real cost of UI infrastructure debt isn't in any single component violation — it's in the aggregate productivity tax levied on every engineer, every day, compounded invisibly over quarters. A 5% reduction in component reuse doesn't feel like a crisis to anyone watching it happen. But compounded across 30 engineers over 18 months, it represents thousands of hours of duplicated implementation, inconsistent behavior in production, and an onboarding experience that takes 4 months instead of 6 weeks. VelocityHealth's core insight is that infrastructure health is a flow metric, not a stock metric: you need to see the slope of the trend to understand when intervention is justified, not just the current state. A health score of 72/100 that is declining at 4 points per quarter is more urgent than a score of 55/100 that is stable.

principles: Trend over snapshot — always show the direction and rate of change, not just the current value; a healthy-looking score that is declining is more actionable than a mediocre score that is stable

Every metric tied to a business cost — component reuse rate is meaningful only when translated into estimated engineer-hours of duplicated work this quarter; never show a raw percentage without the dollar context
Weekly cadence, not real-time — engineering leaders need a reliable artifact that fits into existing review rhythms, not another live dashboard to monitor; the report comes to them on Monday morning

Actionable by the platform team — every red metric must link to a specific, executable intervention (consolidate these 3 deprecated components, enforce these 2 pattern violations) so the dashboard produces work, not just awareness
No new login required for the executive — deliver the report via email and Slack; the tool that requires a CTO to build a new daily habit will be unused within two weeks of installation

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Engineering leaders will recognize UI infrastructure health as a distinct, reportable category worth paying for separately from their existing analytics tools. The risk is that CTOs file VelocityHealth under 'another dashboard' and deprioritize it because their existing stack (DORA metrics, sprint tracking, DataDog) feels like 'enough visibility.' The product only works if leaders believe that the invisible UI debt is a real, quantifiable problem — which is something they currently have no data to confirm.
clickTest.testMethod: Manual report pilot: Build the weekly Infrastructure Health Report by hand for 3 pilot companies using existing codebase analysis tools (grep-based component usage analysis, git log history, CI/CD export). Deliver it via email for 6 weeks as a 'UI Infrastructure Audit Service' without revealing that it comes from a tool. In week 6, conduct a 30-minute call with each CTO or VP: 'Would you pay for this report to be generated automatically every week? What would you pay? Did it change any decisions?' Separately, ask the platform team leads: 'Was anything in this report news to you? Did it help you make a case internally?'
clickTest.successMetric: At least 2 of 3 pilot CTOs confirm that a metric from the VelocityHealth report directly influenced a real decision — budget allocation, headcount request, debt paydown sprint prioritization — within the 6-week pilot. At least 1 CTO uses a VelocityHealth metric in an external context (board deck, investor update, all-hands engineering review). Willingness to pay: at least 2 of 3 pilots express willingness to pay ≥ $500/month for automated delivery. Failure condition: all 3 CTOs say the information was 'interesting' but couldn't point to a specific decision it influenced — this means the data is diagnostic but not decision-relevant at the executive level, and the product needs to move down-market to the platform team.

milestones: M1 — Manual report pilot: Build the Infrastructure Health Report template and deliver manually to 3 pilot companies for 6 weeks. Use static analysis (component import frequency via grep/AST), git history (drift detection via PR review patterns), and manual onboarding velocity data. Validate metric selection, report format, and whether the data changes executive decisions (2 weeks to build, 6 weeks to run)

M2 — Data ingestion pipeline: Automated collection of raw metrics from GitHub (file-level component import analysis, PR comment patterns), CI/CD pipeline (PR rejection rates categorized by violation type), and optionally OnboardIQ (query volume, time-to-first-PR for new engineers). Output: raw metric tables updated weekly via GitHub App (4 weeks)

M3 — Infrastructure Health Score algorithm: Define the composite score from 5 weighted sub-metrics. Calibrate weights using pilot company data — which metrics best predict the subjective 'this is bad and getting worse' judgment that platform teams make manually. Document the formula so CTOs can explain it to their board. (6 weeks)

M4 — Automated report generation and delivery: Weekly PDF + Slack digest generated automatically. Configurable delivery: email to CTO, Slack message to #engineering-leadership, or both. Report includes: score with trend, top 3 risks with estimated business cost, one recommended action. No login required. (8 weeks)

M5 — Interactive web dashboard: Drill-down view for platform team leads. Shows metric trend charts (12-week rolling), component-level breakdown (which components are drifting), team-level breakdown (which squads are contributing to drift), and a deprecated component inventory with active usage counts. (12 weeks)

M6 — Intervention recommendation engine: Auto-generated remediation plan with prioritized tasks, effort estimates, and expected score impact. 'Consolidating these 3 deprecated components would increase your reuse rate from 64% to 71% in an estimated 4 engineer-days.' Closes the loop from observation to action. (16 weeks)
blockers: Data access is the existential blocker: VelocityHealth requires read access to the customer's codebase (GitHub App) and CI/CD pipeline data. Enterprise procurement friction — security reviews, legal approval for repo access — will extend sales cycles significantly and may block mid-market companies entirely. Mitigation: start with companies that already use GitHub Apps (OnboardIQ, GuardRail AI) and have pre-approved the trust model; use the narrowest possible permission scope (read-only, specific repos).

Metric validity is a product risk: the Infrastructure Health Score is only credible if platform team leads agree it reflects reality. If the score says 'healthy' when the team knows it isn't, or vice versa, the tool loses executive credibility immediately. Mitigation: calibrate the score weights manually against 3 pilot companies before automating — don't ship the algorithm until at least one CTO says 'yes, that score matches what we observe.'

Executive attention is scarce: the weekly report must deliver value in under 2 minutes of reading or it will be filtered as noise within 3 weeks. Every word, metric, and visual must earn its place. Mitigation: test the report format with 3 CTOs before automating — present a paper prototype and time how long they spend on it before making a decision. Target: 90 seconds to absorb the key insight and recommended action.
blueprint.timelineNotes: The manual pilot (M1) is non-negotiable before any engineering investment. If the manual report doesn't change decisions, the automated version won't either — and building the automation first is $200K in engineering cost to validate a hypothesis that a $0 spreadsheet could have tested. M4 (automated delivery) is the product's first releasable state; M5 (interactive dashboard) is the second. Do not build M5 before M4 is generating paying customers. M6 (intervention recommendations) is the highest-value feature for retention but requires the longest time to validate — skip it in the MVP and add it only after 6 months of weekly report data establishes what interventions actually produce score improvement.

sources.title: VelocityHealth product brief
sources.content: Target Pain Point: The compounding cost of infrastructure debt being invisible until it is catastrophic. Functionality: An executive-level reporting dashboard that visualizes the 'health' of the UI infrastructure. It tracks KPIs such as component reuse rates, drift frequency, and time-to-first-feature for new hires. By making the 'invisible debt' visible, it provides CTOs and VPs of Engineering with the data needed to justify investments in governance and maintenance before it becomes a structural crisis.

journey.persona: Rashida Okonkwo — VP of Engineering, Series C SaaS, 160 engineers
journey.goal: Produce a defensible, data-backed case for platform team investment before the next budget cycle — and build the early warning system that prevents the next design system incident from being a surprise

stages.name: The Budget Rejection — Good Metrics, Invisible Problem
steps: Platform team lead presents the quarterly infrastructure report: component library drift is accelerating, deprecated components still in active use across 38 files, reuse rate estimated at 64% and declining
Rashida requests 2 additional platform engineers in the Q3 budget cycle, citing the platform team's qualitative assessment
CFO and CEO review: deployment frequency is up, MTTR is improving, sprint velocity is stable — 'the metrics look fine, let's revisit next quarter'
Budget request denied. Platform team continues with 4 engineers serving 160 consumers of the component library
painPoints: No metric exists that translates platform team concerns into CFO-legible terms
DORA metrics actively obscure the infrastructure debt problem — 'the metrics look fine' is true at the deployment level and misleading at the architecture level
opportunities: VelocityHealth's core value proposition is clearest in this exact moment — the platform team is right and can't prove it
The budget rejection is the conversion event: if Rashida had seen a VelocityHealth report before this meeting, the conversation would have been different

stages.name: The Incident — Invisible Debt Becomes Visible Crisis
steps: Design system team releases a major update: 3 deprecated components are removed, 2 prop interfaces are changed for the new patterns
The update breaks 183 component instances across 47 files — most using deprecated patterns that were supposed to be migrated 6 months ago
2 weeks of unplanned remediation: 6 engineers, 80 engineer-hours, 3 product features delayed to the next sprint
Post-mortem: the drift had been accumulating for 8 months. The platform team knew. The data existed in the codebase. No tool surfaced it at the leadership level before it became a crisis
painPoints: The post-mortem reveals that the incident cost 80 engineer-hours — 5x what proactive migration would have cost
The platform team had flagged the risk. The data existed. The missing link was a leadership-level report that would have made the risk legible in time to act
opportunities: The incident creates the psychological opening for infrastructure investment — Rashida now has a $40,000 remediation cost to reference in the next budget cycle
VelocityHealth's 'cost of inaction' projection is exactly the tool she needed before the incident; now she needs it to prevent the next one

stages.name: The Search — Looking for a Tool That Doesn't Exist Yet
steps: Rashida searches for 'UI infrastructure health monitoring' and 'component library governance metrics' — finds nothing purpose-built
Reviews LinearB, Swarmia, CodeClimate, SonarQube — all measure adjacent things (deployment velocity, code quality) but none have a concept of 'component reuse rate' or 'design system drift'

Posts in a VP of Engineering Slack community: 'Has anyone found a tool to track the health of their component library at the leadership level?' Gets 23 reactions and 8 responses — all describing the same problem, none with a solution
Comes across VelocityHealth mentioned in a GitHub repo discussion about UI infrastructure monitoring tools
stages.emotion: Validated but still stuck — the problem is real, no solution exists
painPoints: The market gap is real: no tool exists at the intersection of UI architecture health and executive reporting
The Slack community response (23 reactions, 8 VPs describing the same problem) is a strong demand signal that no one has yet built for
opportunities: Being the first result when a VP of Engineering searches 'component library health metrics' or 'UI infrastructure dashboard' is a high-leverage SEO/content opportunity
The VP of Engineering Slack community is both a discovery channel and a word-of-mouth amplifier — one strong VelocityHealth advocate in that community reaches hundreds of potential customers

stages.name: First VelocityHealth Report — The Number That Changes the Conversation
steps: Rashida signs up for the VelocityHealth pilot after connecting with the team via GitHub
Grants read access to 4 key repositories via GitHub App — approval takes 3 business days (security review)
Monday, 8:42am: receives the first weekly Infrastructure Health Report in her inbox

Score: 61/100 (▼ 11 points over 90 days). Reuse rate: 63%. Drift frequency: 14 violations/week. Top risk: 14 deprecated components with active usage in 47 files — estimated 6.2 engineer-days to remediate before next major design system release. She forwards it to her CTO with one line: 'This is the number we didn't have last quarter.'
stages.emotion: Relief — the data exists, it matches intuition, it's now speakable
painPoints: The security review delay (3 business days) is friction in the activation flow — need to reduce this with clearer scoping documentation
The first score of 61/100 is worse than Rashida expected — she needs context to know whether this is average, bad, or catastrophic
opportunities: The moment she forwards the report to her CTO is the product's highest-value moment — it has crossed into the executive conversation it was designed for
Industry benchmarks ('companies with 100-200 engineers average 68/100 at this stage of library maturity') provide the context that makes 61/100 legible

stages.name: Budget Cycle — The Data-Backed Case
steps: Rashida includes a VelocityHealth slide in the Q4 budget deck: Infrastructure Health Score trending from 72/100 to 61/100 over 12 months. Estimated cost of continued drift without platform investment: 2-3 major design system incidents per year at $40K-$80K each

CFO asks: 'What would 2 additional platform engineers achieve?' VelocityHealth projects: reuse rate from 63% to 74% in 2 quarters, drift frequency from 14 to 4 violations/week, estimated prevention value: $120K/year in avoided remediation
Platform team headcount request approved: 2 additional engineers, $280K annual budget
Rashida sends the VelocityHealth team a message: 'You gave me the number I needed. Three budget cycles and I finally have a platform team.'
stages.emotion: Vindicated — the investment case was always there; the data just needed to be made visible
painPoints: The 'projected prevention value' calculation needs to be defensible — if the methodology is opaque, a skeptical CFO will push back on the numbers
12 months of trend data (from M1 pilot to budget cycle) is ideal; real customers will want to accelerate this by importing historical git data
opportunities: The budget approval is VelocityHealth's most powerful case study — the moment the tool paid for itself by enabling a $280K investment decision
Historical git data import (backfilling trend data from commit history) is a high-value feature that lets new customers show trend data on day 1, not week 52

says: 'I know we're accumulating UI debt — I can feel it in the PR review times and the hiring ramp-up cost. But I can't put a number on it, and I can't justify platform team headcount without a number.'

'Our DORA metrics look great. Deployment frequency is up, change failure rate is down. But the last design system update broke 180 components and cost us two weeks of unplanned remediation. Those don't show up in the same dashboard.'
'The platform team tells me the component library is degrading, but I can't take that to the board. I need a metric, not a feeling.'
'Every time I try to budget for infrastructure investment, the answer is: your velocity metrics look fine. And they do look fine — right up until they don't.'
thinks: 'If I had one number — one score I could trend over time — I could build a budget case that any CFO could understand. The problem is the number doesn't exist yet.'

'We're flying blind on UI infrastructure health. The engineers who know it's bad are too deep in the code to produce a business-level summary. The people I report to are too removed from the code to understand the technical explanation.'

'The incident last quarter was avoidable — anyone who looked at the component drift data would have seen it coming. The problem is nobody was looking at component drift data because nobody had a tool to produce it.'
'I'm spending more in reactive remediation than proactive investment would have cost. I know this intuitively. I just can't prove it yet.'
does: Reviews DORA metrics weekly — deployment frequency, MTTR, change failure rate — and uses them to report to the board, even though they don't capture UI infrastructure health
Relies on anecdotal reports from the platform team lead ('the library is getting worse') to form intuitions about infrastructure health, without any quantitative backup
Pays for reactive remediation sprints (2–4 engineer-weeks) after design system updates break components, then writes them off as 'tech debt paydown' in the roadmap
Loses budget battles for platform team headcount because the business impact of proactive infrastructure investment can't be quantified in the terms the CFO uses
feels: Accountable for engineering velocity but blind to one of its largest invisible drains — the compounding cost of infrastructure debt that doesn't register in current metrics

Frustrated that the tools built for engineering leaders (LinearB, DORA dashboards, DataDog) measure the wrong things for this problem — production system health and deployment velocity, not code architecture health
Embarrassed that a $300K remediation sprint appeared on the roadmap as 'unexpected' when the platform team had been warning about drift for two quarters — just without data to back it up
Motivated to solve this because she knows other VPs of Engineering face the same problem and the first tool to solve it well will win an entire market
pains: No metric exists for UI infrastructure health at the leadership level — the data exists in the codebase but no tool aggregates it into a reportable score
DORA metrics and sprint velocity are the only engineering KPIs that translate naturally to the CFO level — but they're blind to architectural quality

Platform team credibility suffers when they say 'the library is degrading' and can't produce a chart to support it — the budget request gets filed under 'engineering concerns leadership doesn't need to worry about'

Reactive remediation is expensive and unpredictable — the cost of fixing drift after it breaks something is 5-10x the cost of preventing it, but prevention is invisible until it's been demonstrated to work
gains: A single Infrastructure Health Score she can present in a board meeting, with a 12-week trend and a projected cost of inaction — the artifact that transforms 'trust us, it's getting worse' into 'here is the evidence'
A weekly report that appears in her inbox Monday morning, costs 90 seconds to read, and gives her the top 3 risks and the one action her platform team should prioritize this week
The ability to defend platform team headcount in a budget cycle with data that connects UI infrastructure investment to engineering velocity outcomes
A way to recognize infrastructure degradation at the trend level — before it produces an incident — so remediation can be planned rather than reactive

persona.name: Rashida Okonkwo
persona.role: VP of Engineering at a Series C B2B SaaS company (160 engineers, 22 on frontend/design system)
persona.quote: 'I know we're accumulating UI debt — I can feel it in the hiring ramp and the PR review cost. But I can't put a number on it, and I can't justify platform team headcount without a number.'
persona.bio: Rashida joined as VP of Engineering 3 years ago after a stint as CTO at a Series A startup. She's deeply technical — 10 years as a staff engineer before moving into leadership — but now operates at the business level where translating engineering work into CFO-legible outcomes is her primary daily challenge. She manages 6 engineering directors, each responsible for a product domain. The platform team (4 engineers, 1 lead) reports to one of her directors and is responsible for the component library, design system, and shared infrastructure. She trusts her platform team's judgment but can't advocate for their budget without data. Her board asks her for DORA metrics every quarter. She has never been asked about component reuse rate — but she knows it's the metric that explains why onboarding is slow and why the last design system update was so painful.
goals: Produce an 'engineering infrastructure health' section for the board deck that goes beyond DORA metrics and captures architectural quality
Win the platform team headcount request in the next budget cycle with a data-backed ROI argument, not a trust-based one
Reduce new engineer time-to-first-feature from 4 months to 6 weeks by making the component library discoverable and its patterns visible
Build a system for detecting infrastructure debt accumulation early — before it produces a remediation crisis — so that debt paydown can be planned, not reactive
frustrations: DORA metrics are the only engineering KPIs that translate to the CFO level — but they measure production system health, not code architecture quality, and they look fine even when the architecture is degrading
The platform team's reports are accurate but anecdotal — 'the library is getting worse' without a chart doesn't survive a budget conversation with a CFO
Reactive design system remediation sprints appear as 'unexpected tech debt' on the roadmap every 2-3 quarters, costing 2-4 weeks of unplanned engineering time, with no early warning system
Every tool she's tried measures something adjacent to the problem (code quality, deployment velocity, production uptime) but nothing that directly addresses UI infrastructure health as a category
behaviors: Reviews a customized DORA metrics dashboard every Monday morning — it's the core of her weekly rhythm
Does a monthly 1:1 with her platform team lead specifically to get a qualitative health check on the component library — this is the only infrastructure health signal she currently has
Presents an 'engineering health' section in every board meeting but it's limited to deployment frequency and incident counts — she wants to add infrastructure health but has no metric for it

Builds engineering investment cases by connecting proposed work to historical cost data (e.g., 'the last 3 design system incidents cost us X engineer-weeks') — she's comfortable with quantitative arguments but needs the data to exist first
motivations: Building an engineering culture where infrastructure investment is recognized as velocity investment — not overhead
Creating the metrics infrastructure that makes engineering quality legible to the CFO and board, expanding what 'engineering leadership' means at this company
Being the VP who solved the platform team budget problem — the leader who put a number on what used to be a feeling
Protecting her engineers from the burnout cycle of reactive remediation by building better early-warning systems
personality: Comfortable translating between technical and business domains
Impatient with tools that require more effort than they return

competitors.name: LinearB / Swarmia
competitors.description: Engineering analytics platforms built around DORA metrics — deployment frequency, change failure rate, MTTR, and lead time for changes. Excellent at measuring engineering velocity at the deployment and PR level. Have no concept of UI component library health, design system drift, or architectural quality. Their 'code quality' metrics (PR size, review time) are proxies for process health, not infrastructure health. Rashida already uses one of these tools; VelocityHealth is additive, not competitive, at the metric level — but competes for her attention and her team's willingness to install another data connector.
competitors.targetMarket: Engineering managers and VPs who report on engineering velocity to the business
painPoints: No UI infrastructure health metrics
No concept of component reuse or architectural drift
Measures process quality (PR size, review time) not architectural quality
Requires significant data setup and ongoing maintenance

competitors.name: CodeClimate
competitors.description: Code quality platform that tracks technical debt at the file and function level — complexity, duplication, maintainability. Closer to the problem than DORA tools, but operates at the code micro-level (individual functions and files) rather than the architecture macro-level (component library health, design system governance). Engineers use it; VPs of Engineering rarely look at it. Has no model for 'component reuse rate' or 'design system coverage' as architectural-level metrics. The output is a list of files with quality issues, not an Infrastructure Health Score with a business cost estimate.
competitors.targetMarket: Engineering teams focused on code quality at the function and file level
painPoints: Operates at micro-level (files/functions), not architectural level
No concept of component library or design system health
Output not legible to executive level — requires engineering context to interpret
No business cost attribution for debt items

competitors.name: SonarQube
competitors.description: Open-source static analysis platform for bugs, security vulnerabilities, and code smells. Widely used in enterprise engineering. Produces a 'Reliability', 'Security', and 'Maintainability' rating per repository. Has no model for UI architecture health — cannot distinguish between a governed component usage and a direct DOM manipulation that bypasses the design system. Its 'technical debt' metric is a time estimate to fix all code smells, but it doesn't understand what 'a component that should be using DataTable but is using a hand-rolled table instead' looks like.
competitors.targetMarket: Development teams focused on code correctness, security, and maintainability
painPoints: No UI architecture health model — doesn't understand component libraries
Output is per-file bug and smell counts, not executive-level health scores
Free tier requires self-hosting which creates infrastructure overhead
No business cost attribution

competitors.name: Stepsize
competitors.description: Technical debt management tool linked to issue trackers (Linear, Jira). Engineers create 'debt issues' that are tagged and tracked alongside product issues. Tracks debt volume and prioritization but relies entirely on engineers manually flagging debt items — it doesn't detect drift or measure component reuse automatically. Good for tracking known debt; useless for detecting unknown/accumulating debt. Requires behavioral change from engineering teams to create and maintain debt issues consistently, which rarely happens in practice.
competitors.targetMarket: Engineering teams that want to track and prioritize known technical debt alongside product work
painPoints: Manual — relies on engineers proactively flagging debt, which doesn't happen consistently
No automated detection of drift or reuse degradation
No executive-level health score
Cannot surface unknown/invisible debt accumulation

competitors.name: Manual platform team reports
competitors.description: The true incumbent: quarterly or ad-hoc codebase audits conducted by platform team leads using a combination of grep scripts, bundle analysis, and institutional knowledge. Results are shared in a Google Doc or Notion page as a qualitative narrative ('the component library is degrading, we found 14 files using the deprecated DataTable'). Accurate when done by a skilled platform engineer. Takes 2-3 days per audit. Not repeated frequently enough to show trend data. Doesn't translate to CFO-legible business cost estimates. The platform team lead who does this work gets no leverage from it — the report exists, gets read once, and is forgotten until the next incident triggers another audit.
features: Completely accurate when done by the right person
Can capture nuance that automated tools miss
Platform team builds familiarity with the codebase through the audit process
competitors.targetMarket: Every engineering team with a component library — universal baseline
painPoints: Takes 2-3 engineer-days per audit — happens at most quarterly
No trend data — single snapshots don't show rate of change
Not legible at the executive level without significant translation work
Results live in a doc that's forgotten until the next incident
Platform team gets no leverage — same information is rediscovered every audit
competitors.pricing: 2-3 engineer-days per audit at $150-250/hr = $2,400–$6,000 per audit

positioningAxes.xLabel: Scope specificity (Generic code quality → UI infrastructure health specifically)
positioningAxes.yLabel: Audience level (Engineering team tools → Executive / VP of Engineering reporting)

items.label: Business cost attribution per metric
items.description: Every metric must be tied to an estimated dollar or engineer-hour cost — 'reuse rate 64%, estimated 2.1 engineer-months of duplicated implementation this quarter'

items.label: Trend data (slope, not point)
items.description: The health score's direction and rate of change is more important than its current value — a 72/100 declining at 4 points/quarter is a crisis; a 55/100 stable for 3 quarters is a maintenance problem

items.label: Automated weekly delivery (email/Slack)
items.description: The report must appear without requiring a login — leaders who have to visit a dashboard don't build the habit; leaders who get a Monday morning email do

items.label: 90-second executive readability
items.description: The report must deliver its key insight in under 90 seconds — score, trend, top risk, one recommended action. Anything longer gets filed as noise

items.label: Automated codebase ingestion (no manual tagging)
items.description: Metrics must be generated automatically from the codebase — tools that require engineers to manually flag debt items don't produce reliable data

items.label: Actionable intervention recommendations
items.description: Each red metric links to specific, executable platform team tasks — not just awareness but a prioritized to-do list with effort estimates

items.label: Component reuse rate tracking
items.description: The % of UI built from governed components — the foundational metric for measuring whether the library is actually being used

items.label: Drift frequency tracking
items.description: How often per week components deviate from their canonical patterns — the early warning signal that precedes reuse rate decline

items.label: Time-to-first-feature for new hires
items.description: The onboarding velocity metric that connects infrastructure health to hiring cost — already tracked manually, VelocityHealth automates the connection

items.label: General code quality metrics (complexity, duplication)
items.description: File-level code quality data — already solved by CodeClimate and SonarQube; not a differentiator, but useful as supplemental context

userFlow.persona: Rashida Okonkwo — VP of Engineering, Monday morning weekly review
userFlow.goal: Extract the key infrastructure health insight from the VelocityHealth report in under 2 minutes, share the most relevant finding with her platform team lead, and add one action to this week's priorities
userFlow.entryPoint: Rashida opens her email at 8:30am Monday. The VelocityHealth Weekly Infrastructure Report is in her inbox, sent at 7:00am.
userFlow.exitPoint: Rashida has shared the drift frequency breakdown with her platform team lead via Slack, added 'Review deprecated component remediation plan' to her weekly priorities, and mentally noted the score for the board meeting prep she'll do Thursday.

steps.label: Open the weekly Infrastructure Health Report email
steps.description: Rashida opens the VelocityHealth email. Subject line: 'Infrastructure Health: 64/100 ▼ 3pts this week — 1 urgent risk'. The email preview already shows the score and the direction — she knows whether she needs to read carefully or skim before opening.
steps.systemState: Email rendered. The first visible block is the score (64/100), the week-over-week delta (▼ 3 points), and the single most urgent risk (deprecated component usage up 22% in the reporting period).

branches.condition: If the score is stable or improving
branches.outcome: Rashida spends 30 seconds scanning — no immediate action needed, she'll reference it in Thursday's prep

branches.condition: If the score has dropped significantly or a new risk is flagged
branches.outcome: Rashida reads the risk section carefully and forwards to her platform team lead before 9am

steps.friction: Subject line must communicate enough to calibrate urgency before opening — if every subject line says 'Infrastructure Health Weekly', Rashida stops reading the preview and the open rate drops
steps.errorPath: If the email doesn't arrive by 7:30am Monday, Rashida will have already moved through her morning routine and the report becomes a Tuesday afterthought — timing is part of the product

steps.label: Read the score card — 60-second scan
steps.description: Rashida reads the score card: Infrastructure Health Score 64/100, down 3 points from last week, down 8 points from 90 days ago. Five sub-metric pills show green/yellow/red status. The top-of-fold area of the email contains everything she needs to assess urgency.
steps.systemState: Score card rendered with 5 sub-metric status pills (Component Reuse Rate: 🟡 63%, Drift Frequency: 🔴 17/week, Coverage Score: 🟡 78%, Deprecated in Use: 🔴 14 components, Time-to-First-Feature: 🟡 3.4 weeks). The most urgent risk is called out in a red banner.

branches.outcome: Rashida notes the score for her board deck and archives the email — 45 seconds total
Rashida reads the red metric's detail and the recommended action — she decides whether to act now or discuss in her weekly platform team 1:1

steps.friction: The score card must be renderable in email clients (no JavaScript, no web fonts) — if it falls back to a table of numbers with no visual hierarchy, Rashida can't absorb it in 60 seconds

steps.label: Drill into the Drift Frequency risk
steps.description: Drift frequency is 17/week (up from 11 last week) and marked red. Rashida clicks 'View breakdown →' which opens the VelocityHealth dashboard in a browser, scoped to the drift frequency detail view. The browser view shows: which teams are generating the most drift, which components are drifting, and the recommended action.
