experienceMap.overview: VelocityHealth's customer journey moves engineering leaders from 'flying blind on infrastructure health' — where debt accumulates invisibly until it becomes a crisis — to 'proactive infrastructure stewardship', where health trends are visible in the Monday morning rhythm and interventions are planned before they're forced.

phases.name: Pre-VelocityHealth: The Data Blindspot
touchpoints: Budget cycle deck with no infrastructure metrics
phases.experience: Engineering leaders responsible for infrastructure quality have no tool that speaks their language. DORA metrics and code quality tools measure adjacent things. The platform team knows the library is degrading but can't translate it into business terms. The gap between 'the architecture is getting worse' (felt by engineers) and 'here is the business cost and the trend' (needed by the CFO) is unbridged. Leaders make infrastructure investment decisions based on trust, not data — and lose budget cycles as a result.
phases.insights: Marketing VelocityHealth requires creating awareness that the problem exists and is solvable — most VPs of Engineering don't know to look for 'UI infrastructure health monitoring' because they don't believe such a tool exists. The market doesn't know what it needs because the product category hasn't existed before.

phases.name: Discovery: Finding VelocityHealth After the Incident
phases.channel: VP of Engineering peer Slack communities, GitHub discussions, word of mouth
phases.experience: The design system incident creates the emotional opening for infrastructure tooling adoption. Rashida is motivated to find a solution by a specific, costly event — not by abstract concern about future debt. This is when she's most open to a new tool and most motivated to make it work. The discovery path is peer-to-peer (VP Slack community, GitHub discussions) rather than paid search — the product needs to be present in the conversations where engineering leaders process painful incidents.
phases.emotion: Motivated to solve a concrete problem
phases.insights: The incident-driven adoption pattern means VelocityHealth's best marketing is content that meets engineering leaders during or after an infrastructure crisis — post-mortems, retrospectives, 'how did we not see this coming' moments. Content marketing that targets 'design system incident prevention' and 'how to justify platform team investment' will find customers at their highest conversion moment.

phases.name: Activation: The First Report Changes the Conversation
touchpoints: GitHub App installation and repo access approval
First use of a VelocityHealth metric in an external artifact (board deck, all-hands)
phases.experience: The activation moment is the first time Rashida forwards the VelocityHealth report to someone above or beside her — the CTO, a peer VP, a board member. That forward is the proof that the product has crossed from 'tool I use' to 'data I share' — and sharing is the behavior that creates organizational value and drives retention. The security review delay (3 business days for GitHub App approval) is the biggest friction point in this phase and the most important thing to reduce.
phases.emotion: Relief and credibility — 'the data matches what we felt and now we can say it'
phases.insights: Measure the 'forward rate' (% of weekly reports forwarded to at least one other person) as the primary activation metric. A report that stays in Rashida's inbox is a half-converted customer; a report she forwards to her CTO is a fully converted customer. Track forward rate by cohort and by report content — which risk types drive the most forwards?

phases.name: Retention: The Monday Morning Ritual
touchpoints: Monthly score trend discussion in engineering all-hands
phases.experience: VelocityHealth earns its place in Rashida's Monday routine by being consistently useful in under 2 minutes. The retention risk is report fatigue — if every report says the same thing without variation or actionable urgency, Rashida stops reading carefully and the tool becomes background noise. The weekly email must feel like a briefing, not a status report: it should have a clear hierarchy of 'this week's most important thing' rather than a flat list of metrics.
phases.emotion: Dependent — this is now part of her infrastructure mental model
phases.insights: Report open rate declining over time is a leading indicator of churn. If 12-week open rates drop below 60%, the report content needs to be recalibrated — either the metrics aren't changing enough week-to-week to be interesting, or the format isn't communicating urgency effectively. A/B test subject lines and report structure with cohorts of similar companies.

phases.name: Expansion and Advocacy: VelocityHealth in the Budget Conversation
phases.channel: Budget decks (Google Slides), Board materials, Peer VP Slack communities
touchpoints: VelocityHealth Infrastructure Health Score in the board meeting
Budget request using VelocityHealth trend data to justify platform team headcount
VP of Engineering peer community share: 'here's the tool that helped me win the platform team budget'
phases.experience: The highest-value moment in the customer lifecycle is when a VelocityHealth metric appears in a board deck or a successful budget request. This is when the tool has fulfilled its core promise — making the invisible legible at the level where resource allocation decisions are made. Every customer who wins a budget battle with VelocityHealth data becomes an organic advocate in the VP of Engineering community, where word-of-mouth is the dominant discovery channel.
phases.emotion: Vindicated and vocal — Rashida becomes an advocate
phases.insights: Create a structured success story program: when a customer wins a budget cycle using VelocityHealth data, document the specifics (original score, trend, decision made, outcome) with their permission and share it in the VP of Engineering communities where their peers are. The 'I won the platform team headcount' case study is the most credible possible marketing for this product.

serviceBlueprint.overview: VelocityHealth delivers UI infrastructure health visibility as an automated service — weekly data collection, metric calculation, and report delivery — with a dashboard layer for teams that want to drill deeper. The core experience is a report that arrives, not a tool that must be visited.

steps.name: Codebase Ingestion
steps.customerAction: Engineering leader or platform team lead installs the VelocityHealth GitHub App and grants read access to the relevant repositories. Selects which repos to include in the health score (component library, product repos that consume it).
steps.frontstage: GitHub App installation flow: permission scope clearly explained (read-only, no write access). Repo selection UI. Confirmation: 'VelocityHealth will analyze 4 repos. First report will be ready in 48 hours.'
steps.backstage: GitHub App webhook triggers initial codebase crawl. AST analysis extracts: component import frequency by file, import source resolution (governed library path vs. local duplicate), deprecated component usage count. Git history analysis extracts: drift frequency (new pattern violations per week), churn rate in component files. Output: raw metric tables stored per workspace.
steps.support: GitHub App (repo read access), AST parser (TypeScript/JavaScript), Git log processor, cloud data store (workspace-scoped metric tables)
steps.evidence: Email to the installer: 'VelocityHealth has analyzed [repo count] repos and [file count] TypeScript files. Your first Infrastructure Health Report will arrive Monday at 7:00am.'

steps.name: Weekly Metric Calculation
steps.customerAction: No customer action required — runs automatically every Sunday at 11pm.
steps.frontstage: Nothing visible — the weekly calculation is silent until the report arrives Monday morning.
steps.backstage: Weekly job: (1) pull latest codebase snapshot via GitHub API, (2) run component import analysis, (3) calculate 5 sub-metrics (Reuse Rate, Drift Frequency, Coverage Score, Deprecated in Use, Time-to-First-Feature from OnboardIQ if connected), (4) compute composite Infrastructure Health Score using calibrated weights, (5) calculate week-over-week and 90-day deltas, (6) identify top 3 risks using threshold rules and trend analysis, (7) generate recommended actions per red metric, (8) render report as HTML email + PDF.
steps.support: Weekly calculation job (cron), GitHub API (repo snapshot), metric calculation engine, health score algorithm, risk threshold rules, report rendering pipeline
steps.evidence: Internal alert to VelocityHealth ops: 'Week 34 calculations complete. 47 workspaces processed. 3 workspaces flagged with significant score changes (>10 points). Reports queued for 7:00am delivery.'

steps.name: Report Delivery
steps.customerAction: Rashida opens her email at 8:30am Monday. Subject line: 'Infrastructure Health: 64/100 ▼ 3pts this week — Drift frequency requires attention'.
steps.frontstage: HTML email: score card (Infrastructure Health Score, delta, trend direction), 5 sub-metric pills with green/yellow/red status, top risk highlighted in red banner with one recommended action, 'View full breakdown →' link to dashboard. Renders correctly in Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail. No images required for core content — readable in plain-text fallback.
steps.backstage: Email rendered from template using metric data. Magic link generated for the 'View breakdown →' click (no re-authentication required, valid for 7 days). Slack message queued if Slack integration is configured (delivers to the configured channel 30 minutes after email send).
steps.support: Email delivery service (SendGrid), magic link authentication, Slack API (for Slack notification), PDF renderer (for downloadable version)
steps.evidence: Email open tracking event logged. 'View breakdown →' click tracked as activation event.

steps.name: Dashboard Drill-Down
steps.customerAction: Rashida clicks 'View breakdown →' to investigate the drift frequency spike. The dashboard opens directly to the Drift Frequency detail view, pre-loaded with the week's data.
steps.frontstage: Dashboard: Drift Frequency trend chart (12-week rolling), breakdown by team (which squads are generating violations), breakdown by component (which components are drifting most), list of specific violation instances with file paths and suggested fixes. 'Share breakdown' button generates a pre-formatted Slack message. 'Download for board deck' exports the trend chart as a clean PNG.
steps.backstage: Dashboard served from the magic link session (no login). Drill-down data fetched from the metric data store. Slack message pre-generated from the current drill-down context. PNG export renders the chart at 2x resolution with the VelocityHealth branding strip.
steps.support: Web dashboard (React), metric data API, Slack message pre-generator, PNG chart export
steps.evidence: Dashboard session recorded. 'Share breakdown' click logged as a high-value engagement event (indicates the report is influencing team communication).

steps.name: Platform Team Remediation
steps.customerAction: Rashida shares the drift breakdown with her platform team lead via the pre-generated Slack message. Platform team lead sees the specific violations, creates a remediation ticket in Linear, and assigns it to the sprint.
steps.frontstage: Pre-generated Slack message includes: drift frequency chart (as inline image), team breakdown table, specific component violations list, recommended action ('Enforce Modal pattern — 8 instances, est. 3 engineer-hours'). Platform team lead clicks through to the dashboard for the full violation list.
steps.backstage: Slack message sent via Rashida's Slack workspace (via the share flow). Dashboard session shared with any recipient of the Slack link. VelocityHealth tracks whether the recommended action is 'resolved' in the following week's report — if the Modal violations drop, the recommended action is marked complete in the next report.
steps.support: Slack API, shared dashboard session, remediation tracking pipeline (compares violation counts week-over-week for recommended action items)
steps.evidence: Following Monday's report: 'Drift frequency: 9/week ▼ 8 from last week. Modal pattern violations resolved (was 8, now 0). Score: 67/100 ▲ 3pts.'

storyboard.scenario: Rashida is 3 years into her VP of Engineering role at a 160-engineer Series C SaaS company. She's lost 3 consecutive platform team budget requests because 'the metrics look fine.' A major design system incident just cost the company 2 unplanned engineer-weeks. This is the week she finds VelocityHealth — and the week the data that was always there becomes visible.
storyboard.persona: Rashida Okonkwo — VP of Engineering, Series C B2B SaaS, 160 engineers

frames.description: Q3 budget meeting. Rashida presents the platform team's request: 2 additional engineers, $280K/year. The platform team lead's qualitative report is projected on the wall: 'Component library drift accelerating, estimated reuse rate at 64%.' CFO: 'Your DORA metrics are strong. Deployment frequency is up 40% year-over-year. Let's revisit this next quarter when we have more data.' The budget request is denied for the third consecutive cycle.
frames.dialogue: 'More data. Every quarter it's more data. The data exists — it's just not in a form anyone here can read.'

frames.description: Three weeks later, 9:47pm. Rashida gets a Slack alert: the design system update that shipped at 5pm has broken the Checkout and Reporting flows in production. 183 component instances using deprecated backdrop behavior in Modal. Engineering team is rolling back. This is the third design system incident in 18 months.
frames.dialogue: 'How did we not see this coming? Marcus said the drift was bad. Why doesn't anyone have a dashboard for this?'
frames.emotion: The clarity of hindsight — expensive and preventable

frames.description: Post-mortem document, slide 7: 'Timeline of drift accumulation.' The data was there — in the git history, in the component import analysis, in the PR review patterns — for 8 months before the incident. A VelocityHealth infrastructure analysis, run retroactively on the git history, shows the health score declining from 74/100 to 61/100 over that period. Every red metric was predictable. 'We had the data. We just didn't have a tool that surfaced it to me.'
frames.dialogue: 'This is the report I needed 8 months ago. Instead I'm reading it in a post-mortem.'
frames.emotion: Retrospective clarity — the problem was solvable

frames.description: Monday, 6:52am. Rashida's inbox. Subject: 'Infrastructure Health: 61/100 ▼ 8pts (90-day) — 1 urgent risk: deprecated component active in 47 files'. She opens it. The score card takes 30 seconds to absorb. The top risk is exactly what she expected. She scrolls to the business cost estimate: '14 deprecated components × average 3.2 engineer-hours to migrate = estimated 44 engineer-hours before next major release.' She forwards it to her CTO with one sentence: 'This is the number I've been trying to produce for 3 years.'
frames.dialogue: 'There it is. The number that was always there but never surfaced.'

frames.description: Q4 budget meeting. Rashida's slide: 'Infrastructure Health Trend — Q1 to Q4 2026.' The VelocityHealth chart shows the score declining from 74/100 to 61/100 over 12 months. Below it: 'Without investment: 2-3 design system incidents/year at $40-80K each = $80-240K projected annual cost. With 2 additional platform engineers: reuse rate increases to 74%, drift frequency to < 5/week, projected prevention value: $120-160K/year.' CFO: 'Why didn't we have this slide last year?'
frames.dialogue: 'Because the tool didn't exist last year. It does now.'
frames.emotion: Vindicated — data wins where trust couldn't

frames.description: 6 weeks later. VelocityHealth report: Infrastructure Health Score 68/100 ▲ 7pts (6-week). Drift frequency: 6/week (down from 17). Deprecated components in active use: 6 (down from 14). The platform team, with their 2 new engineers, has been working from the VelocityHealth remediation queue for 5 weeks. Rashida screenshots the trend chart and sends it to her engineering all-hands channel: 'This is what proactive platform investment looks like on a chart.'
frames.dialogue: 'Three budget cycles to get here. But this is the chart that makes the next request automatic.'

frames.description: VP of Engineering Slack community, #tools channel. Rashida's post: 'For anyone who's lost budget cycles because their DORA metrics look fine but they know the architecture is degrading — VelocityHealth. It's the tool I didn't know I needed and then couldn't do a budget cycle without. Happy to share the report format if it helps anyone make a case.' 31 reactions. 12 DMs. 7 trial signups from engineering leaders in her network.
frames.dialogue: 'If I can save one platform team from 3 years of losing budget battles, this was worth sharing.'

informationArchitecture.overview: Two primary user types: engineering leaders (Rashida) who consume the report in their email workflow and need < 2 minutes of effort; and platform team leads (Marcus) who drill into the dashboard to identify specific interventions. The executive experience is email-first; the platform team experience is dashboard-first.

nodes.label: Weekly Report (Email)

nodes.label: Score Card
nodes.description: Infrastructure Health Score (0-100), week-over-week delta, 90-day trend arrow. Five sub-metric pills: Reuse Rate, Drift Frequency, Coverage Score, Deprecated in Use, Time-to-First-Feature.

nodes.label: Top Risk Banner
nodes.description: The single most urgent risk this week with a business cost estimate and one recommended action. Red if score dropped >5 points or a metric crossed a critical threshold.

nodes.label: Score Trend Chart
nodes.description: 12-week rolling score trend as an inline image. Screenshot-ready for board decks. Clean export with no browser chrome or login state visible.

nodes.label: Share and Export CTAs

nodes.label: Interactive Dashboard
nodes.description: For platform team leads who need to drill beyond the email summary. Accessible via magic link (no re-authentication). Shows metric trends, breakdowns, and intervention queues.

nodes.label: Health Score Overview
nodes.description: Composite score trend (24-week), sub-metric trend charts, industry benchmark comparison (anonymized peer group at similar company size and library maturity).

nodes.label: Component Reuse Rate
nodes.description: % of UI built from governed components, trend by week. Breakdown by team/squad. Files with lowest reuse rate. Import path analysis showing library vs. local duplicate usage.

nodes.label: Drift Frequency
nodes.description: Pattern violations per week, trend chart. Breakdown by team and by component. Specific violation list with file paths, violation type, and suggested fix. 'Share this breakdown' button.

nodes.label: Coverage Score
nodes.description: % of UI surface area with governed component coverage — identifies blank spots in the library where engineers have no governed option and must build from scratch.

nodes.label: Deprecated in Active Use
nodes.description: Inventory of deprecated components with file counts, usage frequency, and estimated migration effort. Sorted by business risk (proximity to design system release dates).

nodes.label: Onboarding Velocity
nodes.description: Time-to-first-feature trend by hire cohort (requires OnboardIQ integration or manual cohort data input). Correlates infrastructure health score with onboarding velocity over time.

nodes.label: Remediation Queue
nodes.description: Prioritized list of debt interventions generated from red metric analysis. Each item has: description, estimated engineer-hours, expected score impact, assignable to a team.

nodes.label: Deprecated Component Migrations
nodes.description: Specific deprecated component instances to migrate, sorted by usage count and proximity to next design system release. One-click issue creation in Linear or Jira.

nodes.label: Pattern Enforcement Targets
nodes.description: Files and teams where drift violations are highest. Links to GuardRail AI or similar enforcement tooling for automated remediation.

nodes.label: Coverage Gap Backlog
nodes.description: UI patterns that lack governed components — areas where engineers are building from scratch because the library doesn't cover the use case. Seeds the platform team's roadmap.

nodes.label: Configuration
nodes.description: Setup and maintenance: repositories, delivery schedule, notification channels, integration connections, team definitions.

nodes.label: Repository Settings
nodes.description: Which repos are included in the health score. Component library repo vs. consumer repos. Exclusion patterns (e.g., exclude /legacy/ directories from reuse calculations).

nodes.label: Delivery Settings
nodes.description: Report recipients (email), Slack channel for Slack delivery, delivery time (default Monday 7:00am, configurable), PDF attachment toggle.

nodes.label: Integrations
nodes.description: OnboardIQ (for onboarding velocity data), GuardRail AI (for drift detection enrichment), Linear/Jira (for remediation ticket creation from the queue).

nodes.label: Team Definitions
nodes.description: Map code ownership (GitHub CODEOWNERS or team-level repo access) to team names for the team breakdown in drift frequency and reuse rate reports.

nodes.label: Executive Artifacts
nodes.description: Shareable outputs designed for the board meeting, budget cycle, and all-hands — not the internal dashboard view.

nodes.label: Board-Ready Score Chart
nodes.description: Clean PNG export of the Infrastructure Health Score trend. No dashboard chrome. VelocityHealth branding strip. Designed to drop directly into a Google Slide.

projects.name: OnboardIQ: Architectural Context Engine

hypothesis.problem: A company's component library is the most valuable piece of institutional knowledge its frontend team has built — and it's almost entirely inaccessible to new engineers. Storybook is incomplete or out of date. Confluence docs reference component names that were renamed two quarters ago. The codebase has 4 different implementations of the same pattern, and a new engineer has no way to know which one is canonical. The only reliable source of truth is a senior engineer, and senior engineers are fielding the same 'where is the pattern for X?' questions on repeat, draining their time and creating a bottleneck that gets worse as the team grows. AI coding tools (Copilot, Cursor) don't know your library — they hallucinate generic solutions that bypass your governed components entirely, compounding the drift problem GuardRail was designed to catch.
hypothesis.solution: OnboardIQ — an LLM-powered architectural context engine that ingests your UI infrastructure library (components, patterns, tokens, usage guidelines, ADRs) and makes it queryable in natural language. A new engineer asks 'How do I implement a data table with multi-role column visibility?' and gets back: the exact component, the right variant, a working code snippet pulled from a canonical usage example in the codebase, a direct link to the Storybook page, and the ADR explaining why the pattern was designed this way. OnboardIQ is available as a VS Code extension, a Slack bot, and a web interface — so engineers can query it wherever they're already working, without switching context.
hypothesis.hook: Stop explaining your component library. Let it explain itself.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Teams without an established component library — OnboardIQ has nothing to index. Solo developers or very small teams (< 5 engineers) where direct mentorship still scales. Companies with no documentation at all, where the library exists only in tribal knowledge — OnboardIQ can't surface what was never written down. Teams whose onboarding pain is primarily cultural or process-related rather than informational.

advantage.capability: OnboardIQ can be built on top of existing documentation sources — Storybook, Zeroheight, Notion, Confluence, GitHub — without requiring teams to create new documentation. The ingestion pipeline treats the component library itself (component APIs, prop types, usage examples in the codebase) as the primary source of truth, with documentation as supplemental context. A RAG pipeline over this structured knowledge base produces answers that are specific, source-cited, and linked to canonical implementations rather than generic best-practice suggestions. The IDE integration (VS Code extension) creates a zero-friction query surface: engineers ask questions inline while writing code, without leaving their working context.
advantage.motivation: The cost of slow onboarding is quantifiable in a way that most DevX tools are not. A mid-level frontend engineer at $150K/year fully loaded costs approximately $12.5K/month. If the average time to first productive commit is 9 days and OnboardIQ cuts that to 3 days, that's 6 days × $625/day = $3,750 recovered per hire — before accounting for the senior engineer time freed from answering repetitive questions. At 10 hires/year, that's $37,500 in direct cost recovery plus hundreds of hours of senior engineer time returned to product work. The ROI story writes itself for any engineering lead who has sat through a quarterly headcount review.
advantage.insight: Every company's component library already contains all the information a new engineer needs — it's just not queryable. The architecture is in the code. The reasoning is in the ADRs. The patterns are in the canonical usage examples. What doesn't exist is a layer that extracts this structured knowledge and makes it answerable in natural language, specific to this team's exact library. Generic AI tools fail here for the same reason generic docs fail: they don't know your library's specific component hierarchy, naming conventions, or usage constraints. OnboardIQ's moat is the schema it builds from your library — not just embeddings of documentation, but a structured graph of component relationships, pattern dependencies, and usage constraints that makes answers specific enough to actually use.

principles: Specificity over generality — always return the exact component, variant, and file path, never a category or a guess
Source-first — every answer must cite its source (Storybook page, ADR, canonical usage example) so engineers can verify and learn the reasoning, not just copy the output
No confident hallucination — if the answer isn't in the indexed library, say so explicitly and suggest where to look next, rather than synthesizing a plausible-sounding but unverifiable response
Integrate where engineers already work — IDE extension, Slack bot, GitHub PR comment; the query surface must have zero-friction access, not require a context switch to a separate app
Measure velocity, not volume — the product's north star is engineer time-to-first-productive-commit, not query count; optimize everything for that outcome

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: New engineers will trust OnboardIQ's answers enough to act on them without asking a colleague to verify — because a single confidently-wrong answer (wrong component, deprecated pattern, incorrect usage) will break trust immediately and cause engineers to revert to asking humans. The precision bar for OnboardIQ is higher than for a general-purpose AI tool: a new engineer has no baseline to evaluate whether the answer is correct, so errors are invisible until they cause a PR rejection.
clickTest.testMethod: Shadow mode trial with 3 new engineers during their first 4 weeks. Deploy OnboardIQ alongside the existing onboarding process — no changes to docs, no reduction in Slack access. Log every query and result. After each session, prompt the engineer to rate the answer: 'Was this answer directly applicable to your task?' (yes/no/partially). Track: (1) answer helpfulness rate, (2) follow-up question rate as a proxy for answer completeness, (3) time to first PR submitted, (4) time to first PR merged. Compare against the previous 3-engineer cohort's baseline metrics.
clickTest.successMetric: 80% of answers rated 'directly applicable' by engineers during the 4-week trial. Time-to-first-PR reduces by at least 30% vs. the previous cohort's average. At least 2 of 3 trial engineers replace at least one Slack 'how do I?' question with an OnboardIQ query in week 1. Zero instances of OnboardIQ confidently recommending a deprecated or incorrect pattern (tracked via PR review feedback).

milestones: M1 — Library ingestion pipeline: CLI tool that crawls Storybook, Zeroheight, or a local component directory and builds a queryable context store — component names, prop APIs, usage examples, links to source files. Validates that the store accurately represents the library by running a test set of known questions and checking answers (2 weeks)

M2 — Natural language query engine: RAG pipeline over the context store that accepts a free-text question and returns the relevant component, canonical usage example, source link, and (where available) the ADR or design rationale. Runs as a local CLI tool and REST API (4 weeks)

M3 — VS Code extension: In-editor query panel triggered by a keyboard shortcut. Engineers type a question without leaving their file; OnboardIQ returns the answer inline with a link to the Storybook page and the canonical code example. Usable in the first week of onboarding (6 weeks)

M4 — Slack bot: `/onboardiq [question]` slash command that returns a formatted answer in-thread — component name, code snippet, source link. Covers the 'I'm about to ask a colleague in Slack' moment before it becomes a DM (8 weeks)

M5 — Answer quality tuning: Collect thumbs up/down feedback on every answer. Use accepted vs. rejected answers as training signal to tune retrieval and reranking. Target: precision improves from 70% at launch to 85%+ by week 8 of production (10 weeks)

M6 — Engineering lead dashboard: Shows library coverage (% of components indexed), most-asked questions (surfaces doc gaps), answer quality trend over time, and time-to-first-PR cohort comparison for engineers onboarded with vs. without OnboardIQ (12 weeks)
blockers: Answer precision is an existential blocker: a single confidently-wrong answer that causes a new engineer to ship broken code will destroy trust with the entire team. The retrieval pipeline must be tuned to return 'I don't know, but try X' rather than a plausible-sounding wrong answer. Conservative retrieval beats confident hallucination every time.

Documentation quality gates: if the existing Storybook or docs are severely out of date (component names changed, deprecated patterns still documented), OnboardIQ will surface bad answers from bad sources. Need a documentation freshness audit before onboarding any customer — and a clear 'last verified' timestamp on every indexed source.

Library ownership for multi-framework repos: companies with mixed React/Vue/Angular or with multiple component libraries (one per product line) complicate the ingestion schema significantly. Scope the MVP to single-framework repos with one primary component library and expand after initial validation.
blueprint.timelineNotes: M1–M2 in 4 weeks is the minimum viable demo — a CLI tool that answers questions from a Storybook export. Get this in front of 2 pilot companies before building any UI. The VS Code extension (M3) is the highest-leverage distribution surface — prioritize it over the web app. M4 (Slack) is a high-adoption moment because it intercepts the 'I'm about to ask a human' impulse. Do not build the analytics dashboard (M6) until there are real queries to analyze — at least 100 queries from real engineers.

sources.title: OnboardIQ product brief
sources.content: Target Pain Point: Onboarding bottlenecks and the loss of engineering velocity. Functionality: An LLM-powered context tool that maps the entire UI infrastructure library. New engineers can ask natural language queries like 'How do I implement a data table with multi-role permissions?' or 'Where is the existing validation pattern for admin forms?' Instead of digging through stale files, the tool points them to the governed, standardized component and provides a direct link to the implementation guidelines.

journey.persona: Yuki Tanaka — Mid-level Frontend Engineer, first 30 days
journey.goal: Implement a data table with multi-role column visibility for the reports feature — first significant task after completing starter tickets

stages.name: Task Assignment and False Confidence
steps: Yuki is assigned the reports data table feature on day 8
Searches Storybook for 'DataTable' — finds 3 results: DataTable (deprecated), DataTable v2, and DataGrid
Reads the DataTable v2 story — no mention of role-based column visibility
Searches Confluence for 'role-based table' — finds a 14-month-old doc that references a HOC called RoleColumnFilter that doesn't appear anywhere in the codebase
painPoints: No way to know which DataTable variant is canonical without asking
Documentation references components that don't exist in the codebase in that form
opportunities: OnboardIQ's value is highest at this exact moment — the search has failed and the next step would be to ask a human
Intercept this moment with a zero-friction query: 'Which DataTable should I use for role-based column visibility?'

stages.name: The Grep-and-Copy Fallback
steps: Yuki greps the codebase for DataTable usages — finds 11 files, each with slightly different prop patterns
Picks the most recent file that looks similar to what they need and copies the implementation
The copied pattern uses a local permissions check instead of the team-standardized usePermission hook
Submits PR — gets a review comment: 'Use usePermission from the auth module boundary instead of inline role checking'
painPoints: Grep finds examples, not canonical examples — no way to distinguish the right implementation from a legacy one
The cost of the wrong pattern is a PR rejection, which is demoralizing in week two
opportunities: OnboardIQ should distinguish canonical examples from legacy ones — index the approved pattern, not all patterns
The PR rejection message ('use usePermission from the auth module boundary') is exactly the kind of answer OnboardIQ should return proactively

stages.name: Discovery: The DevX Lead Mentions OnboardIQ
steps: Yuki mentions the PR rejection to their DevX onboarding buddy
DevX lead: 'Oh — have you tried OnboardIQ? It's a beta tool we're piloting. Try asking it your original question.'
Yuki opens VS Code, types into the OnboardIQ panel: 'How do I implement a data table with role-based column visibility?'
OnboardIQ returns: DataTable component + RoleVisibility prop + usePermission integration pattern + code snippet + link to Storybook + link to ADR-014 (auth boundary)
painPoints: Discovery of the tool was accidental — should be standard onboarding, not a tip from a colleague
opportunities: OnboardIQ should be introduced on day 1 of onboarding, not discovered by accident
The moment of seeing a specific, sourced, correct answer after 3 days of searching is the product's strongest conversion moment — make it reproducible

stages.name: First Correct Implementation
steps: Yuki applies the pattern returned by OnboardIQ directly from the IDE
Clicks the Storybook link in the answer — sees the exact story that demonstrates the component
Clicks the ADR link — reads the 3-paragraph explanation of why the auth module boundary was designed the way it was
Submits corrected PR — it gets approved without structural comments
painPoints: Time lost to the first failed attempt: 3 days. Time to implement correctly with OnboardIQ: 2 hours.
opportunities: The before/after contrast (3 days vs. 2 hours) is the product's strongest marketing story — capture it with a survey at the moment of first successful PR
The ADR link is high-value — new engineers want to understand the reasoning, not just the answer. This is a differentiator vs. Storybook alone.

stages.name: Habitual Use and Self-Sufficiency
steps: Yuki starts querying OnboardIQ before searching Storybook or Confluence for any new pattern
Query volume is high in weeks 2–3, drops significantly by week 5 as the mental model of the library solidifies
Yuki stops asking senior engineers 'how do I' questions in Slack — queries go to OnboardIQ first
By week 6, Yuki answers a teammate's Slack question about form validation with: 'Ask OnboardIQ — query the validation pattern for admin forms'
painPoints: A few OnboardIQ answers reference Storybook pages that are incomplete — creates brief confusion before Yuki learns which source types to trust more
OnboardIQ doesn't yet surface related patterns ('if you're using DataTable, you probably also need PaginationControls') — this would accelerate adoption further
opportunities: Query volume over time is the retention metric — show engineering leads a chart of each engineer's query volume declining as they internalize the library
Related pattern surfacing ('engineers who asked this also needed X') is a high-value feature for week 2 of the roadmap

says: 'I've been reading the Storybook for three days and I still don't know which DataTable to use — there are four of them and I can't tell which is current.'
'The Confluence docs say to use FormValidator but when I grep the codebase half the forms use something called useFormValidation instead. Which one is right?'
'I hate pinging senior engineers on Slack with basic questions. I know they're busy. But I've been stuck on this for two hours.'
'My first PR got rejected because I reimplemented a component that already existed. I had no idea it was there — the docs don't mention it.'
thinks: 'Everyone else seems to know this stuff instinctively. Am I the only one who doesn't understand the codebase?'
'If I could just find one good example of how this is supposed to work, I could figure out the rest myself. The problem is finding that example.'
'There must be a pattern for this — this can't be the first time someone needed a permission-gated form. But I can't find it.'
'I don't want to ask the same question twice. I need to remember the answer this time, whatever it is.'
does: Opens Storybook, searches for the component they need, finds multiple versions with no indication of which is current — closes Storybook
Greps the codebase for similar patterns, copies the first working example they find, which may itself be a deprecated pattern
Posts in the team's #frontend-help Slack channel and waits — response time ranges from 15 minutes to 2 days depending on who's online
Asks their onboarding buddy the same question they've already asked twice, embarrassed to be asking again
Spends the last 30 minutes of every day reverse-engineering what they built to check if it matches what they see in production
feels: Overwhelmed by the volume of undiscoverable institutional knowledge — everything they don't know feels like a landmine
Reluctant to ask questions too frequently for fear of being seen as slow or high-maintenance
Frustrated that the tools meant to help (Storybook, Confluence) are themselves a source of confusion rather than clarity
Anxious that their first month impression is being shaped by their onboarding experience, not their actual engineering ability
pains: No single queryable source of truth for 'how do I implement X in this codebase' — the answer is distributed across Storybook, Confluence, Slack history, and senior engineer memory
Generic AI tools (Copilot, ChatGPT) suggest patterns that don't exist in the library and sometimes contradict the team's architecture
Documentation freshness is invisible — there's no way to know if the Storybook page was updated last week or two years ago
The cost of a wrong answer is high: a PR rejection in week one sets back productivity and confidence simultaneously
gains: A single natural language query that returns the right component, the right usage pattern, and a direct link to a working example — resolving in 30 seconds what currently takes 3 hours
Confidence that the answer is sourced from the team's actual governed library, not a generic best practice that might violate the architecture
The ability to self-serve answers without interrupting a senior engineer, preserving both their time and the new engineer's dignity
Visible evidence of growing competency — query volume decreasing over time as the new engineer internalizes the architecture

persona.name: Yuki Tanaka
persona.role: Mid-level Frontend Engineer, first 30 days at a Series B fintech (90 engineers, 12 in frontend)
persona.quote: 'I have 4 years of React experience, but I've spent my first two weeks basically learning how to ask for help. I know how to build things — I just don't know how to build them the right way here yet.'
persona.bio: Yuki is a competent, motivated engineer who performed well in the interview process and impressed the team with their depth of React knowledge. On paper, they're exactly who the team wanted to hire. In practice, their first month has been a cycle of false starts: implementing patterns that already exist in the library, building forms without the validation hook the team standardized on, asking the same two senior engineers repeated questions in Slack. None of this reflects their actual ability — it reflects an onboarding environment where the institutional knowledge is inaccessible. Yuki knows this, but it doesn't make the experience any less demoralizing.
goals: Ship a meaningful feature PR that gets merged without structural corrections within the first 3 weeks
Build enough familiarity with the component library to self-serve answers without interrupting colleagues
Understand the reasoning behind the team's architectural decisions, not just the what but the why
Make a positive first impression that reflects their actual engineering ability rather than their onboarding friction
frustrations: Storybook is the official docs source but 30% of its content references components or prop names that no longer exist in those forms
Every question answered in Slack lives in chat history that disappears — there's no institutional memory of what was already explained
AI coding tools suggest solutions that look right but bypass the team's governed components, resulting in PR rejections that feel arbitrary until the pattern is explained
The gap between 'I know how to build this' and 'I know how to build this the way this team does' is invisible from the outside — Yuki can't see what they don't know
behaviors: Spends 30–60 minutes per unknown before asking for help — prefers to self-serve but often can't find the answer
Keeps a personal Notion doc of patterns they've learned, knowing this information isn't captured anywhere accessible
Looks for canonical usage examples in the codebase before reading docs, because examples are often more current
Checks the git blame on files they're editing to find who last modified them — then DMs that person directly rather than posting publicly
motivations: Proving that their technical ability is real and not masked by onboarding friction
Building a mental model of the codebase that lets them contribute without constant guidance
Establishing a reputation as a self-sufficient engineer who ships quality work without requiring hand-holding
Finding the shortest path from 'new hire' to 'trusted contributor'
personality: High standards for their own work
Quick learner once the mental model clicks

competitors.name: GitHub Copilot Chat
competitors.description: GitHub's general-purpose AI coding assistant. Excellent at general code generation and standard library knowledge. Has no awareness of the team's specific component library, architectural patterns, or naming conventions. Confidently suggests generic solutions that bypass governed components — the exact behavior that causes new engineers to ship structurally incorrect code.
competitors.targetMarket: All engineers — virtually universal adoption on teams using GitHub
painPoints: No awareness of team-specific component libraries
Suggests deprecated or non-existent patterns when asked about internal tools
Cannot distinguish between canonical and legacy implementations in the codebase
High false confidence — wrong answers look the same as right answers

competitors.name: Notion AI
competitors.description: AI layer on top of Notion workspace. Useful for searching and summarizing documentation stored in Notion. Not engineering-specific — cannot query a component library, cannot return code examples linked to actual source files, and cannot distinguish between current and stale documentation. The output is prose summaries, not actionable component references.
competitors.targetMarket: Teams using Notion as their primary documentation platform
painPoints: Summarizes docs but cannot point to code-level canonical examples
No awareness of component APIs, prop names, or usage constraints
Cannot distinguish between a current ADR and a superseded one
Docs-first, not code-first — misses the most authoritative source of truth

competitors.name: Storybook (as documentation)
competitors.description: The de facto standard for component library documentation. Excellent when up to date. In practice, Storybook documentation drifts significantly — components get renamed, deprecated, or updated without the stories being maintained. For new engineers, Storybook is a starting point, not a reliable answer. It also requires knowing what to search for — it can't respond to a natural language question about how to implement a pattern.
competitors.targetMarket: Frontend teams documenting their component libraries
painPoints: Static — can't answer 'how do I combine these components to implement this pattern?'
Documentation drift — stories go stale as components evolve
Search requires knowing the component name — can't discover the right component from a use-case description
No connection to canonical usage examples in the actual production codebase

competitors.name: Zeroheight
competitors.description: Design system documentation platform that aggregates component docs, design tokens, and usage guidelines. Better than Confluence for design system content, but the same fundamental limitation: it's a static documentation layer, not a queryable knowledge engine. Documentation still requires manual maintenance, still drifts, and still can't respond to natural language implementation questions.
competitors.targetMarket: Design system teams documenting for designers and engineers simultaneously
painPoints: Static documentation — can't answer implementation questions
Still requires manual maintenance to stay current
No awareness of how components are actually used in the production codebase
Primarily design-system-level, not codebase-level

competitors.name: Senior engineer tribal knowledge
competitors.description: The incumbent solution: asking a senior engineer in Slack or a 1:1. Perfectly accurate, context-aware, and able to explain reasoning — but scales to exactly one question at a time per available senior engineer. Onboarding velocity is directly capped by how many questions can be answered per day. Doesn't improve as the team grows — it degrades, because the ratio of new engineers to senior engineers answering questions gets worse with every hire.
features: Perfectly accurate for the engineer who answers
competitors.targetMarket: Every engineering team — universal baseline, but more painful as teams grow
painPoints: Doesn't scale — each answer requires a senior engineer's synchronous attention
Knowledge lives in chat history and disappears — same questions get answered repeatedly
Creates dependency and social friction — new engineers are reluctant to ask frequently
Answers vary by respondent — different senior engineers explain the same pattern differently

positioningAxes.xLabel: Library-specificity (Generic knowledge → Your team's exact component library and patterns)
positioningAxes.yLabel: Queryability (Static documentation → Natural language implementation Q&A)

items.label: Answers are library-specific, not generic
items.description: The answer must reference your team's actual component, not a generic React pattern — 'use DataTable at src/components/data/DataTable with the RoleVisibility prop' not 'you can use a table with conditional rendering'

items.label: Every answer cites its source
items.description: Engineers need to know where the answer came from — Storybook page URL, ADR number, canonical file path — so they can verify it and learn the reasoning

items.label: Natural language query — no need to know component names
items.description: A new engineer doesn't know if the component is called DataTable, DataGrid, or TableView. They describe what they need; OnboardIQ maps it to the right component

items.label: Zero-friction query surface (IDE + Slack)
items.description: The tool must live where engineers already work — VS Code extension and Slack bot — not require a context switch to a separate web app

items.label: High answer precision — no confident wrong answers
items.description: A wrong answer from OnboardIQ causes a PR rejection and breaks trust permanently. Precision over recall: better to say 'I don't know' than to confidently hallucinate

items.label: Surfaces implementation reasoning (the 'why')
items.description: New engineers don't just need the answer — they need the reasoning (ADR, design decision) so they can apply the pattern to adjacent cases

items.label: Documentation search (keyword-based)
items.description: Static keyword search over Storybook or Confluence — already solved by those tools' built-in search, though poorly

items.label: General code generation
items.description: Writing boilerplate code — already solved by Copilot and other AI tools, not a differentiation point

userFlow.persona: Yuki Tanaka — Mid-level Frontend Engineer, 2 weeks into onboarding
userFlow.goal: Get a correct, source-cited answer to 'How do I implement a data table with multi-role column visibility?' without interrupting a senior engineer
userFlow.entryPoint: Yuki is in VS Code, implementing the reports feature. They need to implement role-based column visibility and don't know the correct pattern. They trigger the OnboardIQ panel with Cmd+Shift+I.
userFlow.exitPoint: Yuki has the correct DataTable component, the RoleVisibility prop usage, a code snippet, and a link to the Storybook page and the relevant ADR. They close the panel and implement the pattern — which gets approved on first review.

steps.label: Trigger OnboardIQ in VS Code
steps.description: Yuki presses Cmd+Shift+I (or clicks the OnboardIQ icon in the activity bar). The OnboardIQ panel opens in the sidebar alongside their code. The query field is focused automatically.
steps.systemState: Panel open, context from the current file available (OnboardIQ reads the open file for context enrichment)

branches.condition: If OnboardIQ detects the file contains a table-related import
branches.outcome: Panel pre-populates a context hint: 'I see you're working with data display. Ask me about table patterns.'
Blank query field with placeholder: 'Ask about any component, pattern, or implementation in this library'

steps.friction: Keyboard shortcut must be discoverable — surface it in the onboarding welcome message and in the VS Code status bar
steps.errorPath: If the extension isn't installed, the welcome email and team onboarding doc should include the install link with a one-click setup

steps.description: Yuki types: 'How do I implement a data table with role-based column visibility?' and submits.

branches.outcome: Returns exact component + usage + source in < 3 seconds

branches.outcome: Returns clarifying question: 'Are you looking for (a) column-level role filtering or (b) row-level permission gating?'

steps.friction: Response latency must be < 3 seconds — anything longer breaks the inline flow and engineers will close the panel

branches.outcome: OnboardIQ logs a copy event — signals high-confidence answer acceptance

branches.condition: If Yuki clicks the Storybook link
branches.outcome: Counts as deep engagement — engineer wants context beyond the snippet

Shows follow-up: 'What was missing? (a) Wrong component (b) Missing context (c) Outdated pattern (d) Other' — one-click selection

experienceMap.overview: OnboardIQ's customer journey moves engineers from 'lost in undiscoverable institutional knowledge' — where velocity is capped by documentation quality and senior engineer availability — to 'self-sufficient library navigator', where the right component and pattern is one natural language query away.

phases.name: Pre-OnboardIQ: The Documentation Dead-End
touchpoints: Opens Storybook — finds multiple versions of the component
Greps codebase — finds 4 different pattern implementations
phases.experience: The information exists but is inaccessible in the form needed. New engineers spend 60–80% of their first 4 weeks in search mode: looking for the right component, the right usage, the right pattern. The search itself is exhausting and demoralizing because it doesn't feel like work.
phases.insights: Marketing OnboardIQ should quantify this cost: '3 days to find the right DataTable pattern without OnboardIQ. 2 hours with it.' The before/after is visceral.

phases.name: First Query: The 'Oh, That's What I Needed' Moment
touchpoints: Opens OnboardIQ panel in VS Code
Receives structured answer in < 3 seconds with component name, code snippet, and source links
phases.experience: The first query response is the most important product moment. If the answer is specific, correct, and source-cited, the engineer's reaction is immediate: 'This is what Storybook should have been.' The specificity — naming the exact component, showing the exact prop, citing the exact ADR — is what creates trust that generic AI tools never build.
phases.insights: Capture a screenshot or quote from this moment for marketing. 'I asked OnboardIQ what took me 3 days to figure out manually and got the answer in 8 seconds.' That's the testimonial that converts.

phases.name: Adoption: Building the Query Habit
touchpoints: Uses Cmd+Shift+I before Storybook for every new pattern
Uses /onboardiq in Slack when about to post a help question
Clicks Storybook links from OnboardIQ answers to verify and deepen understanding
phases.experience: Engineers who get 3 correct specific answers in their first week establish OnboardIQ as their first-line resource — before Storybook, before Slack. The query habit forms quickly because the answer quality is consistently higher and faster than alternatives. The Slack bot catches the moment of 'I'm about to ask a human' and intercepts it.
phases.insights: Track the shift from VS Code queries to Slack queries as the engineer's context evolves — VS Code queries = implementation questions, Slack queries = architecture questions. The ratio tells you where to improve the product.

phases.name: Self-Sufficiency: Query Volume Drops
touchpoints: Query volume peaks in week 2–3, drops significantly by week 5–6
Engineer starts recognizing component names and patterns without querying
Begins directing colleagues to OnboardIQ instead of answering their questions directly
phases.experience: The paradox of OnboardIQ's success is that its best customers use it less over time. A declining query volume per engineer signals that the mental model has been built — the tool has worked. Engineering leads should see this as the health metric, not worry about churn.
phases.insights: Declining query volume per engineer is the retention story: show engineering leads a chart of 'queries/week vs. weeks on team' showing the natural decline as engineers internalize the library. This is the proof that OnboardIQ actually builds knowledge, not dependency.

phases.name: Advocacy: Sharing OnboardIQ with the Next New Engineer
touchpoints: Answers a new engineer's Slack question with 'try OnboardIQ — query X'
Mentions OnboardIQ in their 30-day retrospective as a tool that changed their onboarding
Asks the DevX team to add OnboardIQ to the day 1 onboarding checklist
phases.experience: Engineers who had a transformative OnboardIQ moment become the most effective advocates — and the most credible ones, because they lived the before/after. The advocacy cycle is: saved time → told colleagues → colleagues onboarded faster → more engineers using OnboardIQ → more feedback → better answers.
phases.insights: The referral loop is organic if the tool works. Capture it with a prompt at the 30-day mark: 'Has OnboardIQ changed how you navigate the codebase? Share your experience with your team lead.'

serviceBlueprint.overview: OnboardIQ delivers library-specific architectural knowledge as infrastructure — automated ingestion of the component library, a queryable RAG engine, and a zero-friction query surface in the tools engineers already use — VS Code and Slack.

steps.name: Library Ingestion
steps.customerAction: Engineering lead or DevX team runs the OnboardIQ CLI: `onboardiq index --source storybook --url [storybook-url] --repo [github-repo]`
steps.frontstage: CLI progress output showing components indexed, patterns extracted, source links verified. Completion message: '143 components indexed, 89 usage patterns extracted, 14 ADRs linked.'
steps.backstage: Crawler fetches Storybook stories, component prop definitions, usage examples from the codebase. Builds a structured knowledge graph: component → variants → props → canonical usage locations → linked docs and ADRs. Generates embeddings for semantic search.
steps.support: Storybook API, GitHub API (for codebase crawl), embedding model, vector database (Pinecone or Weaviate), knowledge graph database
steps.evidence: Slack notification to DevX channel: 'OnboardIQ index complete. 143 components ready. Run `onboardiq test` to validate answer quality on sample queries.'

steps.name: Query Resolution
steps.customerAction: Engineer types a natural language question in the VS Code panel or Slack bot: 'How do I implement a data table with role-based column visibility?'
steps.frontstage: Structured answer returned in < 3 seconds: (1) exact component and import path, (2) code snippet with correct prop usage, (3) Storybook story link, (4) ADR or design rationale link if available
steps.backstage: Query is embedded and run against the vector store for semantic similarity. Top K results are re-ranked by freshness (last codebase update timestamp) and usage frequency (how often the component appears in canonical implementations). LLM generates a structured answer grounded in the retrieved context. Response is returned with source citations baked in.
steps.support: Embedding model, vector database, reranking model, LLM (Claude claude-sonnet-4-6 or equivalent), caching layer for repeated queries
steps.evidence: Answer card in VS Code panel or Slack thread — component name, code snippet, source links. Response timestamp shows < 3 seconds.

steps.name: Feedback Collection
steps.customerAction: Engineer clicks thumbs up or thumbs down on the answer. Thumbs down triggers a one-click follow-up: 'What was missing? (a) Wrong component (b) Missing context (c) Outdated pattern'
steps.frontstage: Single-click feedback prompt below each answer. Confirmation: 'Thanks — this helps improve future answers.'
steps.backstage: Feedback event logged with query text, answer text, and rating. Negative feedback triggers a review queue for the DevX lead. Positive signals reinforce the retrieval ranking for that query type. Weekly retraining job updates retrieval weights based on accumulated feedback.
steps.support: Feedback event store, review queue dashboard, weekly retrieval retraining pipeline
steps.evidence: DevX lead receives weekly email: 'OnboardIQ feedback this week: 94% positive (186 queries). 11 thumbs down — review queue has 11 items.'

steps.name: Library Update Sync
steps.customerAction: Component library is updated — new component added, prop renamed, pattern deprecated. DevX lead pushes an update: `onboardiq sync --changed-since [date]`
steps.frontstage: CLI output showing what changed: 'DataTable v3 added. DataTable v2 marked deprecated. 4 affected usage patterns updated.'
steps.backstage: Incremental re-crawl of changed components and files. Updated entries replace previous embeddings. Deprecated components flagged with a 'DEPRECATED — use X instead' annotation that appears in any answer referencing them.
steps.support: GitHub webhook (triggers sync on component library PR merge), incremental embedding update pipeline
steps.evidence: OnboardIQ answers referencing the updated component immediately reflect the change — no manual cache clear required.

steps.name: Engineering Lead Analytics
steps.customerAction: Engineering lead opens the OnboardIQ dashboard to review onboarding velocity for the latest hire cohort
steps.frontstage: Dashboard shows: (1) queries per engineer per week (by cohort), (2) answer quality score over time, (3) most-asked questions (documentation gap report), (4) time-to-first-PR trend by cohort (with vs. without OnboardIQ)
steps.backstage: Aggregation pipeline computes cohort metrics. Most-asked questions are ranked and annotated with 'this question has no good Storybook answer' or 'this ADR is missing' to surface documentation debt.
steps.support: Query analytics database, cohort tracking, PR timeline data from GitHub API
steps.evidence: Monthly email to engineering lead: 'OnboardIQ cohort report — Aug 2026. Avg time-to-first-PR: 3.2 days (vs. 8.7 days for pre-OnboardIQ cohort). Most-asked unanswered: form validation in admin context (no ADR linked).'

storyboard.scenario: Yuki is 10 days into their new role. They've been given their first real feature: a reports table with role-based column visibility. They've been stuck for 3 days. The documentation is a maze and asking for help feels like admitting defeat. This is the week they find OnboardIQ.
storyboard.persona: Yuki Tanaka — Mid-level Frontend Engineer, Series B fintech, 10 days in

frames.description: Day 10, 9:30am. Yuki opens Storybook for the fourth time this week. Searches 'DataTable'. Three results: DataTable (deprecated tag), DataTable v2, DataGrid. Clicks DataTable v2 — no mention of role-based columns anywhere in the story. Closes Storybook with a sigh.
frames.dialogue: 'Which one is even current? Why are there three of them? This shouldn't take this long.'

frames.description: Day 10, 11am. Yuki greps for 'DataTable' across the codebase. 11 files. Each uses a slightly different prop pattern. Picks the file that looks most recent — copies the implementation. The copied pattern uses a local role check instead of usePermission.
frames.dialogue: 'This looks right. Similar enough. I'll just use this.'

frames.description: Day 11. PR submitted. First review comment arrives: 'Hey Yuki — we use usePermission from the auth module for role checks, not inline comparisons. This is a pattern we enforced last quarter. See ADR-014.' Yuki stares at the comment. They had no way of knowing this.
frames.dialogue: 'I had no idea this even existed. How was I supposed to find this?'

frames.description: Day 12. Yuki mentions the PR comment to their DevX onboarding buddy in a 1:1. The buddy pauses: 'Oh — did we not set you up with OnboardIQ? It's a tool we're piloting. Open VS Code, hit Cmd+Shift+I, and just ask it your original question.'
frames.dialogue: 'Ask it... like, in English? Like I'd ask a person?'

frames.description: Yuki types into the OnboardIQ panel: 'How do I implement a data table with role-based column visibility?' 8 seconds later: 'Use DataTable at src/components/data/DataTable with the RoleVisibility prop, integrated with usePermission from src/auth/usePermission. See usage example: src/features/reporting/ReportView.tsx:34. Storybook: [link]. ADR-014: [link].'
frames.dialogue: 'This is... exactly what I needed. This is the answer I was looking for for three days.'

frames.description: Yuki clicks the ADR link. Reads the 3-paragraph explanation of why the auth module boundary was designed the way it was — the incident that caused the change, the decision made, the pattern that followed. Implements the corrected PR in 40 minutes. It gets approved with no structural comments.
frames.dialogue: 'I actually understand why now, not just what. I won't make this mistake again.'

frames.description: Week 5. Yuki's query volume has dropped from 15 queries/week to 4. They answer a new hire's Slack question: 'For form validation in admin context — don't search the docs, just ask OnboardIQ. Query: validation pattern for admin forms.' The new hire gets their answer in 12 seconds.
frames.dialogue: 'This is what I wish someone had told me on day one.'

informationArchitecture.overview: Two primary users: new engineers (who query) and engineering/DevX leads (who configure, monitor, and tune). The query experience must be zero-friction — in the IDE and Slack. The admin experience must surface doc gaps and velocity metrics that justify the tool's existence.

nodes.label: VS Code Panel
nodes.description: In-editor query panel. Cmd+Shift+I to open. Shows query input, answer card with component name, code snippet, source links, and feedback prompt.

nodes.label: Slack Bot
nodes.description: /onboardiq [question] slash command. Returns formatted answer in-thread with component, snippet, Storybook link, ADR link.

nodes.label: Web Interface
