projects.name: GuardRail AI: Structural Debt Scanner

hypothesis.problem: AI coding assistants produce code that is functionally correct and passes every linter — but violates your architecture. A component exists; it was rebuilt anyway. A pattern is established; it was ignored. A boundary was crossed that shouldn't be. Standard linters are architecture-agnostic: they enforce syntax and style, not your specific composition rules, import boundaries, or component hierarchy. The only tool that catches structural drift today is a senior engineer in code review — who is now reviewing three times more PRs because AI has accelerated output without raising the structural IQ of the code it writes. 'Vibe-coded' PRs accumulate silently as structural debt until a refactor, a performance incident, or a new engineer's onboarding makes the inconsistency expensive.
hypothesis.solution: GuardRail AI — an AI agent that learns your codebase's architecture, component patterns, and composition guidelines from your existing source, then runs as an automated gatekeeper on every PR before merge. It reviews each PR against your actual architecture (not generic best practices), identifies structural debt hotspots, suggests specific refactors aligned to your patterns, and can block merges on high-severity violations. It reads and enforces what your most senior engineers know but never had time to codify into a linter.
hypothesis.hook: Your AI is shipping. Your architecture is dying. GuardRail makes sure they survive each other.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Teams without an established architecture or component library — GuardRail has nothing to enforce. Solo developers or very early startups where architectural consistency is not yet a constraint. Organizations where 'it runs and tests pass' is genuinely the quality bar. Teams already running extensive Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) and automated ArchUnit-style tests — they've solved the problem with process.

segments.name: Engineering leads, staff engineers, and platform/DevX teams
segments.description: Engineering leads, staff engineers, and platform/DevX teams at companies with 20–300 engineers who have adopted AI coding tools (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code) and are beginning to see the downstream effects: PRs that pass review but violate architectural patterns, components rebuilt instead of reused, module boundaries crossed in subtle ways that only surface during refactors or incidents.
segments.painPoint: AI coding assistants produce code that is functionally correct and passes every linter — but violates your architecture. A component exists; it was rebuilt anyway. A pattern is established; it was ignored. A boundary was crossed that shouldn't be. Standard linters are architecture-agnostic: they enforce syntax and style, not your specific composition rules, import boundaries, or component hierarchy. The only tool that catches structural drift today is a senior engineer in code review — who is now reviewing three times more PRs because AI has accelerated output without raising the structural IQ of the code it writes. 'Vibe-coded' PRs accumulate silently as structural debt until a refactor, a performance incident, or a new engineer's onboarding makes the inconsistency expensive.
segments.resolution: GuardRail AI — an AI agent that learns your codebase's architecture, component patterns, and composition guidelines from your existing source, then runs as an automated gatekeeper on every PR before merge. It reviews each PR against your actual architecture (not generic best practices), identifies structural debt hotspots, suggests specific refactors aligned to your patterns, and can block merges on high-severity violations. It reads and enforces what your most senior engineers know but never had time to codify into a linter.

advantage.capability: GuardRail can be built as a GitHub App that integrates into the PR review flow with no changes to developer workflow. The core intelligence is a fine-tuned or RAG-augmented model that ingests the team's existing codebase, extracts structural patterns (import graphs, component hierarchies, naming conventions, composition rules), and uses these as the evaluation criteria for each incoming diff. Unlike linters, the rules are derived from the codebase itself — not written by a human — which means they stay current as the architecture evolves.
advantage.motivation: The cost of structural debt is non-linear: it's nearly invisible when it accumulates but exponentially expensive when it surfaces. A staff engineer spending 30% of review time on AI-generated PRs at a 50-engineer company is burning $150K/year in engineering time on pattern-enforcement that could be automated. The problem is accelerating — AI coding tool adoption doubled year-over-year in 2024 and is still climbing, meaning the volume of structurally inconsistent PRs is growing faster than the reviewer bandwidth to catch them.
advantage.insight: The reason standard linters fail here is not a data problem — it's a context problem. ESLint knows nothing about your architecture. GuardRail's insight is that the architecture already lives in your codebase: in the patterns of how components are composed, in the import graph, in the naming conventions, in which abstractions are used where. The architecture just needs to be extracted and made queryable. This is a RAG problem, not a rules-writing problem — and that means the enforcement is automatic and self-updating.

principles: Enforce architecture, not aesthetics — flag structural violations, not style preferences that linters already handle
No false-positive fatigue — precision over recall; a GuardRail comment must always be actionable and accurate
Self-updating rules — the enforcement model should learn from merged code, not require manual rule maintenance
Zero workflow disruption — run in CI as a non-blocking reviewer by default; escalate to blocking only when explicitly configured
Explainability over black box — every flag must cite the pattern it violates and the location in the codebase where the correct pattern lives

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Engineering leads will trust GuardRail's structural violation flags enough to act on them without a senior engineer's second opinion — because if engineers override or ignore GuardRail comments at the same rate they'd ignore a bot, the tool adds ceremony without reducing debt.
clickTest.testMethod: Shadow-run GuardRail on 4 weeks of merged PRs for 3 pilot teams. Present the flagged violations to each team's senior engineer who reviewed those PRs and ask: 'Would you have flagged this? Is the suggested refactor correct?' Measure agreement rate. Separately, measure how often GuardRail flags something the senior engineer missed.
clickTest.successMetric: Senior engineer agreement rate above 85% on flagged violations. GuardRail catches at least 1 structural violation per week that the human reviewer missed. Zero instances of GuardRail blocking a structurally sound PR (0% false-positive block rate on the pilot teams).

milestones: M1 — Architecture ingestion: CLI tool that scans a repository, builds an import graph, extracts component composition patterns, and outputs a structured architecture manifest. Validates that the manifest accurately represents how the codebase is actually structured (2 weeks)

M2 — Diff analyzer: Given a PR diff and an architecture manifest, identify structural violations — wrong import source, component reimplemented instead of reused, abstraction boundary crossed, naming convention violated. Runs locally before GitHub integration (4 weeks)
M3 — GitHub App: PR review bot that runs M1+M2 on every PR, posts inline comments on violations with refactor suggestions, and reports a summary check. Non-blocking by default (7 weeks)
M4 — Accuracy tuning: Fine-tune the model on a labeled dataset of flagged vs. valid structural patterns from 5 pilot companies. Target: 85%+ precision on structural violation detection (10 weeks)

M5 — Blocking mode + severity tiers: Allow teams to configure which violation categories block merge vs. warn. Add severity scoring (critical / major / minor) based on blast radius and architectural centrality (12 weeks)

M6 — Architecture drift dashboard: Weekly email report showing structural debt trends over time — new violations introduced, violations resolved, components most frequently re-implemented, and teams with highest structural debt density (16 weeks)
blockers: Precision is existential: a single high-profile false positive (GuardRail blocking a valid PR) that slips through will destroy trust with an engineering team. The model must be conservative by default and tuned aggressively on real codebases before enabling blocking mode

Architecture extraction quality varies widely by codebase — a well-structured monorepo gives GuardRail rich signal, while a legacy codebase with inconsistent patterns gives it noise. Need to define a minimum architecture quality threshold for onboarding

GitHub App security review can take 2-4 weeks if the app requests code read access at org level. Plan for this in the M3 timeline and consider a self-hosted option for enterprise security-conscious customers
blueprint.timelineNotes: M1-M2 in 4 weeks can be validated entirely locally without GitHub integration — this is the fastest path to showing a pilot customer a working violation detector on their own codebase. Do not build the GitHub App until at least 2 pilot customers have validated the diff analyzer's accuracy on their PRs. M4 (accuracy tuning) is the make-or-break milestone — ship M3 first, collect real violation data, then tune.

sources.title: GuardRail AI product brief
sources.content: Target Pain Point: Unmaintainable, 'vibe-coded' AI-generated code. Functionality: Unlike a standard linter, this specialized AI agent evaluates code against your specific component architecture guidelines. It identifies 'structural debt' hotspots — areas where code is functional but inconsistent or poorly composed — and suggests refactors. It acts as an automated governance gatekeeper that reviews AI-generated PRs before they are merged, ensuring the code remains production-ready rather than just 'it runs'.

journey.persona: Priya Venkataraman, Staff Engineer / Tech Lead
journey.goal: Prevent structurally inconsistent AI-generated PRs from merging without burning her own review time to catch every one

stages.name: The Slow Burn
steps: Team adopts GitHub Copilot — PR velocity increases 40% within 8 weeks
Priya notices the same structural mistakes appearing repeatedly: wrong import paths, rebuilt components, violated boundaries
She adds an 'architecture-review' label and begins personally reviewing all AI-assisted PRs
painPoints: No automated way to detect structural violations — relies entirely on human pattern recognition
PR volume has increased faster than review capacity
opportunities: GuardRail could be introduced at adoption time — 'AI coding tool + GuardRail' as a bundle
Early onboarding: connect to the repo before the debt accumulates

stages.name: The Incident
steps: An AI-generated PR rebuilds a core auth abstraction in a way that bypasses the permission model
It passes tests, passes ESLint, gets merged on a Friday afternoon
A production incident 9 days later traces back to the structural violation
Post-mortem action item: 'improve code review process for AI-generated code'
painPoints: No tool exists that would have caught 'this bypasses the permission model' as a structural violation
The post-mortem generates process debt (more manual steps) rather than tooling solutions
opportunities: GuardRail's highest-value pitch is to engineering leads who have just had this conversation
The incident provides quantified cost of structural debt — exactly what GuardRail's dashboard surfaces proactively

stages.name: Tool Discovery
steps: Priya searches for 'architecture linting AI', 'PR governance AI', 'structural debt scanner'
Finds GuardRail via Engineering Enablement Slack community or a referral from another staff engineer
Reads the post on how GuardRail scans the existing codebase to derive architecture rules — no manual rule-writing
painPoints: Skeptical of AI code review tools after experiencing CodeRabbit's false positives
Concerned about the security implications of a third-party tool with repo read access
opportunities: The 'no manual rule writing' angle is the key differentiator — lead with this in marketing
Offer a self-hosted option or SOC2 certification to address enterprise security concerns

stages.name: Shadow-Run Trial
steps: GuardRail shadow-runs on 4 weeks of already-merged PRs — no blocking, just analysis
Priya receives a report: '23 structural violations in the last month. 8 component re-implementations. 4 boundary violations. 11 pattern inconsistencies.'
She validates 20 of the 23 flags herself — 87% precision
Shows the report to her engineering manager: 'This is the cost of unreviewed AI output'
painPoints: Needs to validate precision before enabling blocking mode — shadow run is essential
Getting budget approval requires showing the cost of the status quo, not just the value of the tool
opportunities: The shadow-run report is the sales artifact — it converts by showing the customer their own debt
87% precision builds trust faster than any demo

stages.name: Live Gating
steps: GuardRail enabled in warning mode on all PRs — inline comments but no blocking
Two weeks later: switched to blocking mode on critical-severity violations (boundary violations, component re-implementations)
PR cycle time increases by 8 minutes on average — engineers fix violations before requesting review
Priya's architecture-review time drops from 35% to 12% of her week within the first month
painPoints: Some engineers push back on GuardRail blocking their PRs — need clear escalation path for disagreements
False positives at the margin still require Priya's judgment to override
opportunities: The 'Priya's review time: 35% → 12%' is the retention metric — track it and surface it in the product
Override workflow is a product feature: 'senior engineer override' creates an audit trail of intentional exceptions

says: 'We've been using Copilot for 6 months and the PRs are faster but code review is taking longer because I can't trust the structure.'
'Junior engineers using AI are shipping code that works but breaks every pattern we've established. It runs, it tests, it merges — and then three months later it's a nightmare to change.'
'I reviewed a PR last week where someone rebuilt our DataTable component from scratch because the AI suggested it. The existing one was right there.'
'We need architecture linting. ESLint isn't enough — it doesn't know that you shouldn't import directly from the auth module outside the auth boundary.'
thinks: 'If AI is writing 40% of our code, and that code doesn't follow our architecture, we're accruing debt 40% faster than before AI existed.'
'I can't write a linter rule for every architectural decision we've made over 4 years. There are hundreds of implicit patterns that senior engineers just know.'
'The next incident is going to be caused by an AI-generated PR that nobody noticed was structurally wrong. It runs. It passes tests. It's silently broken.'
'I'm the bottleneck. Every structural violation that slips through is either caught by me in review — burning 30% of my week — or it becomes tech debt I deal with later.'
does: Adds 'architecture review' as a PR label and tries to personally review AI-generated PRs before merge — doesn't scale
Writes custom ESLint rules to enforce import boundaries and naming conventions — covers maybe 20% of the actual architecture
Creates architecture docs in Confluence/Notion that AI coding tools don't read and new engineers don't find until it's too late
Runs a weekly 'architecture sync' meeting where structural debt is discussed but rarely resolved due to feature pressure
feels: Anxious about the rate at which AI-accelerated output is outpacing the team's ability to maintain structural quality
Frustrated that the same architectural mistakes keep appearing in AI-generated PRs despite being documented and discussed
Overwhelmed by the volume of PRs requiring structural review — the review queue is longer than ever despite (or because of) AI tooling
Resigned to the idea that some structural debt is inevitable given the pace of AI-assisted development
pains: Standard linters enforce syntax and style but have no concept of your architecture — they can't know that you have an existing EmptyState component that should be reused
AI coding tools are trained on generic patterns, not your codebase's specific composition rules and module boundaries
Senior engineers are the only humans who catch structural violations, but their review bandwidth hasn't scaled with AI-accelerated PR volume
Architectural drift is invisible until it's expensive — it shows up in refactor costs and incident post-mortems, not in green CI checks
gains: An automated reviewer that catches structural violations before merge — not after they've been deployed and are expensive to unwind
Architecture rules derived from the codebase itself, not written by hand — self-updating as the architecture evolves
A quantified view of structural debt trends over time — finally able to show leadership that 'vibe-coded' AI output has a measurable cost
Senior engineers freed from pattern-enforcement review so they can focus on the design decisions that actually require human judgment

persona.name: Priya Venkataraman
persona.role: Staff Engineer / Tech Lead at a Series B SaaS company (85 engineers, 7-person platform team)
persona.quote: 'The PRs are coming in 40% faster since we rolled out Copilot. My review queue is 3x what it was. And half of what I'm reviewing is me explaining why we already have an abstraction for this.'
persona.bio: Priya has been a staff engineer for 3 years at a fast-growing B2B SaaS company. She architected the current frontend component system, the service boundary model, and most of the import conventions the team follows. She's a strong writer — most of the architecture docs exist because she wrote them. She's now spending 35% of her time on code review, up from 12% before the team adopted AI coding tools. She's watching the codebase she designed drift in ways that ESLint can't catch and docs can't prevent.
goals: Keep the codebase's architecture consistent as the team grows and AI coding tools accelerate output
Free her review time for decisions that require architectural judgment, not pattern enforcement
Quantify structural debt so she can make the case to leadership for investment in code quality tooling
Ensure new engineers (and AI tools) can't inadvertently violate architectural boundaries they don't know exist
frustrations: AI tools produce functionally correct code that violates structural patterns — and the violations are subtle enough to slip past tired reviewers
Custom ESLint rules cover import boundaries but can't enforce composition rules, abstraction reuse, or naming conventions that exist in practice but not in config
Architecture docs go stale immediately and AI tools don't read them anyway
The only reliable enforcement mechanism is Priya herself — which means she's both the architect and the quality gatekeeper at 3x the PR volume
behaviors: Personally reviews all PRs labeled 'AI-assisted' or touching core architectural modules before merge
Writes architecture review checklists that get ignored under feature pressure
Runs quarterly 'structural debt sprints' where the team refactors the worst violations from the previous quarter
Maintains a private list of components that have been re-implemented by AI-generated PRs — currently at 11 duplicates
motivations: Protecting the architecture she designed from drift she can't prevent at current scale
Reducing the review burden so she can contribute to product features again
Making the implicit architecture explicit and enforceable without having to write every rule by hand
Demonstrating to leadership that code quality has a measurable ROI — not just a 'nice to have'

competitors.name: ESLint + custom rules
competitors.description: The dominant JavaScript/TypeScript linter. Highly configurable with custom rules, plugins, and shareable configs. competitors.targetMarket: All JavaScript/TypeScript teams — virtually universal adoption
painPoints: Rules are static and architecture-agnostic
Cannot detect that a component was rebuilt instead of reused

competitors.name: SonarQube / SonarCloud
competitors.description: Widely adopted code quality platform with static analysis, code smells, duplication detection, and security scanning. painPoints: Generic quality rules, not architecture-specific

No concept of component reuse or composition patterns

competitors.name: Trunk.io
competitors.description: Developer experience platform that manages and runs linters, formatters, and static analysis tools in a unified CI check. painPoints: Orchestration layer, not analysis intelligence

storyboard.scenario: Priya is 3 months into her team's Copilot rollout. PR velocity is up. Her review queue is full. A critical incident last week traced back to an AI-generated PR that bypassed the auth boundary. This is the week she finds GuardRail.
storyboard.persona: Priya Venkataraman — Staff Engineer / Tech Lead, Series B SaaS, San Francisco

frames.description: Monday morning. Priya opens Linear and sees her review queue: 18 PRs waiting. Half are tagged 'AI-assisted'. Her calendar shows 4 hours blocked for code review. She opens the first PR — an AI-generated auth middleware — and immediately spots a boundary violation.
frames.dialogue: This is the third time someone's reimplemented the permission check instead of using the hook we built. The AI doesn't know our architecture. Neither does ESLint.

frames.description: Post-mortem meeting for last week's incident. Root cause: AI-generated PR bypassed the auth abstraction. The action item on the board reads: 'Improve governance of AI-generated PRs.' Everyone nods. Nobody has a concrete tool in mind.
frames.dialogue: This is a process problem and a tooling problem. We need something that understands our architecture — not just our syntax.

frames.description: Priya searches 'architecture linting AI' and 'PR governance for AI code'. She finds GuardRail through a post in the Engineering Enablement Slack community: 'We ran it on our repo and it flagged 31 violations we'd already merged — with 89% accuracy.' She clicks through.
frames.dialogue: No manual rule writing. It learns from your codebase. That's exactly what I need.

frames.description: Priya installs the GuardRail GitHub App, connects it to their main frontend repo. 20 minutes later: the shadow analysis report lands in her inbox. '27 structural violations in the last 30 days. 9 component re-implementations. 5 boundary violations. 13 pattern inconsistencies.'
frames.dialogue: Five boundary violations. In one month. And I only caught two of them in review.

frames.description: Priya walks her engineering manager through the shadow report. Total structural debt: 27 violations, estimated 40+ hours of future refactor work. She shows the cost of the auth incident. GuardRail budget approved in the same meeting.
frames.dialogue: The shadow report was the entire sales pitch. I didn't have to argue for the tool — the data argued for itself.

frames.description: GuardRail is live in warning mode. A Copilot-assisted PR opens — the engineer accidentally reimplemented a DataTable component. GuardRail posts an inline comment within 90 seconds: 'Structural violation (Major): Use existing DataTable at src/components/data/DataTable. See usage at src/features/reports/ReportView.tsx:34.' Engineer applies the fix before Priya sees the PR.
frames.dialogue: It cited the exact file. Not just 'a component exists' — the file, the line, an example. The engineer fixed it themselves.

frames.description: Four weeks later. Priya's architecture-review time: 12% of her week, down from 35%. Structural violations per week: 3, down from 8. The engineering manager asks for the monthly report — Priya shows a chart of 'violations detected vs. merged' trending sharply in the right direction.
frames.dialogue: I'm designing features again. That's what I should be doing.

projects.name: Unified Component Registry

hypothesis.problem: When an engineer needs a UI pattern, they have no fast way to know whether a production-ready component already exists, who owns it, whether it handles all required states (loading, error, empty, partial, permission-denied), or whether it is actively maintained. The result is the 'archaeology' phase: searching Storybook, Slack, GitHub, and Figma separately before concluding — wrongly — that the component doesn't exist and rebuilding it from scratch. The 'ownership vacuum' compounds this: components exist but nobody is accountable, so they drift out of spec, break quietly, and accumulate technical debt.
hypothesis.solution: A centralized component registry dashboard that serves as the single source of truth for every governed UI component in the codebase. CatalogX surfaces each component with: named ownership status (or a flagged vacuum), a production state coverage score across loading / error / empty / partial / permission-denied, recent usage analytics showing which teams are consuming it, and direct deep-links to Storybook, Figma, and source. Engineers search once and know immediately whether to use, adapt, or build.
hypothesis.hook: Stop rebuilding what already exists. Find it, own it, ship it.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Solo developers or small teams (under 10 engineers) with no shared component library. Teams whose entire component system lives in a single file with no governance model. Organizations already fully committed to a vendor-locked design system platform (e.g. Salesforce Lightning) that surfaces this natively.

segments.name: Frontend engineers, design systems leads, and engineering ma
segments.description: Frontend engineers, design systems leads, and engineering managers at mid-to-large product companies (50–500+ engineers) who maintain a component library but lose hours every sprint to duplication, ownership confusion, and production-readiness uncertainty.
segments.painPoint: When an engineer needs a UI pattern, they have no fast way to know whether a production-ready component already exists, who owns it, whether it handles all required states (loading, error, empty, partial, permission-denied), or whether it is actively maintained. The result is the 'archaeology' phase: searching Storybook, Slack, GitHub, and Figma separately before concluding — wrongly — that the component doesn't exist and rebuilding it from scratch. The 'ownership vacuum' compounds this: components exist but nobody is accountable, so they drift out of spec, break quietly, and accumulate technical debt.
segments.resolution: A centralized component registry dashboard that serves as the single source of truth for every governed UI component in the codebase. CatalogX surfaces each component with: named ownership status (or a flagged vacuum), a production state coverage score across loading / error / empty / partial / permission-denied, recent usage analytics showing which teams are consuming it, and direct deep-links to Storybook, Figma, and source. Engineers search once and know immediately whether to use, adapt, or build.

advantage.capability: CatalogX can be built as a thin metadata layer over existing infrastructure — Storybook, Figma, GitHub, and npm — without requiring teams to migrate their tooling. The registry ingests data from these systems via APIs and webhooks, meaning the source of truth stays where engineers already work. The production state coverage score is the core proprietary signal: no existing tool surfaces this automatically.
advantage.motivation: Every hour an engineer spends on archaeology or rebuilding a duplicate component is an hour not spent on product. At 50 engineers rebuilding one medium-complexity component per sprint, the annual waste exceeds $300K in engineering time. The ownership vacuum creates a compounding problem: ungoverned components become liabilities that slow every team that touches them.
advantage.insight: The bottleneck isn't component creation — it's component discovery and trust. Engineers don't reuse existing components because they can't quickly verify that the component handles their specific edge case and won't break when their PM adds a permission-gated feature next sprint. The production state coverage score solves the trust problem; the ownership field solves the accountability problem. Together they make reuse the path of least resistance.

principles: Discovery before creation — make finding a component faster than building one
Trust is earned, not assumed — every component must prove its production state coverage
Ownership is non-negotiable — every component has a named owner or is flagged as a vacuum
Zero migration cost — work with existing Storybook, Figma, and GitHub setups
Analytics over anecdote — usage data replaces 'I think this is used' guesswork

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Engineers will trust CatalogX's production state coverage score enough to use an unfamiliar component without verifying it manually in source code — because if they still feel the need to open GitHub to verify, the tool hasn't solved the archaeology problem.
clickTest.testMethod: Give 8 frontend engineers a task: 'Find a component for a permission-denied empty state and use it in a PR.' Half get Storybook only, half get CatalogX. Measure time-to-decision and whether the chosen component was actually production-ready.
clickTest.successMetric: CatalogX users pick a production-ready component in under 3 minutes with no GitHub archaeology. Storybook-only users average 12+ minutes or build their own. At least 6 of 8 CatalogX users say they would use the tool daily.

milestones: M1 — Registry MVP: manual component entry with owner, state coverage checklist, and Storybook/Figma/GitHub links. Ship as an internal tool for one design systems team (2 weeks)
M2 — Automated ingestion: GitHub Action that scans component files and auto-populates registry entries; Storybook sync that pulls story titles and status (4 weeks)

M3 — Production state coverage scoring: static analysis of component source to detect which states (loading, error, empty, partial, permission-denied) are handled; surfaces a coverage score per component (7 weeks)
M4 — Usage analytics: npm download tracking per component, import frequency from codebase scanning, and team-level attribution showing who consumes what (10 weeks)
M5 — Ownership vacuum detection: automated alerts when a component has no named owner, usage spikes with no owner response, or hasn't been updated in 90+ days (12 weeks)
M6 — Public launch: Figma Community plugin + npm package for self-hosted teams; SaaS offering for teams that want hosted infrastructure (16 weeks)
blockers: Production state coverage scoring via static analysis is technically non-trivial — detecting whether a component handles an error state requires understanding component prop contracts and render branches, not just string matching
GitHub/npm ingestion requires OAuth scopes that some enterprise security teams will block — need a self-hosted option from day one
Ownership definition varies by org: some use CODEOWNERS, some use Slack aliases, some have no system at all — the registry must be flexible enough to support all three without forcing a migration
blueprint.timelineNotes: M1-M2 in 4 weeks validates the core discovery and trust hypothesis before building any automated scoring. Do not build M3 until at least 2 teams are using M1-M2 actively. Full 16-week build assumes one full-stack engineer. Static analysis engine (M3) is the highest-risk milestone — time-box to 3 weeks and descope to manual coverage entry if blocked.

sources.title: CatalogX product brief
sources.content: Target Pain Point: Reusability bottlenecks and the 'ownership vacuum'. Functionality: A centralized dashboard that acts as the single source of truth for all governed UI components. It doesn't just show the component; it displays metadata including ownership status, production state coverage (loading, error, empty, partial, permission-denied), and recent usage analytics. This eliminates the 'archaeology' phase of onboarding, as engineers can search for pre-built, production-ready solutions rather than rebuilding patterns.

journey.goal: Find and confidently use an existing empty-state component for a permission-denied scenario without building from scratch

stages.name: Task Trigger
steps: PM adds a ticket: 'Handle permission-denied empty state on the dashboard'
Devon opens Storybook and searches 'empty state'
Returns 12 results — no indication of which handle permission-denied
painPoints: Storybook search returns component names, not state coverage
No way to filter by state type without opening each component
opportunities: CatalogX search returns components tagged with 'permission-denied' coverage immediately
State coverage badges visible in the search results list — no click-through needed

stages.name: Archaeology Phase
steps: Devon opens 4 candidate components in Storybook to check for permission-denied story
Only one has it — but it looks abandoned (last updated 14 months ago)
Searches GitHub for the component to find the owner via CODEOWNERS
CODEOWNERS points to a team alias that no longer exists
painPoints: State coverage is invisible without opening source or stories individually
Ownership vacuum means no path to verify maintenance status
No signal for when the component was last actively maintained vs. updated by a bot
opportunities: CatalogX surfaces last-human-commit date separately from last-update date
Vacuum flag shown inline on search result — instant signal to avoid or adopt
Usage analytics show whether other teams are actively importing this component this month

stages.name: Slack Archaeology
steps: Devon posts in #design-systems: 'Does a maintained empty state component with permission-denied exist?'
Waits 40 minutes for a response
Gets two conflicting answers pointing to different components
painPoints: Institutional knowledge lives in Slack and in specific engineers' heads
Conflicting answers with no authoritative source to resolve them
40 minutes of blocked time while waiting for a response
opportunities: CatalogX is the authoritative answer — no Slack archaeology needed
Surface the 'last asked about in Slack' signal as a trust indicator

stages.name: Decision Point
steps: Devon decides the existing component is too risky to adopt without an owner
Opens a blank file and starts building a new empty state component from scratch
Spends 3 hours implementing what already exists
painPoints: The safer decision (build from scratch) takes longer and creates more debt
No way to adopt an existing component and simultaneously flag it for ownership
opportunities: CatalogX allows one-click adoption registration: 'I am using this component' — creates accountability and alerts the owner
Vacuum adoption path: claim ownership temporarily while a proper owner is designated

stages.name: Discovery via CatalogX
steps: Devon searches CatalogX for 'permission-denied'
One result: EmptyState component with a 5/5 state coverage score including permission-denied
Owner: @sara.kim — last active 3 days ago. 7 teams importing this month.
Clicks through to Storybook, confirms the story, uses the component in 15 minutes
painPoints: First time using a component without reading source code — still slightly anxious about edge cases
opportunities: Post-adoption feedback loop: 'Did this component work for your use case?' surfaced after PR merge
Coverage score breakdown visible on click — shows exactly which states are tested

experienceMap.overview: The CatalogX customer moves from defensive duplication — rebuilding components because discovery and trust are broken — to systematic reuse, where finding and confidently adopting an existing component is faster than building one.

phases.name: Awareness
touchpoints: New engineer asks 'where do I find components?' in onboarding
PR reviewer comments 'we already have a component for this'
Sprint retro item: 'We keep rebuilding the same patterns'
phases.experience: The pain of duplication becomes visible when a PR review surfaces a rebuilt component that already existed. The engineering manager or design systems lead recognises the pattern and begins looking for a registry solution.
phases.insights: The discovery moment is usually a PR comment or a retro callout, not a search query. Marketing should target engineering managers who have just had this conversation, not engineers searching for tooling.

phases.name: Evaluation
phases.channel: Product Hunt, Storybook ecosystem, design systems community
phases.experience: The DS lead or engineering manager evaluates CatalogX against Storybook addons and Backstage. The differentiator is immediate: CatalogX surfaces ownership and state coverage without any plugin configuration. The demo on a real Storybook file closes the gap.
phases.insights: Run the demo on the evaluator's own Storybook — show them their existing coverage gaps and ownership vacuums in 60 seconds. Nothing converts faster than seeing your own problem reflected back.

phases.name: Setup and Ingestion
touchpoints: First registry population from existing codebase
phases.experience: The DS lead runs the GitHub Action against their repository. CatalogX automatically populates component entries from Storybook stories and CODEOWNERS. Within 30 minutes, the registry has 80% of their components without manual entry.
phases.insights: The time-to-first-value is critical. If the registry isn't populated with real data within the first session, churn is near-certain. Automate as much ingestion as possible from the existing repo.

phases.name: First Search and Discovery
phases.channel: CatalogX web app, VS Code extension
touchpoints: State coverage score viewed for the first time
phases.experience: An engineer searches for a component and finds it with a full coverage score and a named owner in under 30 seconds. The experience is visibly faster than their previous Storybook + GitHub workflow. The ownership vacuum flag on three other components becomes an immediate action item.
phases.insights: The first successful search — especially if it surfaces a coverage score that immediately answers 'does it handle my edge case?' — is the activation moment. Instrument this carefully.

phases.name: Team Adoption
touchpoints: DS lead presents CatalogX at engineering all-hands
Added to new engineer onboarding checklist
Slack bot integration for component search
phases.experience: The DS lead adds CatalogX to the engineering onboarding checklist. New engineers discover the registry on day one and skip the archaeology phase entirely. Sprint velocity improves as component reuse increases and duplication decreases.
phases.insights: The onboarding checklist placement is the highest-leverage distribution moment. Make it a one-line addition: 'Search CatalogX before building any UI component.'

phases.name: Ownership Governance
touchpoints: Vacuum detection alert for 4 ungoverned components
Monthly ownership review email to DS lead
Breaking change notification to component subscribers
phases.experience: CatalogX surfaces 4 ownership vacuums that had been invisible for months. The DS lead assigns owners, two of whom update and properly test their components within the week. The breaking change notification system prevents two silent regressions.
phases.insights: Vacuum detection and breaking change notifications are the retention features — they create recurring value that doesn't exist without CatalogX. Lead with these in renewal conversations.

storyboard.scenario: Devon is a senior frontend engineer at a fintech. His PM has just added a ticket for a permission-denied empty state. He has 90 minutes before standup. What happens next depends entirely on whether CatalogX exists.
storyboard.persona: Devon Okafor — Senior Frontend Engineer, Series B Fintech, New York

frames.description: Devon opens his Linear board. A new ticket is assigned: 'Empty state for permission-denied users on the dashboard page.' He estimates it at 2 hours and opens Storybook to see if a component exists.
frames.dialogue: If this exists already I can knock it out before standup.

frames.description: Devon searches Storybook for 'empty state'. 11 results appear. None of them show which states they handle in the search results — he has to click into each one. He opens the first three tabs.
frames.dialogue: Which of these handles permission-denied? There is no way to tell from here.

frames.description: Devon finds one candidate — EmptyState v2. It has a permission-denied story. He checks GitHub for the owner. CODEOWNERS points to @platform-core — a team that was reorganised 8 months ago. The alias no longer resolves.
frames.dialogue: Of course the owner is a ghost team. I can't use this without knowing if it's maintained.

frames.description: Devon posts in #design-systems Slack: 'Does a production-ready empty state with permission-denied exist? Who owns it?' He starts a new component file while waiting for a response.
frames.dialogue: I'll build it myself and ask Slack at the same time. Faster than waiting.

frames.description: NOW — With CatalogX. Devon opens CatalogX and types 'permission-denied empty state'. One result: EmptyState, 5/5 state coverage, owner @sara.kim (active 3 days ago), 7 teams importing this month. He clicks through to the Storybook story in 20 seconds.
frames.dialogue: Full coverage, active owner, 7 teams already using it. This is exactly what I needed.

frames.description: Devon copies the import path from CatalogX, pastes it into his file, and has the component rendering in 8 minutes. CatalogX prompts him to register as a subscriber for breaking change alerts. He confirms.
frames.dialogue: Done before standup. I did not write a single line of component code.

frames.description: Three weeks later. Devon's Slack shows a notification from CatalogX: 'EmptyState v3.0.0 removes legacy prop — you are importing this in 2 files. Migration guide linked.' He updates both files in 15 minutes with no regression.
frames.dialogue: That would have been a silent breakage if I had built my own version.

projects.name: UX Case Study Generator

hypothesis.problem: Building a full UX process — personas, journey maps, empathy maps, flows, wireframes — takes weeks and requires coordination across researchers, designers, and PMs. Most teams skip artifacts entirely or produce low-quality ones under pressure, leaving product decisions undocumented and hard to defend.
hypothesis.solution: A web app that takes a pain point, idea, or brief as input and generates a complete, editable UX artifact suite in minutes: personas, journey maps, empathy maps, affinity diagrams, user flows, lo-fi wireframes, hi-fi prototypes, competitive analysis, usability metrics, and interview questions — all structured as a shareable case study.
hypothesis.hook: Go from idea to a full UX case study in one prompt, not one month.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Senior UX researchers who need primary research rigor, or enterprise teams with established design ops and dedicated research functions.

segments.name: Junior-to-mid UX designers and product managers at startups
segments.description: Junior-to-mid UX designers and product managers at startups or agencies who need to run a UX process quickly but lack the time, team, or experience to produce all the artifacts from scratch.
segments.painPoint: Building a full UX process — personas, journey maps, empathy maps, flows, wireframes — takes weeks and requires coordination across researchers, designers, and PMs. Most teams skip artifacts entirely or produce low-quality ones under pressure, leaving product decisions undocumented and hard to defend.
segments.resolution: A web app that takes a pain point, idea, or brief as input and generates a complete, editable UX artifact suite in minutes: personas, journey maps, empathy maps, affinity diagrams, user flows, lo-fi wireframes, hi-fi prototypes, competitive analysis, usability metrics, and interview questions — all structured as a shareable case study.

advantage.capability: Deep integration with Claude API for structured artifact generation, combined with Figma API for wireframe and prototype scaffolding — all orchestrated in a single workflow.
advantage.motivation: We believe the best design decisions are documented ones. Most teams can't afford to do it properly — we want to make the starting framework free and instant.
advantage.insight: Designers don't skip UX artifacts because they don't value them — they skip them because producing them is the bottleneck. AI removes that bottleneck entirely.

principles: Starting framework > polished deliverable (ship a useful draft, not a perfect artifact)
Editable > static (every output must be modifiable by the team)
Contextual > generic (artifacts must feel specific to the input, not templated)
One input > full suite (minimize friction from idea to all artifacts)
Case study ready > internal only (outputs should be presentable to a product team as-is)

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Designers will trust AI-generated artifacts as a legitimate starting point rather than dismissing them as too generic to be useful.
clickTest.testMethod: Build a single-artifact MVP (AI-generated persona only), share with 10 UX designers/PMs, and measure whether they edit and use it vs. discard it.
clickTest.successMetric: 7 of 10 testers keep and edit the generated artifact rather than starting from scratch.

milestones: M1 — Single-artifact MVP: persona generator with editable output and shareable link (2 weeks)
M2 — Core suite: add journey map, empathy map, and user flow generation (4 weeks)
M3 — Visual artifacts: lo-fi wireframe generation via Figma API or SVG renderer (6 weeks)
M4 — Full case study export: all artifacts packaged into a shareable PDF/Notion-style doc (8 weeks)
M5 — Competition analysis + usability metrics + interview questions generation (10 weeks)
blockers: Lo-fi wireframe generation quality — AI-to-visual fidelity is unpredictable without a structured component library
Hi-fi prototype scope — requires Figma API access and a design system; may need to descope to annotated wireframes for v1
Artifact coherence — ensuring all generated artifacts reference the same persona/problem consistently across the suite
blueprint.timelineNotes: Target a 10-week sprint to full artifact suite. Wireframes and hi-fi prototypes are the highest-risk deliverables — validate the text-based artifacts first and gate visual generation on user demand signals.

sources.title: Initial Product Brief
sources.content: A web-based application that uses AI to generate an entire UX process including all artifacts: User Personas (1-3), User Flow, User Journey Map, Empathy Map, Affinity Diagram, LoFi Wireframes, HiFi Prototypes, Competition Analysis, Metrics to measure in Usability Testing, User Interview Questions. Objective: create a starting framework for the UX process — almost like a case study generator which can then be documented and shown to a product team where they can edit and make changes to the process.

journey.persona: Priya Menon, UX Designer at a Series A startup
journey.goal: Go from a new project brief to a complete, shareable UX artifact suite ready to present to the product team

stages.name: Awareness
steps: PM drops a new feature brief in Slack with a 'sprint starts Monday' note
Priya googles 'UX process template 2024' and lands on a Figma Community template
Sees a tweet or LinkedIn post about AI generating UX artifacts in minutes
Clicks through to UX Case Study Generator landing page
painPoints: No time to run a proper UX process before the sprint kicks off
Existing templates are generic and still require hours of content work
opportunities: Clear headline that addresses time pressure specifically ('Full UX suite in minutes, not weeks')
Show a side-by-side: blank template vs. AI-generated artifact from the same prompt

stages.name: Exploration
steps: Reads the landing page — scans the artifact list to see if it covers what she needs
Checks if wireframes and hi-fi prototypes are included (key differentiator)
Looks for social proof: 'Do other UX designers actually use this?'
Signs up for free tier or starts a demo without creating an account
painPoints: Can't tell if outputs will be specific enough to be useful or just generic filler
Unsure if the wireframe quality will be presentation-ready
opportunities: Live demo: let visitors paste a brief and see a persona generated in real time before signing up
Show real example outputs from real briefs — not polished marketing examples

stages.name: First Input
steps: Creates account and lands on input screen
Pastes or types the product brief / pain point
Selects which artifacts she needs for this sprint
Hits 'Generate' and waits for the first output
painPoints: Blank input box is intimidating — not sure how much detail to provide
Anxiety about whether the AI will understand the specific context
opportunities: Provide 3 example prompts to lower the blank-page fear
Show a real-time progress indicator artifact by artifact ('Generating persona… done. Generating journey map…')

stages.name: First Output Review
steps: Reviews the generated persona — checks if the role, frustrations, and goals feel accurate
Scans the journey map stages to see if they match her mental model
Edits 2-3 fields to make the persona feel more specific to her actual user
Generates the empathy map and checks for coherence with the persona
painPoints: Some persona details feel slightly generic — needs to tweak job title and tools list
Journey map has one stage that doesn't apply to her product context
opportunities: Inline editing on every field with a 'regenerate this section' option
Show a coherence indicator: 'All artifacts reference Priya Menon, 29, SF'

stages.name: Full Suite Generation
steps: Generates remaining artifacts: affinity diagram, user flow, wireframes
Reviews wireframes — assesses whether they match the flow she had in mind
Adds context notes to individual artifact sections
Shares a preview link with her PM to get early feedback
painPoints: Wireframe quality is the biggest risk — if it looks bad, it undermines credibility
Affinity diagram feels abstract without real research data behind it
opportunities: Let users annotate wireframes with 'design rationale' notes linked to the journey map
Clearly label affinity diagram as 'hypothetical clusters' to set right expectations

stages.name: Presentation & Handoff
steps: Exports the full artifact suite as a case study document
Walks PM and engineering lead through the case study in a 30-min sync
PM adds comments and requests one artifact change
Updates the artifact in the tool and reshares the link
painPoints: Export format may not match what stakeholders expect (PDF vs. live link vs. Notion)
Needs a way to incorporate stakeholder edits without regenerating everything
opportunities: Shareable live link with comment mode for stakeholders
One-click 'update from feedback' that lets Priya paste a note and regenerate just that artifact

stages.name: Value Realized
steps: Sprint planning references the persona and user flow to make scope decisions
Priya adds the case study to her portfolio
She starts the next project immediately using the tool — it's now her default starting point
Recommends it to another designer at a meetup
painPoints: Needs versioning to show 'before sprint' vs. 'after sprint' artifact evolution
Portfolio sharing needs a public-facing view without editable controls
opportunities: Version history with timeline view for portfolio storytelling
Public portfolio mode: read-only shareable URL with custom branding

says: 'I don't have time to do proper research before this sprint starts.'
'My PM wants wireframes by Friday but I haven't even done a journey map yet.'
'I know I should document this process but there's no template that fits our project.'
'I need to show the team I've thought through the user experience, not just the UI.'
thinks: 'If I skip the personas, the PM will just make up a user anyway — at least mine would be informed.'
'I'm not sure which artifact matters most for this stakeholder presentation.'
'I wish I had a research assistant who could just generate the first draft.'
'Am I even doing this in the right order? Empathy map before or after persona?'
does: Searches Figma Community for persona and journey map templates to start from
Copies artifacts from previous projects and does a find-and-replace on the product name
Sends 3-question Google Forms surveys to colleagues instead of doing proper user interviews
Skips the affinity diagram step entirely and goes straight to wireframes under deadline pressure
feels: Overwhelmed by the volume of artifacts expected in a short sprint
Embarrassed presenting generic-looking artifacts that don't feel specific to the product
Frustrated that no single tool handles the full UX process end-to-end
Anxious that skipping steps will lead to poor product decisions downstream
pains: Context-switching between 4-6 different tools (Figma, Miro, Notion, Google Docs, Maze) to produce one artifact suite
Artifacts from different tools look inconsistent and are hard to package into a coherent case study
Junior designers don't know the 'right' questions to ask at each UX stage — there's no guardrail
Sharing artifacts with non-designers (PMs, engineers, stakeholders) requires heavy formatting work
gains: A complete, coherent artifact suite they can walk a product team through in a single session
Confidence that they've covered the right ground even under time pressure
A shareable case study that demonstrates their UX process and thinking to stakeholders
Time saved on artifact production redirected to actual synthesis and design decisions

persona.name: Priya Menon
persona.role: Mid-level UX Designer at a Series A B2B SaaS startup
persona.quote: 'I know the UX process cold in theory — I just never have enough time to actually run it properly before the next sprint kicks off.'
persona.bio: Priya has 4 years of UX experience, 2 at her current startup where she's the only designer on a 12-person product team. She's expected to cover research, IA, wireframing, and visual design. She's good at her craft but perpetually under-resourced, often needing to produce research artifacts to satisfy process checkboxes rather than drive genuine insight.
goals: Produce a full UX artifact suite quickly enough to actually influence sprint planning
Build a case study portfolio that demonstrates her end-to-end process thinking
Get buy-in from her PM and engineering lead before design decisions are made without her
Level up from 'the UI person' to 'the UX strategist' in how the team perceives her
frustrations: Every project starts with 'we don't have time for research' and ends with 'why didn't we think about the user?'
Figma templates are visually polished but the content is always too generic to actually use
She has to rebuild the same artifact structure from scratch for every new project
Non-designers on her team don't read long research docs — she needs a presentable, scannable format
behaviors: Blocks 2-hour 'UX sprint' sessions at the start of each project to knock out artifacts
Maintains a personal Notion doc of reusable UX frameworks and templates
Screenshots competitor UX flows on her phone during lunch to inform her own designs
Shares work-in-progress artifacts in Slack to get async feedback before design reviews

Shipping products that genuinely improve how her users work
Building a portfolio strong enough to move to a design lead role

userFlow.entryPoint: User navigates to the app and pastes a project brief or pain point into the input field

steps.label: Enter project brief
steps.description: User pastes or types a product brief, pain point, or idea into the main input field. Can choose prompt depth: quick (one line) or detailed (full brief).

branches.outcome: Show inline prompt: 'Add more context for better results — or continue as-is'
Enable 'Select artifacts' step

steps.friction: Blank input box creates uncertainty about how much detail to provide

steps.label: Select artifacts
steps.description: User selects which artifacts to generate from a checklist: Personas (1-3), Journey Map, Empathy Map, Affinity Diagram, User Flow, Lo-fi Wireframes, Hi-fi Prototypes, Competitive Analysis, Usability Metrics, Interview Questions.

branches.outcome: Show estimated generation time (~2 min)

branches.condition: If user selects wireframes or hi-fi
branches.outcome: Show note: 'Visual artifacts take longer — we'll generate text artifacts first'

steps.friction: User may not know which artifacts they need — some guidance or recommended sets would help
steps.navContext: New Project screen — artifact selector panel

steps.label: Generate suite
steps.description: User clicks 'Generate'. System begins generating all selected artifacts in sequence, showing real-time progress per artifact.
steps.friction: Wait time uncertainty — user doesn't know if it's working or stuck

steps.label: Stream artifacts
steps.description: System calls Claude API with the brief as context, generating each artifact in sequence. Each artifact appears progressively as generation completes.

branches.outcome: Artifact appears in the panel; next artifact begins generating
Show per-artifact error with retry button; continue generating remaining artifacts

steps.errorPath: Per-artifact retry — user can regenerate a single failed artifact without restarting the full suite

steps.label: Review personas
steps.description: User reviews 1-3 generated personas. Can edit any field inline (name, role, goals, frustrations, tools, behaviors). Can request a regenerated version of any section.

branches.condition: If user edits a persona field
branches.outcome: Field saves inline; 'Regenerate related artifacts' prompt appears
Generates an additional persona with a different demographic/role

steps.friction: User may be unsure if editing one artifact should cascade updates to the others

steps.label: Review journey & flow
steps.description: User reviews the journey map stages and user flow steps. Can reorder stages, edit step descriptions, add/remove pain points and opportunities.

branches.outcome: Flow diagram updates in real time
Downstream steps renumber; affected branches flag for review

steps.friction: Journey map and user flow may feel redundant — needs clear labeling of what each artifact is for
steps.navContext: Artifact suite view — Journey Map / User Flow tabs

steps.label: Review visual artifacts
steps.description: User reviews lo-fi wireframes and hi-fi prototype scaffolding. Can annotate screens, request alternative layouts, or push wireframes to Figma.

branches.outcome: Wireframes exported to Figma as editable frames via API
User can request a regeneration with more specific layout constraints

steps.friction: Highest risk step — if wireframes look generic or broken, it undermines the whole suite
steps.navContext: Artifact suite view — Wireframes / Prototypes tabs
steps.errorPath: If Figma export fails, offer SVG/PNG download as fallback

steps.label: Review research artifacts
steps.description: User reviews competitive analysis, usability testing metrics, and interview questions. Can edit, add, or remove individual items.

branches.condition: If user adds a competitor manually
branches.outcome: Competitor added to analysis; map repositions automatically

branches.condition: If user wants more interview questions
branches.outcome: 'Generate 5 more' button appends additional questions

steps.friction: Competitive analysis without real pricing/feature data may feel speculative

steps.label: Export as case study
steps.description: User clicks 'Export Case Study'. Chooses format: shareable live link, PDF, or Notion export. All artifacts are packaged into a structured, presentation-ready document.

branches.outcome: Generates a public read-only URL with comment mode
Generates a multi-page PDF with artifact headers and consistent styling
Creates a Notion page via API with each artifact as a sub-page

steps.friction: User may not know which export format their stakeholder prefers
steps.navContext: Export modal — triggered from top nav 'Share' button
steps.errorPath: If Notion API fails, fall back to offering a markdown download

steps.label: Share with team

branches.outcome: Priya gets an email/Slack notification and can update the artifact from within the tool
Shown a message: 'Request edit access from Priya'

projects.name: Insight AI

hypothesis.problem: Student data across attendance, achievement, course access, and discipline is fragmented and dense, forcing educators to manually manipulate static spreadsheets with no ability to surface trends or collaborate on interventions.
hypothesis.solution: An intelligent data analytics platform that translates raw student metrics into intuitive visual narratives, contextual benchmarks, and shareable reports — enabling educators to surface key trends, annotate findings, and align on collaborative interventions.
hypothesis.hook: Turn fragmented school data into decisions — without a single spreadsheet.

segments.name: NYC Public School educators — principals, teachers, counselo
segments.description: NYC Public School educators — principals, teachers, counselors, and district staff
segments.painPoint: Student data across attendance, achievement, course access, and discipline is fragmented and dense, forcing educators to manually manipulate static spreadsheets with no ability to surface trends or collaborate on interventions.
segments.resolution: An intelligent data analytics platform that translates raw student metrics into intuitive visual narratives, contextual benchmarks, and shareable reports — enabling educators to surface key trends, annotate findings, and align on collaborative interventions.

advantage.capability: Real-time aggregation and visualization of multi-source student data (attendance, achievement, course access, discipline) in a single platform with AI-driven trend surfacing and annotation tools
advantage.motivation: Educators spend hours manually cross-referencing spreadsheets and still miss the patterns that matter — they need answers, not more data
advantage.insight: The schools with the best student outcomes do not have more data than others — they have faster, shared visibility into what the data means

principles: Clarity over completeness — show the signal, not the noise
Context beats raw numbers — every metric needs a benchmark
Shared visibility drives shared accountability
Annotations are decisions — make them first-class
Boring reliability > flashy features
Outcome > Output

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Principals and teachers will trust AI-surfaced trends enough to act on them without manually verifying the underlying spreadsheet data
clickTest.testMethod: Show 10 NYC school staff a dashboard with 3 pre-loaded trend alerts and ask them to decide on an intervention — measure how many reference source data vs. act directly from the visual
clickTest.successMetric: 70%+ of participants take or discuss an intervention action within 5 minutes without opening a spreadsheet

milestones: Data ingestion pipeline: connect to NYC DOE data exports (attendance, grades, discipline, course rosters)
Core dashboard: per-student and cohort views with trend lines and benchmark overlays
Annotation layer: educators can flag, comment, and tag any data point or trend
Report builder: generate shareable PDF/web summaries for parent meetings or district review
Collaborative workspace: multi-user access with role-based views (principal, teacher, counselor, district)
blockers: NYC DOE student data access requires FERPA-compliant data agreements — legal process may take months
Data format inconsistency across schools (manual exports, different SIS vendors)
Educator buy-in — getting staff to replace their existing spreadsheet workflows
blueprint.timelineNotes: Target pilot with 3 schools in one district within 6 months. Full district rollout by end of year 1.

phases.name: Status Quo — The Monday Merge
phases.channel: NYC DOE portal, Excel, email, printed handouts
phases.experience: Every Monday morning Maria logs into four separate systems, exports CSVs, and merges them by hand. The process takes 45-60 minutes and the data is already a week old. She flags students in her own spreadsheet and emails snapshots to James, who has already made his own version.
phases.emotion: Exhausted and behind before the week starts
insights: The bottleneck is not data access — it is the manual assembly ritual that consumes the time educators could spend acting on what they find

phases.name: Onboarding — First Unified View
phases.channel: Insight AI web app, existing DOE data feeds
phases.experience: Maria connects the DOE data feeds through a guided setup. For the first time she sees attendance, grades, and discipline on one screen with trend lines and a benchmark band. The week-over-week delta she used to calculate manually is already there.
insights: The trust gate is not features — it is whether the first AI flag matches a student she already suspected

phases.name: Detection — The Flag That Arrives Monday Morning
phases.channel: Insight AI weekly digest email, dashboard
phases.experience: A Monday digest arrives at 7am with three flagged students and a one-line reason for each. Maria taps into the dashboard and sees the attendance drop and grade decline layered on one chart with a plain-language summary. She adds an annotation before 8am.
phases.emotion: Alert and in control instead of overwhelmed
insights: Delivering the insight to the inbox rather than requiring a login is the adoption unlock — she acts before opening Excel

phases.name: Collaboration — One Room, One View
phases.channel: Insight AI shared dashboard, Friday team meeting
phases.experience: Maria shares a live link before the Friday meeting. James opens it on his laptop. For the first time they are looking at the same numbers, the same trend lines, and the same annotation. The 15 minutes usually lost reconciling versions is spent deciding who calls the parent.
insights: Shared visibility does not just save meeting time — it changes what the meeting is about, from data debate to decision-making

phases.name: Follow-Through — The Loop That Closes
phases.channel: Insight AI intervention tracker, next digest
phases.experience: James logs the counselor check-in and parent call in the intervention tracker. The following Monday the digest shows the same student with an attendance uptick flagged green. For the first time Maria can see whether an intervention moved the needle without running another merge.
insights: Closing the loop between action and outcome is what turns Insight AI from a reporting tool into a decision engine

serviceBlueprint.overview: Service blueprint for Insight AI covering the full cycle from data ingestion to an educator acting on a flagged student — showing the school staff experience frontstage and what Insight AI does backstage across data pipelines, AI analysis, and collaboration infrastructure.

steps.name: Data Ingestion and Sync
steps.customerAction: Administrator connects DOE data sources (ATS, grades portal, discipline log) during initial setup.
steps.frontstage: A guided connector shows each source coming online with a data freshness indicator.
steps.backstage: Scheduled pull from DOE APIs and export endpoints normalizes attendance, grade, discipline, and course data into a unified student schema.
steps.support: Data connectors, normalization pipeline, schema mapper
steps.evidence: A live unified student roster with all four data types confirmed as connected

steps.name: AI Trend Analysis and Alert Generation
steps.customerAction: Educator receives weekly digest email Monday morning with flagged students.
steps.frontstage: Digest email listing top flagged students with a one-line plain-language reason per student.
steps.backstage: AI model computes week-over-week deltas, compares against cohort benchmarks, and ranks students by severity of combined signals across attendance, grade, and discipline trajectory.
steps.support: Trend detection model, cohort benchmark engine, digest scheduler
steps.evidence: Digest email with ranked students and a confidence-level indicator

steps.name: Educator Review and Annotation
steps.customerAction: Maria opens the student unified dashboard from the digest deep link and reviews the trend chart.
steps.frontstage: Student profile shows attendance, grades, and discipline layered on one chart with benchmark bands and week-over-week delta.
steps.backstage: Dashboard fetches real-time-synced data for the selected student and renders trend overlays against the school-level cohort baseline.
steps.support: Student data API, visualization layer, benchmark overlay service
steps.evidence: A single chart replacing four separate spreadsheet tabs

steps.name: Collaborative Sharing and Team Alignment
steps.customerAction: Maria generates a shareable report link and sends it to the counselor and lead teacher before the Friday meeting.
steps.frontstage: One-click report generation produces a live-linked view of flagged students with annotations visible to all recipients.
steps.backstage: Report engine assembles the current flagged list, annotations, and trend state into a shareable, role-scoped URL with real-time data refresh.
steps.support: Report generator, role-based access control, live share link service
steps.evidence: One link that all staff open to the same live view during the meeting

steps.name: Intervention Logging
steps.customerAction: Team agrees on actions; James logs a counselor check-in and parent call against the student record.
steps.frontstage: Intervention form tied to the student profile with assignee, action type, due date, and notes.
steps.backstage: Intervention record stored and linked to the student data timeline; progress alerts scheduled based on the assigned follow-up date.
steps.support: Intervention data store, notification scheduler
steps.evidence: A logged intervention visible to all staff alongside the student name

steps.name: Progress Monitoring and Loop Closure
steps.customerAction: The following Monday, Maria sees the same student in the digest with an attendance uptick flagged green.
steps.frontstage: Next digest shows updated student status with a green flag, delta, and a link to the intervention log.
steps.backstage: New data pull re-runs the trend model for all previously flagged students; outcomes are compared against pre-intervention baselines and surfaced in the digest.
steps.support: Trend model re-run, intervention outcome comparator, digest generator
steps.evidence: A green flag on a student who was red last week — confirmation the loop closed

storyboard.scenario: It is the third week of October. A 7th grader named Marcus has been quietly missing school two days a week for three weeks. His math grade has slipped from a B to a D. In the old world, Maria would not see this until the November progress report. In the Insight AI world, it surfaces on a Monday morning before Marcus misses another day.
storyboard.persona: Maria Santos (Assistant Principal) & James Okafor (School Counselor)

frames.description: Maria at her desk at 7am Monday. Laptop open with four browser tabs — the ATS portal, three CSV exports, and a half-finished Excel merge from last week. Coffee is cold. She has 40 minutes before the first bell.
frames.dialogue: "Same drill. Export, merge, color-code, repeat. If I miss something this week I will not see it until November."

frames.description: Three weeks into the Insight AI pilot. Her inbox shows the weekly digest at 7:02am. Three students flagged. Marcus is at the top with a plain-language alert: attendance down six days in three weeks with a recurring pattern, math grade dropped from B to D, counselor check-in recommended.
frames.dialogue: "That is Marcus. I had a feeling something was off. The data actually caught it."

frames.description: Maria taps the deep link. The Insight AI dashboard opens on Marcus's profile. Attendance, math grade, and discipline all layered on one chart with a red trend band below the school benchmark. The recurring absence pattern lines up exactly with the grade drop.
frames.dialogue: "Same two days every week for three weeks. This is not random. Something is happening at home."

frames.description: She types an annotation directly on the chart: possible external schedule conflict, flag for counselor, check in with family. She hits share. James gets a notification and opens the same chart on his phone — same data, same annotation, in real time.
frames.dialogue: James: "Got it. I will pull him out of advisory tomorrow and make the parent call this afternoon."

frames.description: Friday team meeting. The teacher pulls up the shared Insight AI link on the projector. No conflicting spreadsheets, no version debate. The team logs three interventions: counselor session completed, parent call scheduled, teacher check-in assigned for next Tuesday.
frames.dialogue: "We are all looking at the same thing. That argument used to eat the first 20 minutes of every meeting."

frames.description: The following Monday digest. Marcus appears with a green indicator: full attendance both days last week, math grade holding steady. The intervention log shows all three actions completed. Maria reads it while her coffee is still hot.
frames.dialogue: "He was there all week. We caught it in week three instead of week eight. That is the difference."

insights.northStar: Time from a student risk signal forming in the data to an educator taking an informed intervention action — compressed from 3-4 weeks to 72 hours. Not dashboards viewed, not alerts sent: the moment early visibility converts into a documented action on a student who needed it.

metrics.name: Mean time to flag
metrics.description: Elapsed time from a student declining trend beginning to Insight AI surfacing it to an educator
metrics.target: 72 hours or less from trend onset, vs. the current 3-4 week spreadsheet cycle
metrics.measurement: Trend-onset date (retrospectively confirmed) vs. first AI alert timestamp per student

metrics.name: Intervention rate on flagged students

metrics.target: 70% or higher intervention rate within 5 days; current estimated baseline near 0% as no tracking exists

metrics.target: 60% or greater reduction from current 2-3 hour baseline
metrics.measurement: Self-reported prep time survey at start, mid-point, and end of pilot

projects.name: Bakufu

hypothesis.problem: AI agents proliferate faster than governance frameworks can keep pace. Teams have no enterprise-grade layer to manage agents as accountable product contributors — agents self-grade their output, produce inconsistent results across runs, leave no audit trail, and have no accountability chain when they break production.
hypothesis.solution: A multi-tenant governance and control platform built for AI agent fleets. Bakufu operates a structured Roster → Direct → Review → Manage workflow: teams enroll agents, define plain-language rulebooks and immutable deterministic guardrails, run cross-model-family judge panel reviews (eliminating self-grading bias), and get full execution traceability through MCP-connected tools — Figma, GitHub, Specify, and Supernova.
hypothesis.hook: Your AI agents are already running. Bakufu makes sure they are right.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Solo developers or small teams with a single AI assistant. Companies not yet adopting AI agents for product work. Teams needing general-purpose LLM orchestration (LangChain/AutoGPT use cases). Organizations without an existing design system or component library.

segments.name: Design Systems leads, VP Engineering, and Platform Engineeri
segments.description: Design Systems leads, VP Engineering, and Platform Engineering teams at mid-to-large product companies (100–2,000 employees) who are actively deploying AI agents for design token generation, component code production, or frontend engineering work.
segments.painPoint: AI agents proliferate faster than governance frameworks can keep pace. Teams have no enterprise-grade layer to manage agents as accountable product contributors — agents self-grade their output, produce inconsistent results across runs, leave no audit trail, and have no accountability chain when they break production.
segments.resolution: A multi-tenant governance and control platform built for AI agent fleets. Bakufu operates a structured Roster → Direct → Review → Manage workflow: teams enroll agents, define plain-language rulebooks and immutable deterministic guardrails, run cross-model-family judge panel reviews (eliminating self-grading bias), and get full execution traceability through MCP-connected tools — Figma, GitHub, Specify, and Supernova.

advantage.capability: Cross-model-family judge panel architecture: we route agent output to a reviewer from a different model family (e.g. GPT-4 judges Claude output), making it structurally impossible for an agent to validate its own work. Combined with a hybrid inference architecture that selects the optimal model per task, this is technically non-trivial to replicate.
advantage.motivation: AI agents are being deployed faster than accountability frameworks can catch up. Every broken token relationship or non-accessible component that ships because of unchecked agent output erodes trust in AI tooling. We are building the missing accountability primitive — the layer that treats agent output with the same rigor a senior engineer applies to a junior PR.
advantage.insight: Every AI orchestration platform today assumes you trust the agent's self-assessment. No one has built the governance layer specialized for design systems engineering — where correctness is binary (the token ships to production or it doesn't) and the blast radius of a bad output spans every product surface.

principles: Accountability before autonomy
Cross-model validation over single-model confidence
Traceability is a feature, not a constraint
Specialize deeply — design systems, not everything
Ship nothing an agent cannot explain

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Design Systems leads will pay for a dedicated governance layer on top of their existing AI agent tooling — rather than accepting imperfect output or building bespoke internal guardrails.
clickTest.testMethod: Design and pitch a "Governance Pilot" to 8 Design Systems leads at companies actively running AI agents for component or token generation. Offer a free 3-week pilot of the judge panel review layer wired into their existing stack. No custom integration required — MCP handles the connections.
clickTest.successMetric: 3 paid pilot commitments (≥ $500/month) from teams with an active AI agent workflow and a 100+ component design system in production.
