userFlow.persona: Priya Nair, Head of Design Systems at a 300-engineer Series C SaaS company
userFlow.goal: Enroll an AI agent into Bakufu, set deterministic guardrails, run a cross-model judge review, and get a fully audit-traced token output merged to production
userFlow.entryPoint: Priya receives a Slack alert: a design token agent pushed inconsistent color values to staging — brand/primary was #2563EB in Figma but #256FFF in the GitHub PR
userFlow.exitPoint: Judge-reviewed, approved token output is merged via MCP to GitHub and the full execution trace is written to the audit log — shareable with the CTO

steps.label: Triage the incident
steps.description: Priya opens the Bakufu dashboard from the Slack alert link. She lands on the Agent Activity Feed showing the offending agent run — execution ID, timestamp, affected tokens, and the drift delta.
steps.friction: No audit trail exists yet — she cannot see what input the agent received or why it produced a drift. She is working from a diff, not from root cause.

steps.label: Locate the agent in Roster
steps.description: Priya navigates to the Roster tab and searches for the token generation agent by name. The agent exists but is in an unmanaged state — no rulebook assigned, no judge panel configured.
steps.friction: Agent was deployed directly by an engineer without going through the enrollment workflow. No ownership metadata.

steps.label: Enroll agent into Bakufu governance
steps.description: Priya clicks Enroll Agent. She assigns an owner (herself), sets the agent category (Token Generation), and links it to the Figma and GitHub MCP connections already configured for her workspace.
steps.friction: MCP connection verification takes a few seconds — no clear progress indicator on which connection is being validated.

steps.label: MCP connections verified
steps.description: Bakufu verifies the Figma and GitHub MCP connections. Returns a connection health summary: Figma (connected, read/write), GitHub (connected, PR scope), Specify (not connected — shown as optional).
steps.navContext: Bakufu → Roster → Enroll Agent → Connection Status
steps.errorPath: If a required MCP connection fails, enrollment is blocked with a specific remediation link — not a generic error.

steps.label: Author a Rulebook
steps.description: Priya creates a new Rulebook named Token Naming & Value Standards. She writes two plain-language rules: (1) All color tokens must match Figma Variable values exactly — no tolerance. (2) Token names must follow brand/{scale}/{variant} convention. She then adds one immutable deterministic guardrail: reject any output where hex values diverge from Figma Variables by more than 0 characters.
steps.friction: Writing rules in plain language feels ambiguous — unclear whether the agent will interpret them correctly. No preview of how a rule maps to an enforcement check.
steps.navContext: Bakufu → Roster → Agent Profile → Rulebook Editor

steps.label: Rulebook compiled and attached
steps.description: Bakufu parses the plain-language rules through the rule compiler and generates structured enforcement criteria. The deterministic guardrail is locked as immutable (not overridable by judge votes). Rulebook version 1.0 is attached to the agent.
steps.errorPath: If a rule fails to parse, Bakufu highlights the ambiguous phrase and suggests a rewrite — parse errors are non-blocking but uncompiled rules are inactive.

steps.label: Configure judge panel
steps.description: Priya opens the Review Configuration. She selects a 3-model cross-family judge panel: Claude Sonnet (analytical), GPT-4o (conformance), Gemini Pro (creativity/outlier detection). She sets the consensus threshold to 2-of-3 approval required for promotion.
steps.friction: It is not obvious how to interpret divergent scores across model families — no explanation of what a GPT-4o conformance score means vs. a Claude analytical score.
steps.navContext: Bakufu → Roster → Agent Profile → Review Configuration

steps.label: Re-run agent through Bakufu pipeline
steps.description: Priya triggers a fresh agent run from the Bakufu interface against the same Figma file and GitHub branch. The agent executes under Bakufu governance — rulebook enforced, execution trace recording begins.
steps.friction: Run takes 45–90 seconds with no granular progress — just a spinner. Priya cannot tell if it is slow due to Figma API latency or agent processing.
steps.errorPath: If the agent times out, Bakufu surfaces the last checkpoint reached and allows resume — not a full restart.

steps.label: Deterministic guardrail evaluation
steps.description: Before the judge panel runs, Bakufu applies the immutable guardrail: compare every output hex value against the Figma Variable source. This run passes — all 14 color tokens match exactly.
steps.errorPath: If the guardrail fails, the output is immediately rejected without entering the judge queue — Priya gets a token-level diff showing each mismatch. No judge tokens are consumed.

steps.label: Judge panel scores output
steps.description: The 3 judges independently review the token output against the Rulebook. Results: Claude (pass, 94% confidence), GPT-4o (pass, 88% confidence), Gemini (flag — token name brand/blue/500 violates naming convention, 71% confidence). 2-of-3 threshold met but a flag is surfaced.

steps.label: Review judge panel report
steps.description: Priya reviews the judge panel report. She sees the 2-of-3 pass, the Gemini flag on brand/blue/500, the confidence scores, and the Why flagged? explanation: the token name uses a color literal (blue) rather than a scale reference (neutral). She must decide: approve as-is or reject for correction.

branches.condition: Approve — 2/3 pass is sufficient, flag is informational
branches.outcome: Output promoted to merge queue, flag annotated in audit log

branches.condition: Reject — fix the naming violation before merging
branches.outcome: Output sent to revision queue with annotated feedback attached

steps.friction: Priya is unsure whether a naming convention violation from one judge is a blocking issue or a recommendation. The threshold passed, but the flag feels important.

steps.label: Reject and send to revision queue
steps.description: Priya rejects the output. She adds a human annotation to the Gemini flag: Rename brand/blue/500 to brand/primary/500 to match naming convention. The output is queued for agent revision with the annotated feedback attached.
steps.friction: No way to make the fix herself inline — she must wait for the agent to re-run.

steps.label: Agent re-runs with feedback
steps.description: The agent receives the revision feedback via Bakufu. It re-runs with the naming correction applied. The deterministic guardrail passes again. The judge panel re-scores: 3-of-3 pass, all confidence scores above 90%.
steps.errorPath: If the agent produces the same violation again, Bakufu auto-escalates to Priya with a note that the feedback was not actioned — preventing silent loops.

steps.label: Approve and merge via MCP
steps.description: Priya approves the revised output. Bakufu pushes the token file to the GitHub PR via MCP and updates the Figma Variables via the Figma MCP connection. The full execution trace — two runs, all judge scores, guardrail evaluations, human annotations — is written to the immutable audit log.
steps.errorPath: If the GitHub MCP push fails (merge conflict), Bakufu surfaces the conflict file and pauses — does not force-push.

steps.label: Share audit report with CTO
steps.description: Priya opens the Audit Log entry for this execution chain. She generates a shareable report link showing: agent identity, rulebook version, both run traces, judge scores with confidence, human decisions, and the final MCP-push receipt. She shares it with the CTO as accountability evidence.

phases.insights: The production incident is the catalyst — not a feature request. Marketing should lead with the pain moment, not workflow improvement.

storyboard.scenario: Priya is Head of Design Systems at a Series C SaaS. Last Tuesday, an AI-generated token alias broke dark mode across 12 product surfaces and took two days to trace. Today she needs a governance layer.
storyboard.persona: Priya Nair — Head of Design Systems, Series C SaaS, San Francisco

frames.description: Priya is at her desk at 9 PM, Slack filled with red alerts. Her screen shows broken dark mode across the product — every component with a color token is rendering incorrectly. Her engineering lead is pinging her.
frames.dialogue: This is the third AI agent incident this quarter. I need a real solution.

frames.description: Two days later, Priya is at Config, Figma's annual conference. A speaker on stage is showing a slide: Who is accountable when your AI agent ships a broken component? The talk describes her exact problem.
frames.dialogue: Finally someone is talking about governance, not just generation.

frames.description: Priya is at her laptop watching the Bakufu demo. The screen shows a judge panel catching a WCAG AA failure in a Claude-generated component — flagged in real time before any PR was opened. She leans forward.
frames.dialogue: A different model reviewing the agent output. That is the right architecture.

frames.description: Priya is on a video call with the Bakufu founder. She has connected her company Figma file and GitHub repo via MCP in under 10 minutes. The founder runs a governed agent job live on her own token set.
frames.dialogue: No custom integration required. That was the part I was worried about.

frames.description: Three weeks into the pilot. The Bakufu dashboard shows a red alert: an agent generated a semantic token that broke the alias chain for the brand primary color. The judge panel caught it before any PR was opened.
frames.dialogue: This is exactly the incident we had last month, caught before it shipped.

frames.description: Priya is in a meeting room with her CTO. The Bakufu audit trail PDF is open on the projector showing every agent job, model version, rule citation, and verdict from the past three weeks. The CTO is nodding.
frames.dialogue: This is the audit trail our security team has been asking for.

frames.description: Six months later. The Bakufu workspace shows 24 governed agents — design systems and frontend engineering combined. Priya is on stage at a design systems meetup presenting how they scaled AI agents without scaling risk.
frames.dialogue: Bakufu did not slow us down. It is what let us move faster.

projects.name: Pulse

hypothesis.problem: Founders ship products based on assumptions and biased feedback from friends. Traditional user research is slow, expensive, and hard to recruit for. Most products fail not because they are badly built, but because they solve the wrong problem for the wrong user or the problem is too small which in turns questions the scalability of the product.
hypothesis.solution: A platform where founders upload their working prototype and instantly access a curated community of target users — matched by the founder's own persona definitions — who interact and give structured feedback. AI agents trained on persona data also simulate realistic user behavior, giving founders signal 24/7 even when real users are not active.
hypothesis.hook: Get your prototype in front of 100 matched users in 24 hours — plus AI agents that behave like your actual target customers, giving you feedback around the clock.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Enterprise product teams with dedicated UX research budgets, existing user panels, or agency partnerships — they already have structured research pipelines and won't gain enough marginal value.

segments.name: Early-stage founders and indie builders (pre-Series A) who h
segments.description: Early-stage founders and indie builders (pre-Series A) who have a working prototype — clickable Figma or live URL — and need real user validation before committing to a full build or go-to-market push. They need to know whether their idea has potential product market fit before they start allocating resources and time to building a fully functional and/or monetizable version.
segments.painPoint: Founders ship products based on assumptions and biased feedback from friends. Traditional user research is slow, expensive, and hard to recruit for. Most products fail not because they are badly built, but because they solve the wrong problem for the wrong user or the problem is too small which in turns questions the scalability of the product.
segments.resolution: A platform where founders upload their working prototype and instantly access a curated community of target users — matched by the founder's own persona definitions — who interact and give structured feedback. AI agents trained on persona data also simulate realistic user behavior, giving founders signal 24/7 even when real users are not active.

advantage.capability: A dual validation engine: real human feedback from a persona-matched community, plus AI agents that simulate authentic user behavior based on the founder's own persona definitions — providing 24/7 feedback without recruitment lag.
advantage.motivation: Founders pour years and capital into products that never find their market. The best time to catch a wrong assumption is before you scale, not after.
advantage.insight: Validation fails not because founders do not want feedback, but because getting it from the right people at the right moment is nearly impossible today. AI agents that behave like real users — not just answer surveys — change the economics of that entirely.

principles: Signal over noise — one validated insight from the right user beats 1,000 generic opinions
Behavior over stated preference — watch what users do, not just what they say
Matched friction — feedback must come from people who actually resemble the target persona
Agents that behave, not just respond — AI simulation must mirror realistic user journeys
Founder-first UX — the platform itself must be the simplest thing a founder has ever used

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: That AI agent feedback will be trusted and acted on by founders at the same level as real human feedback — and that the behavioral simulation is realistic enough to surface meaningful product insights.
clickTest.testMethod: Run a closed beta with 30 early-stage founders. Each gets 5 real user sessions and 5 AI agent sessions for their prototype. After 2 weeks, run a blind survey asking founders to rate the quality and usefulness of feedback without telling them which was AI vs human.
clickTest.successMetric: 65%+ of founders rate AI agent feedback as as useful or more useful than real user feedback in at least one dimension (UX clarity, feature prioritization, or pain-point identification). Secondary: 80%+ retention after first validation run.

hypothesis.problem: Travel is full of coordination overhead that current tools don't automate: tracking personal belongings across multiple stays, recovering from disruptions like cancellations and delays, understanding the true cost of activities, and getting personalized recommendations that match actual preferences — not generic lists.
hypothesis.solution: An AI-powered mobile travel companion that manages luggage across locations, re-optimizes itineraries in real time when plans change, calculates true activity costs including transport, and surfaces personalized recommendations based on the user's own preference profile.
hypothesis.hook: Your trip does not stop when your plans fall apart — Wanderer re-routes you in seconds.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Casual vacationers who book a single resort and stay put, or budget backpackers whose only goal is to minimize spend.

segments.painPoint: Travel is full of coordination overhead that current tools don't automate: tracking personal belongings across multiple stays, recovering from disruptions like cancellations and delays, understanding the true cost of activities, and getting personalized recommendations that match actual preferences — not generic lists.
segments.resolution: An AI-powered mobile travel companion that manages luggage across locations, re-optimizes itineraries in real time when plans change, calculates true activity costs including transport, and surfaces personalized recommendations based on the user's own preference profile.

advantage.capability: AI itinerary re-optimization, luggage item tracking across multi-stop trips, rideshare cost integration, and a personalized preference engine that improves with each trip.
advantage.motivation: Travel should be experienced, not managed. The overhead of keeping track of things, costs, and contingencies pulls people out of the moment.
advantage.insight: Existing travel apps (TripIt, Google Trips, Airbnb) solve discovery or booking — none solve real-time trip management after departure. The highest-value moment is when something goes wrong and the traveler needs instant re-planning.

principles: Real-time over pre-planned — the app earns its value during disruptions, not before the trip
Accuracy over volume — one right recommendation beats ten generic ones
Never make the user re-enter data — infer, sync, and remember

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Travelers will consistently log their personal items into the app across multiple locations — the luggage tracker only works if users maintain it. In addition, travelers also log all of their preferences into the app which radically improves the accuracy of the recommendations.
clickTest.testMethod: Prototype the luggage tracker and trip re-optimization as standalone features. Run a 2-week beta with 20 multi-destination travelers. Measure daily active logging rate and whether users complete their trip without reporting a lost item or able to complete all of their proposed activities within the prescribed time.
clickTest.successMetric: 70% of beta users log items at least once per location change, and at least 3 users report the tracker prevented a forgotten item.

milestones: Week 1-2: Preference profile + personalized recommendations MVP
Week 3-4: Itinerary builder with disruption re-optimization
Week 5-6: Luggage tracker with location-aware item management
Week 7-8: Cost calculator with rideshare API integration
Week 9-10: Beta with 20 real travelers on multi-destination trips
blockers: Rideshare API access (Uber/Lyft) for real-time cost estimates

blueprint.timelineNotes: Start with the disruption re-optimizer as the hero feature — it is the most defensible and the clearest pain point. Luggage tracker is high-risk adoption; validate it early in parallel.

projects.name: AI Use Case Validator

hypothesis.problem: The gap between 'AI opportunity identified' and 'AI initiative that delivers ROI' is where consulting practices lose credibility and enterprises waste millions. There is no systematic, repeatable process for evaluating whether a specific business process is genuinely ready for AI before resources are committed. Consultants rely on inconsistent judgment, frameworks applied differently by every team member, and vendor-supplied feasibility assessments that are structurally biased toward selling. The result: 60-70% of enterprise AI projects fail to deliver promised value — not because AI does not work, but because the wrong use cases got resourced. Every failure erodes the consulting relationship that took years to build.
hypothesis.solution: A decision-support platform built specifically for AI use case evaluation. The assessment engine applies the Four A's of AI Success and AI Opportunity Intents to score any business process against structured readiness criteria — data quality, task complexity, change management burden, and organizational readiness — producing a defensible, reproducible score with full rationale. The dynamic roadmap builder visualizes the delta between the current manual workflow and the AI-augmented future state side-by-side, making the business case legible to non-technical executives without requiring a separate deck. The cost-benefit calculator models expected ROI, time-to-value, and risk-adjusted returns — calibrated by industry vertical — before a single dollar is committed to implementation.
hypothesis.hook: Stop pitching AI projects you cannot deliver. Know before you commit.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Individual developers or data scientists assessing technical feasibility — they need tooling, not frameworks. AI vendors conducting their own feasibility assessments — the tool is explicitly designed to counteract vendor bias. Small businesses under 50 employees where the evaluation rigor exceeds the scale of the problem.

segments.name: Senior consultants, digital transformation leads, and AI str
segments.description: Senior consultants, digital transformation leads, and AI strategy directors at management consulting firms (Big 4, boutique strategy practices) and enterprise transformation teams at Fortune 500 companies who are personally accountable for recommending — and delivering — AI initiatives. They present AI roadmaps to C-suite clients and bear the reputational cost when those initiatives fail to deliver promised value.
segments.painPoint: The gap between 'AI opportunity identified' and 'AI initiative that delivers ROI' is where consulting practices lose credibility and enterprises waste millions. There is no systematic, repeatable process for evaluating whether a specific business process is genuinely ready for AI before resources are committed. Consultants rely on inconsistent judgment, frameworks applied differently by every team member, and vendor-supplied feasibility assessments that are structurally biased toward selling. The result: 60-70% of enterprise AI projects fail to deliver promised value — not because AI does not work, but because the wrong use cases got resourced. Every failure erodes the consulting relationship that took years to build.
segments.resolution: A decision-support platform built specifically for AI use case evaluation. The assessment engine applies the Four A's of AI Success and AI Opportunity Intents to score any business process against structured readiness criteria — data quality, task complexity, change management burden, and organizational readiness — producing a defensible, reproducible score with full rationale. The dynamic roadmap builder visualizes the delta between the current manual workflow and the AI-augmented future state side-by-side, making the business case legible to non-technical executives without requiring a separate deck. The cost-benefit calculator models expected ROI, time-to-value, and risk-adjusted returns — calibrated by industry vertical — before a single dollar is committed to implementation.

advantage.capability: The Four A's framework and AI Opportunity Intents can be encoded into a structured scoring engine with weighted criteria by industry vertical — making outputs reproducible across consultants and engagements. The roadmap builder is differentiable because it explicitly models the current manual workflow alongside the AI-augmented future state; most consulting tools only show the destination. The cost-benefit calculator can be pre-calibrated with industry benchmarks by vertical (financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, retail) so outputs are immediately credible to a CFO without a custom research engagement.
advantage.motivation: Consulting firms are under enormous pressure to deliver AI initiatives that work. One high-profile AI failure at a major client destroys years of relationship equity and creates principal-level liability. The Validator exists to protect the consultant's credibility as much as to serve the client — that dual motivation is what makes the tool worth paying for.
advantage.insight: The AI readiness evaluation market is dominated by two inadequate options: vendor-supplied assessments (biased toward selling) and generic organizational maturity models (too high-level to assess individual process feasibility). The gap is a tool that is explicitly vendor-neutral, operates at the process level rather than the org level, applies a consistent framework across every evaluation, and produces output the consulting team can stand behind in front of a skeptical CFO. No current tool occupies this position.

principles: Vendor-neutral > Any vendor affiliation
Process-level granularity > Org-level maturity scores
Defensible scoring > Black-box recommendations
Decision support > Decision replacement (consultants own the judgment)
Reproducible output > Bespoke analysis every time

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Management consultants will trust a software tool to structure and score AI feasibility assessments — and will present those scores to clients in a formal deliverable — rather than treating the output as a starting point they immediately override with their own judgment, making the tool invisible in the final work product.
clickTest.testMethod: Build a Google Sheets-based version of the assessment engine and roadmap builder in 3 weeks. Run it with 3 consulting teams on active client engagements — provide white-glove onboarding and run the first assessment alongside them. Measure whether the tool output appears in client-facing deliverables or gets discarded in favor of the team's existing approach.
clickTest.successMetric: 2 of 3 consulting teams include Validator output — the assessment score, readiness rationale, or roadmap visualization — in a client-facing deliverable. At least 1 team requests to use it on a second engagement unprompted. At least 1 team asks about pricing before the pilot ends.

milestones: Phase 1 — Framework validation (weeks 1–3): Build a Google Sheets assessment engine applying the Four A's and AI Opportunity Intents. Run with 3 consulting teams on live engagements. Validate that the framework produces scores consultants trust and will present to clients.

Phase 2 — Web application v1 (weeks 4–12): Assessment engine as a web app. Input: process description, data availability, task complexity, org readiness signals. Output: structured readiness score with per-criterion rationale and a visual summary report exportable to PDF.

Phase 3 — Roadmap builder (weeks 13–20): Side-by-side manual vs. AI-augmented workflow visualizer. Consultant inputs current-state process steps; tool generates an AI-augmented future state with effort delta, timeline estimate, and dependency map.

Phase 4 — Cost-benefit calculator (weeks 21–28): ROI model with industry-specific benchmarks by vertical. Outputs risk-adjusted ROI range, time-to-value estimate, and sensitivity analysis for the three most impactful variables.

Phase 5 — Multi-process comparison (weeks 29–36): Evaluate and rank multiple business processes simultaneously, generating a prioritized AI opportunity roadmap for an entire organization or business unit.
Phase 6 — Enterprise and team features (weeks 37–44): Team collaboration, version history, client-facing export (PowerPoint and PDF), and white-label branding for consulting firm delivery.
blockers: Framework IP: The Four A's of AI Success and AI Opportunity Intents may have existing IP ownership or trademark. Must validate licensing position before encoding proprietary frameworks into a commercial product.

Consultant adoption vs. consultant bypass: Senior consultants may perceive the tool as threatening their expertise rather than augmenting it. Every positioning and onboarding decision must reinforce that this is decision support, not decision replacement — the consultant's judgment is still the product.

Benchmark data sourcing: The cost-benefit calculator requires credible industry benchmarks for AI ROI by vertical and use case type. These do not exist in a clean, licensable dataset — requires proprietary research investment or a data partnership before Phase 4 is credible.

Enterprise sales cycle: Consulting firms have long procurement cycles requiring security reviews, legal sign-off, and partner-level sponsorship before any tool is approved firm-wide. Early GTM must target individual project teams on a per-engagement basis, not firm-wide procurement — and price accordingly.

Scope of 'AI readiness': The tool must define a clear boundary between evaluating a process for AI readiness vs. designing the AI solution. Scope creep into solution design territory will balloon the product surface area and dilute the core value proposition.
blueprint.timelineNotes: Phase 1 (Google Sheets beta) is the only phase that must be completed before any product investment decision. Do not build Phase 2 until at least 2 consulting teams have used Phase 1 output in a client deliverable. Total timeline to feature-complete platform (all 6 phases) estimated at 44 weeks. Phases 5 and 6 should not begin until the product has at least 10 paying consulting teams on Phase 2-4 features.

sources.title: Founder Product Brief
sources.content: The AI Use Case Validator is a decision-support platform designed to help management consulting firms and enterprise transformation teams systematically evaluate business processes for AI readiness. By utilizing frameworks like the Four A's of AI Success and AI Opportunity Intents, the tool assesses feasibility based on factors such as data quality, task complexity, and organizational readiness. Core features include an assessment engine, a dynamic roadmap builder for comparing manual and AI-augmented workflows, and cost-benefit calculators, all aimed at increasing project success rates, reducing wasted resources, and providing data-driven insights before organizations commit significant investment to AI implementation.

projects.name: Chief AI

hypothesis.problem: Every organization runs a hidden layer of critical-but-not-urgent work that falls between the cracks of every project management tool: security training completion for all employees, contract renewals, software licensing renewals and training modules, budget submissions, audit prep, policy sign-offs, onboarding checklists. This work has hard deadlines and real consequences when missed — legal exposure, audit failures, security vulnerabilities, license lapses. But the primary responsibility is with the chief of staff, so it gets tracked in a fragile mix of spreadsheets and calendar reminders. The person responsible is already at capacity. Nobody finds out a deadline slipped until it already has.
hypothesis.solution: An AI Chief of Staff — a web-based bot that acts as a persistent, proactive coordinator for all lateral, deadline-driven operational work. It ingests operational commitments (contracts, renewals, compliance deadlines, training requirements), assigns ownership to specific people, sends targeted reminders, escalates automatically as deadlines approach, and maintains a live dashboard of what is on track, at risk, and overdue. Unlike project management tools, it understands operational context — it knows security training affects all 200 employees individually and tracks per-person completion, not just the parent task. Unlike a human CoS, it never forgets, never sleeps, and never deprioritizes a renewal because a board meeting came up.
hypothesis.hook: The lateral work your Chief of Staff would catch before it became a fire — tracked, owned, and chased automatically.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Startups under 20 people who handle this informally and do not feel the pain yet. Large enterprises with a fully staffed operations function and existing tooling (ServiceNow, Workday) they are locked into. Teams looking for a general project management tool — this is not Asana for lateral work, it specifically excludes core job deliverables.

segments.name: Chiefs of Staff, Operations leads, and COOs at mid-sized com
segments.description: Chiefs of Staff, Operations leads, and COOs at mid-sized companies (50–500 employees) who are personally responsible for making sure cross-functional, deadline-driven operational work gets done — but are currently tracking it across spreadsheets, email threads, shared calendars, and manual follow-ups and a ton of slack follow=ups. Also relevant: any department head who owns compliance and renewal deadlines that sit outside their core job description
segments.painPoint: Every organization runs a hidden layer of critical-but-not-urgent work that falls between the cracks of every project management tool: security training completion for all employees, contract renewals, software licensing renewals and training modules, budget submissions, audit prep, policy sign-offs, onboarding checklists. This work has hard deadlines and real consequences when missed — legal exposure, audit failures, security vulnerabilities, license lapses. But the primary responsibility is with the chief of staff, so it gets tracked in a fragile mix of spreadsheets and calendar reminders. The person responsible is already at capacity. Nobody finds out a deadline slipped until it already has.
segments.resolution: An AI Chief of Staff — a web-based bot that acts as a persistent, proactive coordinator for all lateral, deadline-driven operational work. It ingests operational commitments (contracts, renewals, compliance deadlines, training requirements), assigns ownership to specific people, sends targeted reminders, escalates automatically as deadlines approach, and maintains a live dashboard of what is on track, at risk, and overdue. Unlike project management tools, it understands operational context — it knows security training affects all 200 employees individually and tracks per-person completion, not just the parent task. Unlike a human CoS, it never forgets, never sleeps, and never deprioritizes a renewal because a board meeting came up.

advantage.capability: The AI layer enables three things no checklist tool can do: (1) natural language intake — 'Add our AWS renewal, it's due March 15, owner is Sarah' creates a tracked item instantly; (2) context-aware escalation — the bot knows the difference between a 30-day warning on a $2k SaaS renewal and a 7-day warning on a $500k enterprise contract and escalates accordingly; (3) per-person completion tracking for population-level compliance work like security training, without requiring a separate HRIS integration.
advantage.motivation: Lateral work failures are invisible until they are catastrophic. A lapsed contract, a missed audit, an employee who never completed security training — these do not show up in any OKR dashboard but they end careers and create legal liability. The CoS is the person who prevents this, and that job is currently done with highlighters and calendar blocks.
advantage.insight: Every CoS tool on the market is either too simple (a shared to-do list) or too complex (a full ERP that requires a 6-month implementation). The real insight is that the Chief of Staff's job for lateral work is not project management — it is awareness, follow-through, and escalation. Those three functions, applied only to non-core deadline work, can be fully automated without trying to replace strategic CoS judgment.

principles: Lateral work only > Competing with Asana or Jira
Escalate before the fire > Report after the fact
Natural language in > Structured form entry
Auto-chase > Manual reminder

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Operations leads and Chiefs of Staff will trust an AI bot to autonomously send nudges and escalations on their behalf — without reviewing each one — because the time savings outweigh the loss of control over tone and timing.
clickTest.testMethod: Run the AI CoS workflow manually for 2 paying design partner companies for 4 weeks. Use Claude to draft all nudges and escalations, send them from a shared inbox, and log every response and completion. This is a concierge MVP — no product built yet. Measure whether people complete lateral tasks faster than their baseline.
clickTest.successMetric: At least 1 of 2 pilot companies shows a measurable reduction in overdue lateral tasks (20%+ fewer missed deadlines vs. the prior 4-week period). At least 1 pilot requests to continue the engagement after the manual phase ends and asks when the product will be ready.

milestones: Phase 1 — Concierge MVP (weeks 1–4): Run the CoS workflow manually for 2 design partners using Claude + a shared inbox. No product. Validate that AI-driven nudging and escalation actually changes completion behavior.
Phase 2 — Intake layer (weeks 5–10): Web UI with natural language task intake, deadline setting, owner assignment, and a live status dashboard (On Track / At Risk / Overdue).
Phase 3 — Notification & escalation engine (weeks 11–16): Automated reminder sequences, escalation chains (assignee → manager → exec), and configurable urgency thresholds per work type.
Phase 4 — Integrations (weeks 17–22): Slack (nudges in-channel), Google Calendar (deadline sync), email (for external parties on contracts), and a CSV import for bulk onboarding of renewal calendars.
Phase 5 — Pattern intelligence (weeks 23–28): AI learns which work types and which teams habitually slip, surfaces pre-deadline risk flags before the reminder window even opens.
blockers: Scope boundary enforcement: users will inevitably try to add core project work. The product must redirect this without feeling broken — need a clear 'this is not a fit' UX pattern.

Trust in autonomous AI communications: many orgs will not let an AI send external emails or Slack messages without human approval first. Must validate approve-then-send vs. auto-send preference with pilot partners before building the engine.

HRIS integration complexity: per-employee compliance tracking (security training, policy sign-offs) requires knowing who works there. Integrating with BambooHR, Rippling, or Workday varies enormously by company — must decide whether to start with manual roster CSV import or invest in a native integration.
Liability question: if the bot misses a deadline reminder due to a bug, who is responsible? Need a clear terms-of-service position and a manual audit trail from day one.
blueprint.timelineNotes: Phase 1 is the only phase that matters before raising money or hiring. Do not build Phase 2 until at least 1 design partner pays for Phase 1 and requests Phase 2. Total timeline to public beta: approximately 28 weeks from design partner kickoff.

sources.title: Founder Vision Input
sources.content: Web-based AI Bot that plays the role of a Chief of Staff at an organization. Tracks lateral work that is deadline-related but not directly related to the main job. Examples: getting contracts completed, security training for all employees, budget renewals, licensing renewals for software. Essentially tracks the work that falls between roles and ensures it gets done on time.

journey.persona: Jordan, Chief of Staff at a 150-person Series B SaaS company — reports directly to the CEO, owns everything from board prep to vendor renewals to compliance, has no direct reports, and is currently running all lateral operational work out of a shared Google Sheet and her own memory.
journey.goal: Never have a lateral deadline slip without advance warning again — and stop spending 5+ hours a week manually chasing people for work that is not their primary job

stages.name: The Breaking Point
steps: A key software license lapses because the renewal reminder was buried in an email thread from 90 days ago
IT surfaces the lapse during an incident review — not a proactive catch
Jordan gets called into a CEO meeting to explain what happened and what the exposure was
She spends 3 hours reconstructing the timeline from email and calendar to answer why no one caught this
painPoints: No centralized view of renewal deadlines — each one lives in whoever set it up originally
The person whose calendar had the reminder went on vacation and no one covered it
No escalation mechanism existed — the deadline passed in silence
The tracking spreadsheet had not been updated in 6 weeks
opportunities: The post-incident review is the exact sales trigger — target companies that recently had a compliance miss, audit finding, or license lapse
Position Chief AI as the system that would have caught this 30 and 7 days out and escalated when the first reminder went unanswered

stages.name: Research & Evaluation
steps: Googles 'chief of staff tools' and 'operational compliance tracking' — finds mostly PM tools
Tries a Notion template for ops tracking — abandons it after two weeks because enforcement is still manual
Posts in a CoS Slack community asking how others track renewals and compliance deadlines
Finds Chief AI via a reply in that thread or a LinkedIn post from another ops lead
painPoints: Every tool she finds is either a generic to-do list or a full ERP — nothing scoped to lateral operational work
Skeptical after multiple failed Notion and Airtable setups that required too much manual upkeep
Worried about adding another tool the team will ignore after the first week
Cannot tell from the landing page whether this is just a fancier checklist
opportunities: Lead the homepage with the specific work types (security training, contract renewals, software licensing, budget submissions) not generic task management
CoS Slack communities and ops forums are the primary acquisition channel — be present there, not just on LinkedIn ads
Show a live demo that runs on a real company renewal calendar, not a sanitized toy example

stages.name: Design Partner Onboarding
steps: Gets on a 45-minute call with the Chief AI team to walk through her current tracking setup
Shares her Google Sheet of 35 open lateral items — renewals, compliance deadlines, pending contracts
The team ingests all items, assigns owners, and sets up the first round of AI-drafted nudges for review
Jordan reviews and approves the first 5 nudges before they go out — edits tone on two of them
painPoints: Nervous about an AI sending messages on behalf of the company without her review — especially to external vendors
Two items in the spreadsheet are ambiguous — unclear who the owner is or what done looks like
Onboarding took longer than expected because the spreadsheet had inconsistent date formats and missing owners
opportunities: Default to approve-before-send mode for the first 2 weeks — let Jordan review every draft nudge, which builds trust and teaches the AI her communication style
Surface ambiguous items immediately in onboarding: 'These 4 items have no owner — who should we assign them to?' Fixing this is itself a value moment
Make intake as forgiving as possible — accept messy spreadsheets, inconsistent dates, partial information

stages.name: First Automated Win
steps: Chief AI sends a 30-day warning on an enterprise software contract renewal to the VP of Engineering
VP responds within 48 hours and initiates the procurement process — no nudge from Jordan required
Jordan sees the update on her dashboard: item moved from At Risk to In Progress
She realizes she did not have to do anything for this one — it handled itself
painPoints: Wants a full audit trail — who was notified, when, what they said, and every status change
Wonders why the alert threshold was 30 days — for a contract this size it should have been 60
One nudge went to a person who had already left the company — the contact list needs to stay current
opportunities: Build a complete audit log as a first-class feature — Jordan's accountability depends on being able to show what was sent and when
Make alert thresholds configurable per work type and per dollar value — a $500k contract needs more runway than a $200 SaaS subscription
Add a lightweight team roster or manual contact list to prevent nudges going to departed employees

stages.name: Full Adoption
steps: All lateral work is now in Chief AI — renewals, compliance deadlines, pending contracts, budget submissions
Jordan's weekly ops review is replaced by a 5-minute dashboard scan instead of a 2-hour spreadsheet reconciliation
She uses natural language intake daily: 'Add SOC 2 audit prep, deadline October 1, owner: Head of Security'
CEO asks how the ops review is going — she shows him the live dashboard in under 2 minutes
painPoints: Some employees are ignoring AI nudges after the third reminder — there is no human escalation path built yet
Wants nudges to arrive in Slack, not email — that is where the team actually works
The dashboard does not yet distinguish between a $50k contract and a $5k SaaS renewal — everything looks equally urgent
opportunities: Build the escalation chain as the next must-have: assignee to their manager to Jordan to CEO, with configurable thresholds for when to step up
Slack integration becomes the most-requested feature — build it before the next design partner cohort
Add a dollar value or risk tier field so the dashboard surfaces high-stakes items visually above routine renewals

stages.name: Advocacy
steps: Jordan mentions Chief AI in a CoS Slack community after someone asks how to track software renewals
Three other Chiefs of Staff DM her within 24 hours asking for a referral or demo
She refers them directly to the team — but has no formal way to share her dashboard or a referral link
One of the referred CoS leads at a 300-person company becomes the next design partner
painPoints: No referral mechanism or shareable link — advocacy is happening but the product is not capturing it
She cannot show her dashboard to a prospect without screensharing, which feels awkward
The referral conversation requires her to explain the product from scratch every time
opportunities: Build a read-only shareable dashboard link so Jordan can send a live view to anyone without logging them in
Create a formal referral program — CoS networks are tight and word-of-mouth is the highest-conversion channel for this ICP
Invest in CoS community presence early — one engaged Jordan is worth more than 10 LinkedIn ads

persona.name: Danielle Reyes
persona.role: Chief of Staff at a 200-person Series C company
persona.quote: The CEO thinks everything is running smoothly. That's because I'm the one catching every ball that gets dropped — but I can only catch so many at once.
persona.bio: Danielle is the operational backbone of a fast-growing tech company. She sits at the intersection of every function and is the only person who can see all cross-team dependencies simultaneously. She's deeply trusted by leadership, works 55-hour weeks, and has quietly become a single point of failure. She's been trying to systematize her coordination work for two years but every tool she's tried was built for project managers, not chiefs of staff.
goals: Get every cross-functional commitment tracked and automatically followed up without relying on her memory
Make the operational layer visible to leadership without a weekly status call
Reduce the coordination work that only she currently understands to something a system can hold
Protect high-priority work from falling through the cracks between tools
frustrations: Lateral work — cross-team follow-ups, deadline tracking — has no home in any existing tool
Status dashboards go stale within 48 hours because updates require manual effort from busy people
She finds out things are blocked when it's too late to fix them without an incident
The coordination burden scales with headcount — she doesn't
behaviors: Manually follows up with 5–10 people per week to unblock dependencies
Maintains a personal mental model of every in-flight initiative because no tool does it for her
Sets dozens of calendar reminders as a substitute for real tracking infrastructure
Takes and distributes detailed meeting notes that get acknowledged but rarely acted on
motivations: Making her operational knowledge durable — not trapped in her head
Being able to take a real vacation without the whole coordination layer collapsing
Proving that operational excellence doesn't require a person to be always-on
Building something that survives her — a system, not a dependency

projects.name: Token Intelligence

hypothesis.problem: Design tokens live in three disconnected places — Figma Variables, a design-tokens.json file, and framework configs (Tailwind, Storybook). Any change in one doesn't propagate automatically. Syncs are manual and error-prone, hardcoded values creep back in after every AI-assisted dev sprint, and nobody has visibility into which components are drifting from the token system. The result: the design system is technically maintained but practically ignored by engineers under deadline.
hypothesis.solution: A single Figma plugin with three integrated panels: (1) Token Manager — organize and govern Figma Variables with bulk operations and naming convention enforcement; (2) Token Sync — bidirectional sync between Figma Variables, design-tokens.json, Tailwind config, and Storybook themes; (3) Value Hunter — scans the Figma file for every hardcoded color, spacing value, and typography style and replaces them with the correct token in one pass.
hypothesis.hook: One plugin to manage, sync, and enforce your token system — so your design and code are always speaking the same language, automatically.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Solo designers with no codebase or component library. Teams on Figma Starter (no Variables access). Teams already deeply committed to Tokens Studio who are unwilling to change their export pipeline.

segments.name: Design systems leads and senior frontend engineers at mid-to
segments.description: Design systems leads and senior frontend engineers at mid-to-large product companies (50–500+ engineers) managing a Figma design system alongside a Tailwind/CSS-in-JS/Storybook codebase. They own the token system but spend hours each sprint manually syncing it and hunting down hardcoded values that slipped through.
segments.painPoint: Design tokens live in three disconnected places — Figma Variables, a design-tokens.json file, and framework configs (Tailwind, Storybook). Any change in one doesn't propagate automatically. Syncs are manual and error-prone, hardcoded values creep back in after every AI-assisted dev sprint, and nobody has visibility into which components are drifting from the token system. The result: the design system is technically maintained but practically ignored by engineers under deadline.
segments.resolution: A single Figma plugin with three integrated panels: (1) Token Manager — organize and govern Figma Variables with bulk operations and naming convention enforcement; (2) Token Sync — bidirectional sync between Figma Variables, design-tokens.json, Tailwind config, and Storybook themes; (3) Value Hunter — scans the Figma file for every hardcoded color, spacing value, and typography style and replaces them with the correct token in one pass.

advantage.capability: All three token workflows share the same underlying Figma Variables API and the same token data model — making a unified plugin viable without building three separate products. The sync layer requires a lightweight companion CLI, which is a known pattern (Tokens Studio proved the market exists).
advantage.motivation: Token drift is the single biggest source of design-dev inconsistency. Every hardcoded value that escapes into production is a future refactor. Closing that loop at the source — inside Figma, before handoff — has compounding impact on delivery velocity.
advantage.insight: Tokens Studio and Style Dictionary each solve one part of the pipeline in isolation. The gap no tool closes is the enforcement loop: teams sync once, then drift silently for months. The Value Hunter is the feature that closes this loop — and it is the demo that will sell the entire plugin, because every DS lead who sees it run on their own file immediately sees 40+ violations they didn't know existed.

principles: Enforce > Document (tokens should propagate themselves, not be manually documented)
One source of truth > Multiple independent exports
Catch drift at handoff > Clean up drift in production
Value Hunter first > Full platform later

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Design system leads will adopt a new plugin even if they already use Tokens Studio or Style Dictionary — because the end-to-end enforcement loop (specifically the Value Hunter) is compelling enough to switch or add a tool.
clickTest.testMethod: Live demo the Value Hunter to 5 DS leads — run it on their own Figma file, unannounced, and show it surfacing hardcoded values in under 60 seconds. Measure same-session install rate. Do not pitch the sync features until after the Value Hunter lands.
clickTest.successMetric: 3 of 5 DS leads install the plugin and run the Value Hunter on their own file within 7 days of the demo. At least 1 requests access to the Token Sync beta.

milestones: Phase 1: Value Hunter MVP — scan any Figma file for hardcoded colors, spacing, and typography; surface all violations in a single panel with one-click token replacement. Ship as a standalone public plugin.
Phase 2: Token Manager panel — manage Figma Variables with bulk rename, naming convention linting, and team governance (owner assignment, change log).
Phase 3: Token Sync — bidirectional sync between Figma Variables and design-tokens.json via a companion CLI. One-command push/pull from the terminal.
Phase 4: Framework integrations — Tailwind config sync and Storybook theme sync added as Token Sync output targets.
Phase 5: Figma Community launch — publish to the Figma Plugin Marketplace with a DS-lead-targeted content campaign anchored to the Value Hunter demo.
blockers: Figma Variables API is restricted to Professional plan and above — must validate that the ICP (DS leads at 50+ eng companies) is on Pro or Org tier before building.
Bidirectional sync requires a Node.js companion CLI outside of Figma — adds installation friction. Must test whether DS leads will run a CLI tool or if this kills adoption.
Value Hunter performance at scale: Figma files with 10k+ layers may be slow to scan. Need to profile early and decide if async scanning is required.
blueprint.timelineNotes: Phase 1 (Value Hunter) in 4 weeks — this is the demo-able proof of concept and the market validation tool. Do not build Phase 2 or 3 until Phase 1 has 3 confirmed installs from target ICP. Full platform (all 5 phases) estimated at 18–20 weeks.

projects.name: Omni Repo

hypothesis.problem: No single tool understands the *format* of what you are storing. Everything gets flattened into a document, so a prompt becomes a paragraph, a financial model becomes a wall of text, and a code snippet loses its syntax. Retrieval is slow, re-use is painful, and nothing is structured for how you will actually use it again.
hypothesis.solution: A format-aware central repository with specialized modules for each content type: an AI Prompt Library (tags, folders, one-click copy), a Code Snippet Vault (syntax-highlighted, language-tagged), Financial Spreadsheets (in-app grid), Employee and Vendor Profiles, and a universal search that retrieves by type and tag — not just keyword.
hypothesis.hook: Stop translating your knowledge to fit your tool. Store it in the format it lives in — and retrieve it ready to use.
hypothesis.antiCustomer: Casual personal note-takers who only need free-text journaling (Obsidian, Apple Notes users). Enterprise orgs with existing IT-approved knowledge management platforms they are locked into.

Retrieval is slow, re-use is painful, and nothing is structured for how you will actually use it again.
segments.resolution: A format-aware central repository with specialized modules for each content type: an AI Prompt Library (tags, folders, one-click copy), a Code Snippet Vault (syntax-highlighted, language-tagged), Financial Spreadsheets (in-app grid), Employee and Vendor Profiles, and a universal search that retrieves by type and tag — not just keyword.

advantage.capability: Can be built modularly: each content type is its own renderer (Monaco for code, ProseMirror for rich text, Handsontable for spreadsheets, a prompt schema for AI assets). No single dependency owns the architecture.
advantage.motivation: Context-switching between 6 tools to find one thing is the highest-friction part of modern knowledge work. Solving it means getting hours back per person per week.
advantage.insight: Every competitor (Notion, Coda, Obsidian) treats format as a display concern — they store everything as blocks of text and let the UI dress it up. The insight is that format-awareness at the *data model* level — not just the UI — is what makes retrieval fast and re-use frictionless.

principles: Format-first > Feature-first
Retrieve in one action > Store in ten steps
Structure > Search
Modular depth > Surface breadth

clickTest.riskiestAssumption: Users will maintain a dedicated specialized repo instead of defaulting to Notion or a shared Google Drive, because the format-aware experience is meaningfully faster than searching a generic doc.
clickTest.testMethod: Ship the Prompt Library module as a standalone free tool. Measure if AI practitioners (target: prompt engineers, LLM developers) migrate their prompt collections from Notion/docs within 2 weeks of signing up.
clickTest.successMetric: 40 active users each storing 15+ prompts with tags and folders within 30 days — with a 60% week-2 return rate.

milestones: Module 1: AI Prompt Library — tags, folders, subfolders, one-click copy, search
Module 2: Code Snippet Vault — language detection, syntax highlighting, tag + folder system
Module 3: Financial Spreadsheet storage — in-app grid viewer, import from CSV/XLSX
Module 4: People and Vendor Profiles — structured fields, linked to relevant docs
Module 5: Universal search — cross-module retrieval by tag, type, keyword, and date
blockers: Format breadth creates scope creep risk — need hard module prioritization before build
Multi-user / team sharing model adds auth complexity early — must decide single-user MVP vs. team from day one
Prompt module competes directly with dedicated tools (PromptBase, FlowGPT) — differentiation must be the *integration* with other modules, not the prompt features alone
blueprint.timelineNotes: Phase 1 (weeks 1–6): Prompt Library only — validate core retention assumption. Phase 2 (weeks 7–12): Code Snippet Vault + Universal Search. Phase 3 (weeks 13–20): Spreadsheets and Profiles. Launch Phase 1 publicly before building Phase 2.

sources.title: Founder Vision Input
sources.content: A central repository of notes and information that applies to wide variety of formats: AI Prompts, Code Repos, Financial Spreadsheets, Employee Profiles. Should store most types of data in an appropriate format so it can easily be retrieved and applied. Prompt repo should support tags, folders and sub-folders for easy retrieval and copying.

journey.persona: Marcus, AI Lead at a 40-person growth-stage startup — manages prompt libraries, code snippets, and team documentation across Notion, GitHub, Google Sheets, and Slack
journey.goal: Stop losing 30+ minutes a day hunting for the right prompt, snippet, or reference across six different tools

stages.name: Awareness
steps: Spends 20 minutes hunting for a prompt he wrote last month — finds it buried in a Notion doc
Pastes a code snippet from Slack into VS Code and loses all formatting
Searches Google for "best tool to organize AI prompts and code snippets"
painPoints: No single place stores prompts, code, and financial data in the right format
Generic doc tools flatten everything — prompts lose tags, code loses syntax
Search across tools is keyword-only, returns the wrong format half the time
opportunities: SEO content targeting "AI prompt organizer" and "code snippet + notes manager"
Pain-point-first landing page: lead with the 30-minutes-a-day cost, not the feature list

stages.name: Research & Discovery
steps: Finds Omni Repo via a blog post or Product Hunt listing
Skims the homepage — notices format-aware storage concept
Watches a 90-second demo showing prompt tags, code syntax, and one-click copy
painPoints: Skeptical — has tried Notion, Obsidian, and PromptBase and found them lacking
Unsure if it handles all his formats or just prompts
Doesn't want to migrate everything only to hit a wall with edge-case formats
opportunities: Lead with a live interactive demo (not a video) so he can test his own use case immediately
Show the full module list upfront — Prompts, Code, Spreadsheets, Profiles — to answer the breadth question before he asks

stages.name: Sign Up & First Use
steps: Creates a free account — no credit card required
Lands on the Prompt Library module
Adds his first 5 prompts, tags them by use case, and creates a folder called "Customer Research"
painPoints: Onboarding is blank-canvas anxiety — not sure where to start
Has to manually re-enter prompts already stored elsewhere
Folder/tag structure isn't obvious on first load
opportunities: Offer a one-click import from Notion / CSV on the empty state screen
Show a sample populated library so the structure is immediately clear
Guided first-run: "Add your first prompt → tag it → put it in a folder" in 3 steps

stages.name: Exploration & Habit Formation
steps: Tries the Code Snippet Vault — pastes a Python script, sees syntax highlighting preserved
Uses the one-click copy on a prompt during a real work task
Shares a prompt folder with a teammate via link
painPoints: Not all teammates are onboarded yet — sharing feels one-sided
Wants to link a prompt to the code snippet it was written to generate
No mobile access — uses his phone sometimes when ideas hit
opportunities: Cross-module linking: let a prompt reference a code snippet and vice versa
Frictionless team invite from within a shared folder
Progressive Web App or mobile-optimised view for capture on the go

stages.name: Value Realized
steps: Retrieves and applies a prompt in under 10 seconds for the first time
Team adopts the shared folder for all AI prompts — Notion prompt docs go stale
Exports a snippet set as part of a client deliverable
painPoints: Still switches to Sheets for financial models — not yet fully consolidated
Wants version history on prompts that he iterates frequently
Search still keyword-only — wants semantic / similarity search
opportunities: Version history on prompts is a high-leverage retention feature — build it early
Semantic search ("find prompts similar to this one") as a differentiator over all competitors
Surface a "Time saved this week" metric on the dashboard to reinforce the value habit

Productive in bursts, but the gains erode when retrieval fails
Skeptical a single tool can actually solve format fragmentation without forcing everything into one model

Maintaining a knowledge system takes time that compounds every week it's not done

persona.name: Kai Nakamura
persona.role: AI Product Lead at a B2B SaaS company
persona.quote: I've built probably 400 prompts over the last two years. I can find maybe 30 of them when I actually need them.
persona.bio: Kai builds AI-powered features and spends a significant part of his day working across Notion, GitHub, Sheets, and various LLM interfaces. He's accumulated an enormous knowledge base — prompts, code snippets, evaluation datasets, research notes — spread across too many tools to manage effectively. He rebuilds things constantly because retrieval fails him. He's disciplined about his work but the tools aren't built for what he actually produces.
goals: One place to store prompts, code snippets, datasets, and docs without flattening them into generic notes
Retrieve knowledge in the format it was meant to be used — not as a wall of text to re-parse
Stop losing compound value by rebuilding things he's built before
Build a team knowledge base that survives personnel changes
frustrations: Every tool flattens specialized formats into documents — prompts and code snippets lose their structure
Search is keyword-based, not context-aware or format-aware — retrieval often fails
Maintaining a knowledge system takes time that compounds every week it's neglected
No consistent taxonomy means everything is tagged differently and nothing is findable
behaviors: Saves prompts to Notion but rewrites them from memory because finding them takes longer
Uses file naming conventions as a substitute for proper metadata (e.g. prompt_v3_final_FINAL.md)
Maintains 3–4 parallel 'knowledge bases' across tools for different content types
Copies and pastes code snippets from GitHub Gists, editing them manually each time
motivations: Compound returns on past work — every prompt built once, reused forever
A knowledge system that works for how he actually thinks, not how the tool wants him to think
Getting the last two years of accumulated knowledge into a form that's actually retrievable
Sharing institutional AI knowledge with teammates without losing context in translation

competitors.name: Notion
competitors.description: All-in-one workspace where everything is a block-based document. Widely used for knowledge management but treats all content as text — a code snippet becomes a code block, a financial model becomes a linked database, with no format-native retrieval.
competitors.targetMarket: Teams and individuals who want a flexible, centralized workspace for notes, wikis, project tracking, and lightweight databases
painPoints: No format-awareness — everything is "a block"
Search is keyword-based, not type-aware
Prompts, code, and financial data are second-class citizens

competitors.name: Coda
competitors.description: Document-database hybrid with strong table/formula capabilities. More structured than Notion for data but still document-first — no native prompt or code-snippet types, retrieval is manual.
competitors.targetMarket: Operations and product teams at startups and mid-market companies who need connected documents with database logic
painPoints: Document-first — no native support for code or prompt formats
Steeper learning curve than Notion
No type-aware search or retrieval

competitors.name: Pieces for Developers
competitors.description: AI-powered code snippet manager with context enrichment. Automatically captures code snippets from developer workflow, adds metadata, and enables search by intent. Dev-only — no prompts, financial models, or multi-type support.
features: Auto-capture from IDE, browser, and tools
competitors.targetMarket: Individual software engineers who want a personal code snippet library without manual organization overhead
painPoints: Single format (code) — no multi-type knowledge management
Individual-focused, weak team collaboration
No prompt library or non-code asset types

competitors.name: PromptBase
competitors.description: Marketplace and storage platform for AI prompts. Buy, sell, and store prompts for GPT, Midjourney, and other models. Single-format focused and marketplace-oriented — no code, no financial data, no cross-type search.
competitors.targetMarket: AI hobbyists and creators who want to buy high-quality prompts or monetize their own prompt engineering skills
painPoints: Single format (prompts only)
Consumer/hobbyist positioning — not a professional knowledge management tool
No integration with actual workflows or retrieval across content types

competitors.name: Obsidian
competitors.description: Personal knowledge management with local markdown files, graph view, and a large plugin ecosystem. Beloved by power users but text-only and personal — no format-native rendering, no team collaboration, no structured prompt or code types.
competitors.targetMarket: Individual knowledge workers, researchers, and "second brain" enthusiasts who want full control over their notes locally
painPoints: Personal only — no real team collaboration
Markdown-only — no format-native code or prompt types
Search is text-based, no type-aware retrieval

positioningAxes.yLabel: Collaboration Scope (Individual → Team/Enterprise)

items.label: Centralising cross-tool information
items.description: Knowledge workers who operate across Notion, Slack, Drive, email, and GitHub have no single place that understands all formats natively.

items.label: Finding information across formats
items.description: Searching for a spec that could be in a doc, a Slack thread, a GitHub issue, or a spreadsheet requires checking 4–6 tools manually.

items.label: Keeping stored content current
items.description: Repositories go stale — linked docs get deleted, code snippets become outdated, and there is no freshness signal.

items.label: AI-ready structured storage
items.description: As teams adopt AI assistants, they need information stored with context and structure that LLMs can reason over — current tools were not built for this.

items.label: Tagging and organising content
items.description: Manual tagging in Notion and Obsidian works but is inconsistent without enforcement — a persistent nuisance rather than a blocker.

items.label: Collaboration and sharing
items.description: Sharing specific pages or docs with teammates is handled well by every major tool in the market.

items.label: Version history and rollback
items.description: Notion and Coda provide version history; while imperfect, this is an adequately solved problem for most teams.

items.label: Basic note-taking
items.description: Simple text notes are the most over-solved problem in productivity software — not a differentiating opportunity.
